- - - - A WISH. ask not that my bed of death From bands of greedy heirs be free: For these besiege the latest breath Of fortune's favoured sons, not me. - I aek not each kind soul te keep Tearless when of my death he hears. • Let those who will, if any, weep! There are worse plagues on earth than tears. I ask but that my death may find The freedom to my life denied; : Ask but the folly of mankind Then—then at last to quit my side. 's Spare me the whispering, crowded room, The friends who come, and gape, and go; The ceremonious air of gloom— All which makes death a hideous glow. /for bring to see me cease to live Some doctor full of phrase and fame To shake his sapient head and give The ill he cannot cure a name. Nor fetch to take the accustom'd toll Of the poor sinner bound for death His brother-doctor of the soul To canvas with official breath The future and its viewless things— That undiscover'd mystery Which one who feels death's winnowing wings Must needs read clearer, sure, than he! Bring none of these; but let me be While all around in silence lies, Moved to the window near, and see Once more before my dying eyes, ' Bathed in the sacred dues of morn The wild aerial landscapes spread— The world which was e'er I was born The world which lasts when I am dead. Which never was the friend of one, Nor promised love it could not give, But lit for all its generous sun And lived itself and made us live. Then let me gaze—till I bedome• In soul, with what I gaze on, wed! To feel the universe my home; To have before my mind—instead . Of the sick room, the mortal strife, The turmoil for a little breath— The pure eternal course of life, Not human combatings with death! Thus feeling, gazing. let me grow " Compos'd, refresh'd, ennobled, clear— Then willing let my spirit go To work or wait, elsewhere or here! —Matthew Arnold.

Arrogance is ever accompanied by folly.—Plato. Be guarded in discourse—attentive and slow to speak. No one has a right to mercy who cannot himself show mercy. When the grocer retires from business he weighs less than he did before. It is said that no one can arrest the flight of Time, but who is there who is not able to stop a minute? A HAPPY STATE.—" Social happiness," says Lord Houghton, "consists in being asked everywhere and going nowhere." How TO NAVE AN EASY MlND.—Leave to everyone the care of her own affairs, and disturb not thyself with what is said or done in the world.—Sir Thomas Aquinas. "The single scull race," exclaimed an excited old lady, as she laid down the paper. "My gracious! I didn't know there was a race of men with double skulls." A good temper and an obliging disposition, when com- bined with honesty and industry, are invaluable qualities to everyone who has her way to make in the world. "That's it," exelaimed Mrs. Bascom at the concert, as the singers came out again in response to an encore. "Make 'em do it over again until they get the thing right." Miss Dearleigh (on the tennis ground) : "Won't you join us, Mr. Whiteband ?" Rev. Mr. Whiteband : "I'm sorry to say I haven't the marriage service with me, Miss Dearleigb." You may subdue an angry man by hearing with him but not by answering him; that is as if the steel should try to make the flint leave off giving sparks by striking it again. "I am surprised, John." said an old lady when she found the Irish butler helping himself to some of the finest old port. "Faith. so am I, ma'am. I thought you had gone out," was the reply.

MATRIMONY. "Does marriage change a man?" you ask— His tone and look were sad— " The first week of our wedding tour Took all the change r had." A profound scientist says that nobody need be afraid of a male wasp. This is encouraging. When a gentle- man is stung by a wasp after this, he will know at once that it Is a female wasp, and he can treat it with the courtesy and respect due to the sex. A Scotch clergyman was one day catechising his flock in the church. The bedral, or church-officer, being ' somewhat ill-read in the Catechism, thought it best to keep a modest plaee near the door, in the hope of escap- ing the inquisition. But the clergyman observed and called him forward. "John," said he," what is baptism ?" " Ou, sir," answered John. scratching his head, "ye ken, it's just saxpence to me, and lifteenpence to the precen- tor." A little boy, whose grandfather began life as an errand boy and finished as a millionaire, was wild by his mother a penny a dozen for pins picked RD from the carpet to keep the baby from getting them. "Nurse," said he, as his stock of pennies increased, "Do you know what I am going to do when I have sixpence?" "no." answered the nurse. "I am going to buy a paper of pins, and scatter them all over the floor, and then pick them up," replied the young financier, who was barely six years old. . .

Tug FUNNY MAN FROPOSFS.—He proposed as seriously as a humorous man could—and she laughed. He looked" blue. Then she smiled, and said. "That is a capital joke." "What's a joke ?" he asked, in surprise. "Your latest. Shall you have it printed ?" "That was no joke. I meant it." "You did ? Why, you have written so mach in ridicule of love, courtship, and marriage—" "Well, er-er-yes—but—" "I should never suit you. I write postcripts„ Stop before the mirror, am slow in dressing for church, admire a new hat. sometimes want a new dress, and—" "But, my dear Angelina, I should never object—" "You have shown that happiness ends with marriage, and I have a mother who would be a mother-in-law to you, and who would want to visit me; and—" "Why, I—" "And I may have my animosities, and may look around in church; and you would find such a lot of things to write about." "My precious, I would only write about other people then; the neighbours, the—" "Those horrid Miss Sniffletons?" "For a fact." "And the stuck-up folks over the way ?" "Most cer- tainly." "Enough! lam yours." A CUNNING Fox.—An Oxfordshire farmer one day going his rounds espied a large fox carrying off one of the finest of his geese; he had no dog with him, but he gave chase, hoping that if he could not save the crea- ture's life he might, perhaps, save its carcase, preferring a dead goose to none at all. Ileynard managed to out- strip the speed of the farmer, who placed all his hopes on a wall built of loose stones which happened to come in the line of the fox's retreat, for he judged that the thief could not leap the wall, encumbered as he was with the stolen goose; accordingly, when the wall was reached several unsuccessful attempts were made to leap over, but every time•down came fox and goose on the wrong side of the wall. "Now," said the farmer, "I've got him !" but just, as the wall was reached the wily brute, raisin, himself on his hind legs as high as possible, thrust the bird's beak between two stones as high as he could reach, then sprang to the top of the wall at one bound, stooped down, seized his prep by its neck, lifted it easily over the wall, and the farmer, thus " done " out of his prize, when he looked over the wall, could see nothing but his neighbour's turnips. ARAB TREACHERY IN East. APRICA.—There yet . .

another method of securing many slaves and mach ivory, an instance of which came under my notice some years ago. At the south end of Tanganyika I met the great Arab Kabunda, who had for eight or ten years been established in the valley of the Lofu. His village, some five or six miles from the Lake, was a pi:Aure of peace and fertility. A stream had been turned from its course to irrigate the gardens so that even when the surrounding plains were parched and yellow, this formed a little oasis in the desert; groves of bananas afforded a friendly shade, while fields of rice, maize, millet, and sweet potatoes gave pleasing promise of plenty to the hungry traveller. And not only in the Arab camp did prosperity reign, but the whole- valley was dotted with tranquil and smiling villages. True, even then I had passed over a track of ninety miles of desolation, finding • only blackened stockades and bleaching bones. where Livingstone and other Europeans had received kindly hospitality from friendly natives.. The Arab, while •ostensibly maintaining the most cordial relations with the people of the valley, had sent out his men to collect .slaves and ivory from the surrounding tribes. At last, 'having secured what he considered a sufficient supply of ivory, and wishing to transport it to Zanzibar, Ka- bunda suddenly threw aside his mask of friendship, and with or without pretence of quarrel, surrounded the villages and seized as slaves the whole population of men, women, and children. The man who was guilty of this dark deed of cruelty and treachery was no untutored savage, hut a dignified and cultured Arab. full of courtesy in his dealings with Europeans. Although his ,Caravan numbered three thousand, including. four hun- dred wild warriors to protect his goods an I procure supplies, we being only fifteen, on our visiting him, he I -erected a booth for our receptions and hospitably enter- ' tamed us with the best food at his command.—Murray's Jragazine. WHO PAYS RATES? (By "ECONOMIST.") To a candidate who is soliciting the bond* of election to the Town Council there is nothing so absurdly easy to answer as the question which ks placed at the top of this article. The question has been put and answered several times on platforms in Warrington within the last two or three weeks. It is true the answers vary somewhat. "A candidate, importunate for votes, cannot always say exactly the same thing in a matter of this kind. Your jndicious caedidate when he gets amongst the horny-handed workingmen demonstrates most clearly that it is the people -who live in houses that pay the rates, and that, of course, a lessening of the rates keeps money in their pockets. On the other hand; when he is amongst property owners, and particularly cottage property owners—for " Down with the rates" is the grand formula and battle cry of your cottage property owner—le has little difficulty in showing thatit is they who have to bear the full burden of all local imposts. These t may be said to be the electioneering answees to the t question," Who Days rates ?" On the other side we have what may, perhaps, be properly called the scientific answer—the answer deduced from a con- sideration of economic principles or laws—which is this: That in the end all rates are a deduction from ground rents—from the value of the land upon which houses and other buildings are erected. It may, I think, be safely asserted that the income of working people, and,, indeed, of all people who live in houses for which they pay reiat, is never affected permanently, and, as a rule,not'even temporarily, by the increase or decrease of rates. When the rates are increased rent-payers are, so far as their income and expenditure are concerned, no worse off, and when the rates are decreased they are no better off. In the second place, I assert that rates rarely ever have the effect of preventing property owners from securing a fair profit upon the money invested in their property. And, in the third place, it is easily capable of proof that in very many cases rates are really paid out of an additional value which has been conferred upon building sites, not by the owners of the buildings themselves, but by the inhabit- ants of the town as a whole. "A POOR OpPRESsRD RATEpAYER Two or three week ago a gentleman who was a can- didate for one of the wards in Warrington gave, as an instance of the oppressiveness of the rates to property owners, a case which it Would be instructive to consider for a moment or two. A friend of his owned a piece of property—a shop I believe—for which fifteen or twenty years ago he paid rates on an aseessment of £2O. During the last fifteen or twenty years, however, not only had the rates increased but the assessment had gradually risen to £6O, so that the property owner had now to pay not merely twenty times ss. 6d. or ss. Bd. but sixty times that amount for the same property. Surely, it was argued, nobody could want a more flagrant example of the evil of high rates than this? What with increasing rates on one. hand and rising assessments on the other, was not this poor oppressed ratepayer having his property pared away on both sides till, like King Lear's wits, there was nothing left in the middle? Yet, iet useonsider how he really stood at the end of the twenty years as compared with the beginning. In the first place it is not quite accurate to say that rates are higher to-day in Warring- ton than they were twenty years ago; if they have not fallen they have not risen. Then as to the assessment. The assessment of this kind of proper y is always, I believe, regulated by its letting value, that is to say by the rent which the owner can get for it. The rise in the assessment, therefore, is a clear and incontestable indica- tion that this piece of property is now of three times the annual value it was fifteen or twenty years ago. This added value is not in the building itself—in the bricks ' and mortar, whichof course deteriorate as time goes on— but entirely in the site of the building. Now if we ask ourselves what it is that has given this additional value to the site the answer unmistakably is that it has been given by the growth of Warrington as a town—by the eitensien of its trade and manufactures and the in- crease of its population. In other word...this particular owner's property has been trebled in value by no exer- tion of his own, for if he had slept or lived on the other side of the globe during the last twenty years the result would have been the same. Yet because the commun- ity takes back in the shape of rates about a fourth part of the value it has added, to be used for improving the condition of the town, this is cited as an instance of tho hardships and injustices poor property owners suffer from high rates. Everyone knows that in Warrington, and in all growing towns, cases of this kind are innumer- able, and yet when there is a demand for a fow more pence in the pound out of this "unearned increment" for the purpose of improving the general health, promot- ing education, building baths, acquiring recreation grounds, or freeing libraries, there is an outcry as though it were a pronos-al for the sheer filching of hardly wrought for money. RATES FALL ON GROUND TALLIES. It maybe said that every property owner is not in the fortunate position of the one mentioned above-that every man who owns property in Warrington has not held it for twenty years, and is not enjoying the unearned incre- ment that has accrued in that time. What about the man, it may be asked, who has invested his hard-earned savings in a few houses within the last two or three months or years and yet still has to pay the same heavy rates? Let us take a typical ease and it will be seen that here also rates are a deduction from ground values and not from the fair profits of property owners. A man, we will suppose, has £l,OOO which he is seeking to invest. He knows that by putting it out on Govern- ment or Corporation securities, in railway, bank,or other , shares he may reasonably anticipate a certain yearly interest upon it. but instead of using it for any of these purposes he decides to build houses with it. He knows pretty accurately beforehand what the rates of the town are, what the building of the houses will cost, what expenses the laying out of the street will entail, and the . various other items of expenditure, and on the other side he knowe to a few pence what rent ho will obtain for the kind of buildings lie intends to erect. It is, therefore, a matter of easy computation to ascertain the price he can afford to pay for bis building sites if he is to have a profit on his money not less than he might secure in other investments. Being, like other men, guided by his own interests, this is the price he pays and no more. Now, it is interesting to inquire what would be the reeldt if the rates were lower or the streets made in. a.lexs substantial and ex- pensive way. Would the man who builds houses get the benefit of these reductions? It is easy to see-that he would not. The only difference would be that he I would find himself able to pay a higher price for build- ing sites, and it is as certain as that human nature is at it is, that the ground landlord would equalise matters by demanding that higher price. Here, too, then; it is seen that rates are in the end deducted from ground values, and not from the reasonable profits of owners of house property. It may, perhaps, be objected that ac- cording to this showing the burden and injustice of high rates is simply shifted from one back to another. It must, however, be remembered that ground land- lords owe vastly morn to the community that the com- munity is ever likely to take back in rates. The ground on which Warrington stands if it were not for the fact that it is covered by a growing industrial population, would at most carry the value of ordinary agricultural land, whereas at the present time it is many times that value and is constantly and rapidly getting more valuable. What is taken back in the shape of rates from ground landlords is a mere fleabite when compared with the vast sums that have been and are being put into be pockets of this fortunate class of men by the growth and prosperity of the town. RENTS NOT DEPENDENT ON RATES. Nothing is so often asserted at election times as that all rates, no matter how levied, in the end fall upon work- ing people. If this merely means that all wealth is the outcome of labour of working people the statement is accurate enough, but if it means that a rise of rates causes an increase ot rent and a fall of rates a decrease of rest it is an assertion that is utterly unsupported by facts. The rents of houses and shops do not depend upon the highness or lowness of the rates but upon the demand in relation to the supply. What is it that makes the rent of a shop so much higher at Market Gate than at the extremity of the borough? It is rut the iaequality of the rating, for rates are uniform all over Warrington, but. simply because there is a greater demand for shops in the one place than in the other. And so with regard to cottage property. A working man does not pay more rent for a house near the centre of the town than for an equally good one near the borough boundary because the rating of the town is not uniform, but because there is a greater inquiry after the more convenient houses. Within the last few weeks in some parts of the town thatl know of, the weekly rents of cottages have been raised, and what is the reason given? Is it that the rates are higher than they were? Oh, no, it is simply that there is a greater demand for houses through the influx of people engagedon the Slip Canal. And yet in the very face of tins we have it asserted that high rates are the cause of high rents. 'The fact is that were all the rates abolished to-day the rent-payers of Warrington would not benefit by a single penny. The demand for houses continuing, rents would remain exactly as they are, and if that demand continued to grow rents would rise in spite of the non-existence of rates. The whole benefit of the abolition of rates would be enjoyed by that small and, as a rule, very comfortably provided for class who own the ground plots of Warrington. HIGH HAIRS VERSES LOw RATES. So far from high rates being a discredit to a town they are—always assuming, of course, that they are well spent—one of its chief glories, denoting as they do the public spirit and enlightened views of those who have been entrusted with its government. Other things equal, a town with low rates is a town in which small and selfish class interests prevail, in which all works of public utility are tabooed or carried out on the smallest possible scale, for the sole purpose, and certainly with the sole effect, of augtunenting those "unearned incre- ments" on land which in the, eyes of nearly all right- thinking people are one of the greatest of our social evils. On the other hand it is, generally speaking, a fair infer- ence that where rates are high the interests of the com- munity as a whole have prevailed over that of the small and clamorous section who hold a monopoly of the ground upon which their fellow townsmen live and have their being.
BOBBY,
small I
A LANCASHIRE DICKSHONARY. PUT TOGETHER BI "TUM 0' DICK'S 0' BOB'S." :" Th' Payson," so often alluded to, is compiling the Dictionary, while" Turn" makes the running comment.]
PART I.

APOTR (halfpennyworth). Aw think everybody'll under- stond wod a apoth is when aw mention as ther's 2 apoths in a pennoth ; we used to ha' lota o' gam, when aw wer' a lad, sendin' littler lads into shops for a apoth o' strap oil or a apoth o' pigeon milk.
Ax (ask). Th' payson's just abeawt bit th' nail o' tli'

head wi' th' meeanin' o' this word. AXINS (banns). Aw con remember, as iv id wor but yesterday, wen aw put th' axins up, an'aw remember, too, as me an' th' lass as wer' mixt up l' th' job topt away fro' th' church for three Sunday's just abeawt thad time.
A BOON (above; Heaven). Id will be a boon when some

on us geds up aboon. ADDLE (earn). lieaw, one's varra likely to ged wrang wi' this word iv they're nod keerful, because a mon's heead may be addled, an' his wage may be addled. Th' fost o' these fits th' payson an' th' last doesn't— mony a time. - APPEN (perhaps). Th' payson's reet ageon. ALICKBR (vinegar). Th' best shop i' Lancashire for alicker is a jerryshop aside o' wheer aw live; but yo' hern'd to ax for id by name. Yb' simply sit deawn an' co for a gill o' ale fresh drawn! AGATES Th' payson hed to gi' this up as a bad egg; he wee no better off when aw towd him iv he wee to tek a lass agate when hoo wer' gooin' hooom, an' he coom to a gate, id wod be for him to ged agate o' oppenin' thad gate. Arriancxop (spider). When aw see ony o' these things, or a cobweb, in a heawse aw'm nooan so sure as th' chap's wife as lives theer is as cleyn as boo shod be. Th' payson see as one o' th' kings o' Scotland, when i' prison, wer' wonst watchin' a atercrop as wer' th' same cell, an' throo mein' id fo back an' ged up wi mony times he med up his mind as he'd keep peggin' away at summat as he wanted to do. Aw think th' payson sed as he dud do it, bud aw've a poor opinion of a. chap, king or beggar, as corn'd do owt beawt

hevin' to watch a atteWrop. Buzz (story). Lancashire fooak know wod 'a good buzz is. Neaw aw know a regler stunner abeawt th' payson but he wants me to keep id to missel as he's freetud o' fooak laffin at him, sooa avell oblige him.. BAGGIN (evening meal, tea, or supper). A werkin chap's baggin' is the best meal as he hes, an' even thad gi's him neetmare. An' there's baggin a chap at his werk —thad gi's him neetmare too. Th' payson ses this word 'appen comes fro' a custom as th' Sultan o' Torkey hes o' puttin' .his owder wives i' bags an' chuckin"em th' Bosphorus. Thad boss for vs wodn'd

do. BRASS (money). Aw wish aw .knew as mich abeawt this as th' payson does—ay, aw do sooa! BRAT (apron, child). Booath o' these is teed to lasses, an' mony a time a lot to soon—i' booath eases. BBRRTIN (funeral). Aw've heerd id sed as factry fooalt only geds three good sprees in a lifetime, an' them's ayther at a kessenin', a weddin% or a berryin', an' th' goodest spree is at a berryin'. Id seems a queer thing as id shud be soos, bud, then, th' world's full o' nowt else bud queer things. BnossErr (bursting, fat). As brossen as a pig's a common sayin' Lancashiro, an' it's olez sed abeawt chaps wi' a good corporashun for showin' a wat'At aeon off. 13.smir (baby). This is a wonderful thing, an' heaw mich wonderful depends on id number. Iv id's th' lost id's a hangel ; yo' mertzer id an' weigh id every Betterda' neet, an' book id deawn in a family Bible. An' when id ses " Daddy" an' "Mammy "—wev, yo' wad ad tek th' Nashnal Det for id. Bud iv Ws th'

duzzenth, it's a little imp, an' id geds plenty o' strap; aw know o abeawt id, becos aw've bed 'em—at leeast th' wife has, an' id's o th' same. Boaoairr (ghost). Th' owd style o' hogg,rart's gooan eawt o' date lung sin', them 'at used to be drest white; boggarts as we hey neaw-a-days dress i' black, an' come reawnd a-collectin' brass for th' Deoth list, an' things o' thad sooart. Bilawr (without). fleet, payson. Burry (slice of bread and butter). Childer knows nowt) abeawt butties i' these days ; neaw its a slice o' nice bread wi traycle on id, or else Irish butther at a shillin' a peawnd, bud when aw wer' a lad id wer' a bit o' clap cake dipt P wayter, an' then sprinkled o'er wi' %wt. They wer' co'd sawt-cats then. Buttocx (an animal). Goo' lad thee, payson! Bud tha'rt a little bit eawt on't, for bullockin' a chap meeans berm' him on. Yo' sliud ne'er bullock a chap bigger nor yo'rsel'; th' best way is to ax him, afroa! ova lots' fooak, iv he wer' born i' th' Werkheawse, iv his brother's come eawt o' Preston stooan jug for ateylin' ; iv his sister still lives wi' thad tackler ; an' iv he's bed th' Bumbaileys in latly. Yo'll see heaw he'll laff. BOBBY (policeman). Different fonak bee diff'rent ideeas as to wod a bobby's shop is. Some thinks as he's nowt else to do bud wear them nice clooas an' white gloves, an' get rapput pie fro' servant lasses, for his twenty-six bob a week; aw've sin 'em th' Perk at times dooin' a bit o' cooartin', an' aw've sin 'em geddin' ther heeads weel punsht Norgate. sooa yo' con sooart id eawt for yo'rsels. Ile's welkum to his wage for me, an' as for cooartin'—well, it's a bobby's werk is gooia' to cooart. BBLTINKHR Nayther me nor th' payson con tell adzackly wod th' better end wod ha' to write for this word, bud id meeans a good leatherin' so which on 'em geds hi. BRAWN (bound). " Wheer arta beawn " meeans wheer arta gooin', as everybody knows. BOCK (an animal). Bong ageeau, payson, tho' tha's med a good hit beawt knowin' id, for id is a game; th' way to play id an' th' tackle wanted is as follows : A lad wi' a pickin'-stick an' a buck, an' a chap wi' a window—bigger an' better. Th' lad rises his buck, an' knocks id thro' th' chap's window; th' lad runs away, an' th' chap runs after him. Th' game is catchin' th' lad, an' geddin' to know his name, an' wheer he lives. Iv th' chap doesn'd do this he's lost— th' price o' th' window puttin' in. BLEvrivane, Barms' (crying). When a child's bellin' an' rooarin' some fooak ax id wod id's bletherin' at. BRADE ( ?). This is another word as puzzles th' payson. when anybody ses " brade o' me," or" brade as aw do," they meean yo' to do as they do; that's simple enuff. OBBY-DAEZUBB (a grand one). A lass is a bobby- dazzler when boo's getten a new frock on, but some o' th' other lasses doesn'd say sooa ; bud thad's becos ther mad they limend getten a new 'un on. BaBET (bright). Aw've nowt to say here, only as it doesn' meean owd John Bright, thad gradely Grand Ocvd Mon. • BRITEITES ( ). Th' payson sea nowt heer, an' awill follow his eggsarnple, for it's a queer subject to touch on. Onyway, we're nooan gooin' to let the wimmen wear em', an' thad's streyt.

DACCA (LODBCCO). Wodeve; wad a werkin mon do beawt hie pipe o' bacca ov a neet ! He may ha' bin geddin a good cossin' fro' th' cutlooker, or bin' baited a quarter ov his day's wage, or summat else to upset him, but ther's nowt 'II do him as mich good as a smook. BATED ( ). Payson knows nowt abeawt this, becos he never werkt at th' factry. Iv he'll be any wiser aw may tell him as when a boss is baited id geds summat gi'n id, but when a weyver geds bated he geds summat tekken off him. (To be kontinid.)

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, NOVEM4BER 17, 1888.
• • At oft

A MUNIQIPAL CITATY Ko-Ko. gg, Oh! come and see the Mayor; with his chain of it oia • Come and see the wise men, wise men young and old; Just you twig the Aldermen; see ho' i cute they look; Each might be a "hail," a marquis, or a "dock.!' The Mayo2,4.l4erlnen, and Conncillors of the Borough of Wthinkton. I give yon greeting. shake! You are jolly boys, and I want to have a chat with you. You may muddle things up some-, • timet, and some of you are a bit restive. Rather inclined to pull hard at the traces, some of you young Councillors are, and you forget that it , doesn't do to hurry the old ones. But altenicether you are not half a bad lot, and somehow I kind of cotton to you. I'm not half a bad sort myself, yeti know. If you'll only persevere, you may make something out in time; and just to help you, a bit / I'm going to 'Criticise, so to speak; to have a joust with. you, and put questions, and make remarks, and carry on generally. ,I went to your meeting the other Friday, and was much impressed. Your Worship's robe, and the chain of gold eo poetically , referred to above, have a crushing effect on the unsophisticated, and when your Worship gracefully. ambled to the Mayoral chair I was fain to. exclaim, " What manner of man is that ?" Very imposing, , indeed, bill not held in much awe by some of those ; young cubs around you, sir. Were lin your place, I'd discard the horsecloth, put away the bauble; and—hang custom! Stand on your merits, and putl ; not your confidence in fal-lals. The Big Chiefs also were in full bloom, and it was a great palaver. It , was an imposing function, as a newspaper man ineight say, and I shall never forget it. Even School Attendance George graced the proceedings with his presence, and, really, I thought he never Went to anything under a concert. But this is by the way— the canter preliminary to the race. " Mais revenons A nos moutons." 1 After all, it seems that it is an easy matter to elect a Mayor—when the business has been cut and dried in advance. That part of your proceedings does not require much comment. But how did you like the flattery, Mr. Mayor; those honeyed words of praise so precious to the ear? And why did one of the flatterers give you a back-handed slap by hinting that you held too slack a rein to drive this ponderous corporate coach? It seemed rather a hard rub, but if you don't mind I don't. Anyway, you had a good slap back when you told them all to stick to their copy-books, and avoid all that acrimony and personal recrimination in which we are sometimasapt to indulge." That is good advice, and all you members of the Council will do well to take it to heart—put it in your bosoms 'and hug it. You can't deny that some of your deliberations during the past ' twelve months have been attended with so much "acrimony and personal recrimination" as to make sensible people ashamed of' you, while others have laughed in your faces. Don't take offence; it's true and you can't get out of it. The publie are your masters; mind that nosy sand they expect of you that you should uphold the honotir and dignity Of What you are pleased to call this " good old town." I know you can't agree in everything. We all know it. Discuss as much as you like. Fight as much as you like. It is by discuss- ing and by fighting that abuses are reformed and the way is made clear for progress. nut, for Heaven's sake, gentlemen, be gentlemen. "Acrimony and personal recrimination,' these are not my words • they are those of the chief among you. I should have been inclined to I put them a little stronger, and a little more forcibly. But when you come to think them over—turn them round in your heads, they seem quite strong enough. They are true, and it is in their truth that their strength lies. .No, gentlemen, "acrimony and personal recrimin- ation," and pettishness, and pique, and the like, are not for such as you. ' A word in the aldermanic ear. Your woeks do you honour, and your age commands respect. Individually and collectively you have done good service, and doubt= less you will do good service again, but let me pray you beware of putting on "too much side." It is fitting that you should fancy yourselves somewhat. It is tight that you should hold up your heads and fcel proud. Still you are but mortal, and there are others treading this beautiful earth of ours as well as you. Be proud, but not conceited. Be just, but also be generous. You have reached a pinnacle, and it's nice to turn up your aldermanic noses at those below. But don't do it, let 1110 beg of you. It ie rather annoying to have those younger ones poking into everything, and wanting to know this, that, and the other. But you yourselves were coun- cillors once, and I'll he bound you wanted to be in the " know " in those days. Treat them with Courtesy always, and they will reciprocate. Set the example, and they will follow. "Little children lore one another." Be manly and frank; fair and open, and do unto others as you would have tha. they should do unto you. This is good advice for you all, gentlemen of the Corporation, and if you follow it out the next Mayor will not have to undergo the humility of asking you to avoid ‘1 acrimony and personal recrimination." But lam losing sight of the meeting. Well, it was a kind of an ordinary sort of meeting as things go, but .ft I was a deplorable beginning. Just after that good advice of your Mayor, you straightway went and did the thing he warned you against. Alas! that it should be so, but this human nature of ours is sonsetimes a perverse thing. Temper will out, it seems, say what yeti will. It would be wearying to travel over that storm-in-the-teapot debate, if it can be jestly termed a debate. Personal's', I don't care a rap whether Councillor Bolton is on the Watch Committee or not, but, as a principle seems to be involved, it cannot be denied that any member had a right to raise adi icussion on the point. But it really should have been possible to conduct it decorously, and with an entire absence of that aforesaid "acrimony and per- sonal recrimination," which soon came out in full 'rigour, and blossomed exceedingly. This sort of procedure ' might do for Philippi, the place of note that I mentioned the other week,but I almost think that even at Philippi it could be no worse. [By the way,most genial of hosts,how fares the bottle of chain." that rumour has it awaits the onslaught of Ko-Ko?] Councillor Monks, to his Credit be it said, certainly started off fair, and was tem- perate enough. Councillor Flood, who then made a "splash" with his maiden speech, might have been more careful of the toes of Councillor Bolton, and that gentle- se,an need not have been so very peppery, and so ready to Interrupt other people's remarks. It is rude to ' keep interrupting, and, as Councillor Jolley would put it, a gentleman who has a taste for horticulture ought to be incapable of rudeness. He might have right en his side, ,or he might not. lam not judging that question. I simply speak of the manner of the discussion, and wish to express no particular opinion on the merits of the question under diqute. The height ef absurdity, let me,,' however, remark, in this flash-in-the-pan discussion, was reached when Councillor Jolley took the door. He posed as a man with a grievance, and was prepared to defend the Council from insult. Yes, that is so. "I feel I have received a very serious insult, for some people outside have tried to use their influence on the members of the / Council." Poor Council! Poor thin-skinned Mr. Jolley ! What are you kicking at? Where do you find the insult? I The alleged insult was contained on a post-card which trusted that "a gentleman who is a brewer and the I owner of several licensed houses" would not be put upon the Watch Committee. I repeat, where is the insult? It is invisible to the eyes of most Councillor Jolley, as one of those who were " there to legislate for all sorts and conditions of men," to use his own words. judged the sending round of that post-card as "not the correct thing," and as an "improper thing." Bosh! Are not the members of the Warrington Temperance Federa- tion a part of" the allsorts and conditions of men " that send you to the Council to legislate for them P Certainly they are, but, if they will do the sending, you can do the legislating. Is that the "correct thing ?" Do you mean to say that the Federation, or any other com- bination of the burgesses, for whatever purpose formed, have no right, as a part of the constituency that make such persons as councillors, to express their opinion in any way they choose on a public question? Do those that are greater in die land than you. those who sit in the highest legislative House in the kingdom. feel insulted when petitions and memorials pour in by the ton from " all sorts and conditions of men." Bah ! Not a bit of it. This is a serious question, Mr. Councillor Jolley, and one that affects the public that you may affect to ignore. But the puplic will not be ignored. If I mistake not, the public will think your remarks on this matter something of" an insult." They think that as they send men to legislate for them they have a right to express some opinion,either individually or as a body, as to what their representatives should do. If they do it respectfully, and honourably, can you withhold from them that right ? You dare not do it, and the Council, did it so desire, dare net dolt. This apathetic public, this sleepy multitude, is a very lion when aroused. If you goad it too much, it will shake off its sloth, and take very good care that its rights are respected. Don't take offence. You have simply made a little mistake. I respect you very much. I respect all you gentlemen of the Council very much, but I respect the public more, and feel called upon, in a manner, to speak. The discussion after this point was pretty much of a muchness. Councillor W. Pierpoint expressed his love for the member whose misfortune it is to be a lerewer, and then had a sly whack aS him. Councillor Bolton, in re'ort, did not call him a liar, but said something that pointed suspiciously in that direction: there was a little cross-firing with the Mayor, and then Councillor W. Pierpoint sat down in protest. Councillor H. Roberts, as is his wont, next raised up- his voice, and remarked some sensible remarks, but this demon of personality was 'by this time rampant all over the place. and 'seized him also, although he did not "get it" so strong as some of them % A vote followed, and soon afterwards the school was closed, and the boys went home. Ko-Ko went too, a sadder, if not a wiser man. Just another word or two, and I have done. lam getting strong on municipal matters just now, so on Sunday I went to see the Mayor and the rest of them " procestt" to the Parish Church. This may be a One- honoured custom, but I can't gee much good in it. Of course it gets them to church, but as a procession it is usually a failure. .If they could'briug in the vans, and horses, and watering carts, and road-roller, and the scavengers, it would lengthen the affair out a bit, and add weight, as it were, to the proceedings, though the eclat of the thing would not have much of a look in.

But who cares about the eclat? The Mayor could sit on a watering cart, and chairs could be placed on the vans for the aldermen. See,how convenalft 010 uld be. I should like to have found a seat for Mr. Hunt, but, if he cOtildn't manag,6to steer the road-roller, I am afraid he would have to perambulate. On second thowhts, however, I would allow Alderman Burgess to ride his bobby, and allot to the worthy chief a front seat on the van. On .third thoughts, perhaps it would be better to let things remain as they are, for the mirth that my little arrangement would cause would be sennewhab detrimental to those sober thoughts that we are all sup.; posed to entertain on the Sabbath, and would scarcely be a fitting prelude to the service of the church. Adieu 1 Six and thirty Council men, all marching in a line, Constables and Fire Brigade in uniforms so flue, And when they got to church, the parson told them straight, The Council carried influence, and dignity, and weight. (And then they all felt happy, and puffed out their chests While self-congratulation did fill their manly breasts.) But he might have also told them—he might have told them all, , .They cannot be too careful—Pride goes before a fall:

div.head: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLUB.

A general meeting of the members of this club, to which all persons interested in agriculture were invited, was held at the Farmers' Stores,Warringt on, on Wednesday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. George percival, the president of the club, and there was a good attendance. TIM DISASTROUS HARVEST." •

- The Secretary alfr. Stelfos) proprsed that a resolution be passed and Forwarded to the landowners whose estates lie within the district embraced by the Warrington Farmers' Club, calling attention to the disastrous results of this year's harvest, and to the bad times through which farmers generally had been passing for the last ten years; and, further, calling attention to the fact that a considerable number of landowners had already generously conceded either a permanent reduction or an abatement of rentals, and respectfully requesting them to take these circumstances into favourable con- sideration, with the object of doing something to relieve the over-burdened tenantry.—The proposition was seconded by Mr. John Marsh (Grappeahall) and carried unanimously.

THE COUNTY COUNCILS. The meeting then proceeded 10 " cOnsider the selection of suitable candidates to represent the interests of Owners of Land, Tenant Farmers and Farm Labeurers in the County Council at Chester and in the Local Divisions."—The Secretary introduced the subject by reading a comMunication from Mr. Thomas. Baxter (Chester) who wrote that it was very important that farmers should sea that they were represented on the county boards. If nit, they would lose all control over expenditure, as those boards would have more control than had been exercised by one class alone at the Quar- ter Sessiens. For instance, all rpads over which tipey now had control; and many other things would 'go from them under the new management if they did not see to it and bestir themselves. He was offering himself for Frodsham district, and hoped, if he got on the Council, to meet many more direct representatives of the ratepayers.—The Chairman said that, for their own safety, it was well that they should discuss this question in time. It was to the interest of farmers to send suit- able representatives to the County Councils, and lie knew from experience that there were among the farmers of Cheshire men who were fit to occupy that position.— Mr. Mcltityre (Great Budworth) thought that the ques- tion was etitirely one for farmers , who paid a large amount of money in rates. It would be a great advantage if they could have the first council composed of the right sort of men.—Dr: Mackie said t!Aat the farmers • must themselves make sure of getting the best men within their reach as representatives There were able and experienced men •amongst them.—Mr. T. Dutton (Newton-by-Daresbury) thought that the members of the new council should be men who paid rates, and who would g. in for economy.—Mr. John Darbyshire (Stret- ton) said that the force of circumstances had now put something within the reach of farmers. Were they going to avail themselves of the opportunity Government had afforded them ?—The discussion was also taken part in by Messrs. Dean (Tabby), Barber (Budworth Heath), W. Derbyshire (Morris Brook), Knowles (Appleton), Newton, (Warburton), A. Barber (Whitley), Whitlow (Preston. Brook), and others, and it was ultimately resolved to adjourn the meeting for a week, it being understood that in the meantime it would be aseertained who might be suitable candidates, with a view to their names being submitted to am meeting.

?CHAPTER XX. RAYMOND DISTINGUISHES HIMSELF.

Though Fielding had rowed in the Torpids he was not a great oar, an always protested strongly againat , the absorption of all other interests in the case of so many undergraduates by the "galley slavery." of Oxford rowing. Cricket he loved better. But he was none the less patriotic and reluctant ta see the soilage flag lowered on the river. He took an active part in the University work, which was just then I being planned in East London, and in Oxford itself— 'working plainly and , honestly at such causes as he had at heart without either priggishness or half- heartedness. He had a mild, courteous manner, and was a great favourite in society though no great lover of it, and wherever he moved impressed him- self upon other young men as one of strength and promise. Raymond WU lucky, Ursula considered, even in college life to be under such weighty patronage as that of Fielding: . But the boy had tired of him during his period of tutelage, and did not consider the matter in the stinid light. He said "he was hanged if he was going to be tied to the apron strings of another fellow." • Perhaps Ursula was unwise in skewing her hand. She ought to have concealed from ,Raymond .the very remotest idea that he required " protection " in launching on his "'varsity life." At any rate the issue was most unfortunate. For he avoided Field. big as strenuously as possible. When, out of sheer politeness, he was forced to accept an invitation to breakfast at Fielding's three weeks 'after the begin- ning of the second term (he had refused once before), his friend saw in a moment that things were not at all right with him. Ray was .looking pale and dissipated. He talked about the great expensiveness of college life, adding, when . his hot gave a half-dissent, "if you want to do the thing properlyl" a remark which Fielding had no difficulty in interpreting. . •" What jolly fellows Harding and Hunt are," he went on. "They came to my wine last night —it was very good of them, considering that I am still a fresher." Harding and Hunt were notoriously loose fish, and Fielding had his doubts about their generosity.in bestowing their company upon " Raymond. He answe,red with quite a natural air of patronage—. " I would not advise you to give too many wines your second term." Ursula's talk about "the advantage of Mr. Fielding's help" flashed back on Raymond, and inducattn adder:like deafness to wisdom. Besides he felt the sting of the rebuke all the more keenly because he had left one of 'Harding's wines three nights before—well, not on his own legs alone. His would-be friends had assured him "he would soon I find his legs," and had felt much secret delight , at having • thus finally secured all his money-bags to their set .No other section of the college would admit a freshman who had put such apress-mark upon his, University career. The event had not come to Fielding's ears; but he was a perceptive man, and having had some experience of RaY'f3 weak points, his suspicions were most thoroughly awakened when ,the lad- answered to his remark, "Thanks, I shall give just as many wines as I please." After this reply, which both hurt his friend's feel- ings and .brought home to Fielding that this brother of Ursula's was a conceited coxcomb, as he had once or twice thought before, Raymond relapsed into silence. His late tutor turned away from him, taking no trouble to conceal his offence, and talked for the re- mainder of the meal to the other freshmen present, some of whom reflected inwardly that Raymond Campion would be useful as a model of what not to do in that state of life to which they had been

caned. • Indeed, Ray himself felt a hot blush mount to4his face when it occurred to him that his answer might be interpreted as a piece of coarse rudeness, though he had meant it for a particularly proud and dignified repulse. But he could not recall it. A sense of discom- fort hung heavily on all present during the re- mainder of the breakfast. -Fielding did not address, a word to his quondam pupil till Itaymond.rose to go, when he turned round upon him, and asked Lam abruptly, "4-e you goin to Harding's wine on Wednesday 2" "Tes,—why " Oh, nothing, only I shall meet you there," he an- swered, looking him sun in the face, and unmasking a fierce and critical glance, which quickly caused the lad to lower his own eyes in almost shamefaced con- . , fusion, as he stammered, "Oh, that will be very pleasant." . _

Could Fieklieg have lietin told of his behaviour! As a matter of fact the senior man had not had the slightest intention of going to Harding's wine onWed- nesday, and had not even been asked. But Ray's shuffling manner put him on the alert. As he expected, he easily obtainedan' invitation to the wine—the fast set was somewhat gratified by this sign of grace—he had never before shewn any anxiety to swell their routs with his presence. They felt. as pleased_ as Collins when he gained an addition to his motley flock. So at the first hint he received a cordial invitation from. Harding. When Wednesday evening arrived, at about ten o'clock—the wine began at eight--when the enter- tainmentwas at its height, Fielding entered leisurely and sat down picking up a cigar--no man can act the critic with less awkwardness than the smoker—and taking a modest glass of claret. The effect of his entrance was similar to that pro- duced by it bombshell upon any company of men that are Met together in peace and contentment. Raymond of course had concluded that Fielding was not coining, as lie had not appeared till so late, and had there:, fore, acted as if he had not expressed any intention of being present. This was jest NvhatFielding wanted. He wished to see him, as he really was, and not to allow him time to whiten his sepulchre. Raymond did not notice his entrance, and after en- gaging in, a few minutes' pleasant converse with his host in order to avoid suspicion, Fielding relapsed into silence, and looked round him with apparent in- nocence but really the keenest criticism. The room was large and sumptuously furnished, with pretty casament windows looking directly on the road. It was full of the portraits of prominent actresses which lined the mantelpiece, the, walls and the table. Miss Mary St. John, in a dozen different attitudes, each more languishing than the former; Miss Di Selwyn, with half-a-dozen different grimaces; Miss rernleigh, shewing her teeth in an extremely vicious way; Miss Netta Kelly, laughing, thoughtful, angry, determined, melancholy, sad, dying, and dead; and Miss Rowley, with an eve directed heavenwards, and thoughts obviously earth- ward, or rather, CILIII craw an]. 'After tasting his eye over this array of painted and bedizened womanhood, Fielding concluded that he preferred even the aisthetic movement to this later craze. • ' : On the middle table was the usual pile of fruit and cakes, and.about a dozen empty champagne and wine bottles scattered about. There were about a score of men in the room, all smoking either cigars or cigar- ettes. Through the consequent obscurity of the atmosphere, could see Raymond in the corner, with his profire turned to him' but eyes else- where. He had obviously not seen him come in. He was playing "unlimited Loo "with four other men. He was flushed and excited, with glass con- tinually replenished , from the half-filled champagne bottle at his side. Fielding noticed with indignation that one of the other men was keeping him constantly plied with the fizzing . fluid. He saw in a moment that he were losing heavily. Sovereigns were constantly passing from him to the other men at the table, keeping up a perpetual clink of money. This clink formed a sort of accompani- ment to the reckless witticisms ,of a mere boy on Fielding's right, who was lying at full length in an armchair, and amusing those around him with his sonversation. Fielding listened for a time. There was little real humour in what lie said, and yet lie kept his auditors in a continual roar. The source of amusement in kis sayings was their "riskiness." He was one of those young men who had turned fast from want of real wit. Not being able to derive a healthy pleasure out of life, he had taken to the sport which Tennyson well describes as "playing ducks and drakes on the lake of fire." Fielding heard him now declaiming against the "hideous social restraints of modern life." " Well, you know some moral people I rather like. But they are all commonplace. What genius can you name who has been wholly moral? Why, if a man's moral, it proves he's not a genius! Does our great middle-class our moral Philistine sniddle-class—ever produce geniuses ? " And his supporters " Swinburnites "they called themselves—laughed a loud approving guffaw. " Faites cc que vous voulez, that is my motto," he resumed." Return to nature, liberty, freedom, breathe . the only true air for genius." " Fool I" rauttered Fielding to himself, "he thinks

that because some geniuses are immoral, therefore, if he is immoral, he will be a genius !" And turning wearily away from that part of the room, for he had heard such bro.yings in abundance from many a young dabbler in Parisian titerature-- he listened to the alk of the group on his left. TheY were pledging one another in Harding's champagne —though with discretion—for the modern under- graduate rarely sins against the la,wof sobriety. It was refreshing to find out on listening that these young fellows merely drank and enjoyed themselves front in: stinct, and did not indulge in high talk abon' "liberty and nature." The indulgence of the mere animal instinct for pleasure is more satisfactory to its followers, than false superficial philosophy ashamed to confess base origin. It was even a relief to find that then: interests were'centered on nothing more importany than the " Two Thousand," and that they were dis' cussing the chances if the nval horses with a keenneq worthier of a loftier cause. Bets were being tosseu freely to and fro, one man as jotting down- his en' gagements inhis betting-book. When Fielding had got thus far in his examination of the occupants of the room he was interrupted bl Harding, who raped loudly on the table with fork—the customary way of attracting attention a wine—and called out,"

"Mr. Campion—for a song ! The call was applauded by a loud clinking (4. glasses And thumping of tables on the part of alino? everyone in the room. Raymond got up ' from the card-table nnsteadilY and much flushed. "I say, you fellahs ! " he said, with an adoption of their English vernacular, which he had latter', studied, "don't let us have any rotten songs. d—d sick of them. Let's goand screw up t": Dean "—(he said " letstr")L." I've brought screwst here, and he desherves to be screwed up heist's° he shent down two fellalts last week." The proposal was received with shouts of sr plause from all present card - players, Swin,,, burnites, and betters. The host, however, strenuous opposed the suggestion. He said "the game wa.s no; worth the candle." They would never hear the ona of ' it. They would be half of them sent do" He would be the chief scapegoat, as the frolic! was to be ventured from his rooms. But he was i? a hopeless minority, and was easily overruled They said "screwing up" was nothing ! The DOT wouldn't mind. Besides, .they hated looking forwars• It would make a fine night's . work, and as for morrow, " sufficient for-the day is the evil thereof. "And I expect the Dean will find it sufficient for several days," someone added. But they had to wait till about twelve o'clock, when the .Dean went to bed, and so they spent tin intervening time in singing and drinking. Happen° sang , a song which deepened. Fielding s disgust 10 him and pity for his sister. Suffice it to say that lb had neither wit nor ttifite. •At half-past eleven, yiel ing, as he was obliged to reach his lodgings bef°`" twelve,' was rising to leave, when he was observed 131 Raymond. • - Ray, by this time, had reached the reckless brave stage drinking, and the sight of 'Fielding roused his maudlin faculties to a sort of blind fury. Ile rushed towards him, and seizing a champagne betel flung it at him with all hi,s force. Fielding dode, aside, but it flew past him and struck Harding, host, on the head, inflicting an ugly wound. was also heated with wine, like Alexander, when he slew his friend, and rushing across to Raymond, he felled hint with one blow of his fist. 11 It . Two or three men rushed up to separate them. Harding was not the man to trample on a falle,o6 foe. He shouted, "Stand back, you fellows. Nl' can't have this ass in here any longer. Let's titre him out." And snatching him up in his strong arms, carried him, for Raymond was not remarkable for hlf strength or weight, kicking tow:irds the door. Thu_ men readily opened it and he placed Raymond °Th„ his back on the dusty staircase outside and shut Ow door in his face. This was all done in a moment. The summarine.e, exhibited by Harding in the disposal of his adverssrY was greeted, with loud applause and laughter 11 Ins rowdy companions. He sank back in a chair ha fainting from his wound, which was now bleedill fast,owing to his exertions. His companions crowdei. round and quickly bandaged it up in a rough-sne ready fashion with pocket-handkerchiefs and sashes.,., Meanwhile Raymond, as he rose to an unstead7 perpendicular, after his not very honourable ejectioni found himself face to face with Fielding, who Pa fqlct hiTh iait. The latter locked at him i? troubled, half-pitying way, and P.i.41 fslawly 011. deliberately— . - • to

0)8 0 b ye' for,

" Campiim, you are a fool ! Let me help yo your rooms." Raymond was now perfectly subdued and 1151 f. frightened. Ho was a pitiable sight, his garrnenl disordered by the. rapidity of his translation to t: XataL=hi.s.rechiess. bravado suddenly cooled into mamilin_cowardice and shame. He would have over: whelnied Fielding with the profusest apologies ft) what he had done. But Fielding quicklystoppe' his mouth. a "All right, none of that nonsense," he said, st, if to h' nits, he saw him safPm

hurrying him off to his rooms, . - between the sheets in a few minutes.- .11avi, finished this task of kindnefis- he rushed home Nvi c. all speed, for it was now within five minutes. °. twelve, .and undergraduates who are outside tD lodgings after "the witening hour of night" , .. punished with a draconic severity. Meanwhile the party in Harding's MOMS SheNVCd tendency towards-breaking up. 'The new-born re, 1; larity of Raymond had been turned into gall by ungentlemanly behaviour of that night. Many No'"" loud in their opinion that a freshman ought not telt allowed to cut open third-years' men's heads m Wl; ipunity. Filially it was decided that the rowclille 0 Which Raymond had .tried to turn in the directi,°o of the Dean should he turned on himself. 'Jr maturer thought they decided that "screwing 11. a Dean was stale work, and likely to be followed 10 ' consequences which could be hardly prevented in tr'o nature of things—from interfering with the Ow, pleasure derived liOni a nently-accomplished "sere 0 up." It would be far more ironical and dramatic a hang Haman on his own gallows—to heist ltayialh with his. Own petard—in short, to screw him up ' I,io his own screws. There would be a touch of poe", justice in it. It is always gratifying to see the itilio righteous fall into the very pit they have dug for,ir righteous../slOt only would it be a vindication of t'vee own injured dignity, but it would also be a defell if in anticipation of threatened authority. F°,rAto iaay mond were screwed up himself, lie coup,. ' screw up the Dean. I (To be cantinned. ) —...e.%

• NSW YO, MONDAY.—The newspapers are devoting leach space to speculations concerning the formation of General Harrisons's Cabinet. The weight of opinion seetres to be that Mr. Blaine will not be a member of it. General Harrison's closest friends declare that he is

Under no ptedges to him, and will he his own master. ig suggested that Mr. Blaine might be given the Itnglish mission, but this is met by the statement that the English Government might object on the ground that his association with Patrick Ford and his speech at Pord's Madison-square garden meeting would make him a persona iagrada at the Court of St. James's. It Is thought that Mr. Blaine desires neither a Cabinet position nor a mission, but seeks a seat in the Senate. COLLIERY DISASTER IN HUNGARY.

- -- VIENNA, SUNDAY NIGIIT.—The 20 miners who were 8,111)Posed to have been drowned by the flooding of the oalgotarjan mine in Hungary have, after all, miracu- lously escaped. Although the death of the imprisoned Miners was taken for granted, the work of rescue was eoutinued all Saturday night in the hope of at least finding their bodies, for the reception of which 20 coffins had been prepared, while the wives and children oi the Wariers were waiting in mourning clothes at the mouth Of the pit. The place where the victims were believed to be, and correctly so as the sequel proved, was inac- tessible en account of the rise of water, and the rescue Darty had therefore to force an entrance to this spot from an adjoining pit. To their great astonishment, as 40011 as a breach was effected, they were greeted by faint cheers from the entombed men, who had been in their then position for 61 hours, the whole of the time 'Without food and half-choked by the foul gases caused by the inundation of the pit. TRE REPORTED DEATH OF MR STANLEY. Pis, SUNDAY. —A telegram from Grenoble, published in the So/eil this morning, states that the Swedish ex- Plorer, Theodore Wostinark, when passing through Grenoble, was interviewed by a journalist, to whom he *aid that he had received n letter from a friend now in the Congo State confirtning the report of Mr. Stanley's death published at Lille a fortnight ago. THE MINING DISASTER IN AMERICA. Nam YORK, SATURDAY.—A terrible explosion occurred, yesterday, in a mine near Pittsburg,, Kansas. One hundred and sixty miners were below at the time, and it is feared that all have perished. Nrw YORK, SA I URDAY ErFNlNG.—Further details to hand concerning the torrali explosion which occurred in a mine at Pittsburg, Kansm, state that 90 bodies have been recovered, and it is believed that no less than 46 4re still buried in the debris, biaw YORK. SUNDAY.—A number of men who were in the, mine at the time of the explosion escaped without hurt. The number of those killed is variously estimated at from 60 to 100. Many deal have been brought to surface. The scenes at the mouth of the shaft, where re relatives and friends of the entombed miners were Zahing news of their fate, are described as most ''teous.

Lord Rosiebery writes i—" I do not deny one or two meetings have demanded Scottish Home Rule, but I can- not admit they amount to a national demand." Mr. Chaplin has given notice that he will, on an early day, call attention to the report of the Royal Commission appointed to inquire into the recent changes in the relative values of the precious metals, and move a reso- lution. There is a wides/v.ead belief that the Government in- tend, after all, to introduce this session a bill for authorising the grant of a further sum for advances under Lori Ashbourn,i's Act. Should such a measure be introduced, it will he strongly opposed from the OPposition benches, and if it be persevered with the ReaSiOn will be materially lengthened. The Government. • it is stated, will propose to increase the sum that may be advanced under the Act from £5,000,000 to £10.000,000.

Tax GOVERNMENT AND NATIONAL EDUCATION.—The yellowing resolution was adopted at a meeting of the 1 Education Conference Committee held on Monday ; 'While this committee regards with satisfaction the recent statement in Parliainent of the Vice-President of tile Council that the Government do not intend to make any attempt to destroy the settlement arrived at in con- nection with the Education Act of 1870, it in of opinion that the supporters of an unsectarian system of national education should in no degree relax their efforts to (1) Prevent the granting of additional public money to schools under private management; (2) to secure the extension of the School Board system, and the provision (4 unsectarian schools under public control throughout England and Wales : (3) to obtain increaed facilities for the unsec arian training of teachers; and (4) to prevent the lowering of the standard of elementary education te Meet the exigencies of denominational schools, in regard to all which objects no assurance whatever' has been Oven in the general statement of the Vice-President of the Council." BANQUET TO LORD SALISBURY AND LORD HARTINGTON. Lord Salisbury and Lord Hartington were on Wednes- day evening entertained at a banquet by the Noncon- formist Unionist Association at the Hotel Metropole, Th , London. e Prime Minister, on entering the room 1., Shortly after six o'clock, was received with cheers,which " Nv, ere renewed a few minutes later when the Dissentient reader arrived. The banqueting hall had been specially It. decorated for the occasion. Sir George Hayter Chubb ,- Presided, Lord Salisbury being on his right, and Lord Martington on his left. Among others present were • Viscount Wolmer, M.P., Sir Julian Goldsmid, M.P. Sir A James Corry, M.P., Sir L. Pelly, M.P. Sir John Pulp,;- ton, M.P., Sir 11. M. Havelock-A/1;n, M.P., &c. A letter was read from Mr Balfour, in which the "absentee Minister" referred to the overwhelming value of the f testimony to the policy of the. Government which could e- he given by Irish Nonconformist ministers who were in I• touch with the feelings of the Irish people. An address as presented to the Premier and Lord Hartington on behalf of Nonconformist ministers in Ireland in which they "deprecated in the strongest manner" the es- tablishment of a separate Parliament for Ireland- _ The Marquis of Salisbury, in reply to-the address, said that it was of special value as representing the Noncon- formity. not merely of Ulster, but of the whole of Ire- land. There was, however, a vast amount of opinion lact yet reached, and which looked with terror at the 'insanity that had seized some statesmen in England. Iney were there to protest against the Home Rule policy „,,ef Mr. Gladstone, but they did not know what that Home Rule policy was. The policy of the future was Eedulously concealed—the Radical party sailed under sealed orders. But had they ever thought what the transfer of executive power meant? It meant Parnellite t.tatesmen, Parnellite judges, Parnellite magistrates, and .1-arnellite constables. How happy they would be. sberal statesmen had practically said that when Ireland uemanded separation she should have it ; but he could not think England would be so false to the policy she had d,Plield as to betray the loyal Irishmen who had so long (rusted in her. , Lord Hartington also acknowledged the address, hold- Lag that Protestant opinion in Ireland was opposed to w'e new policy that had lately been presented to it. The nOble Marquis said that Protestant ascendancy no longer elt, isted, but the Protestants were determined not to Vce themselves in the hands of the members of another edoMination whose priesthood exerciesed enormous 'Power.
