div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. .
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. .

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. Mr. Kelly was the first member to put himself en evidence, carrying up to the table a petition from 2,700 persons in South London against Mr. Goschen's wheel tax proposals. QUESTIONS.

_ The questions were then asked.—The Holtz finciurrenr was unable to give any information as to the date when the Employers' Liability Bill would be again brought be- fore the House, or to state what the proposals of the Government might be.in regard to the bill. THE WHITECHAPEL MURDERS.—THE POLICE. ..- RESIGNATION OF SIR C. WARREN. The Home Secretary was questioned b.y Mr. Pickers- gillond Mr. Gent-Davis about the administration of the Criminal Investigation Department. He stated that, although Mr. Monro had resigned his assistant commis- sionership, he (the Home Secretary) still had his advice in all matters relating to crime, and he had been in communication with Mr. Mourn upon the question of the organis.ation of the Crim;nal Investigation Depart- ment. He declined to lay on the table papers showing the exact position in which Mr. Monro now stood and the reason of his resignation. The HOME SECRETAItY stated that. Sir Charles Warren had resigned his post as Chief Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police on the Bth inst., and that it had been accepted.—The announcement was received with loud Opposition cheers, the House at that time being very full. _

In answering questions about the resignation of Sir Charles Warren, Mr. MArrnEws sail the failure to de- tect the person guilty of the W'hitechapel murders was due, not to any new orga.nisation or to any defect in the organisation, but to the extraordinary cunning and secrecy which characterised these atrocious crimes. Mr. CTINNINGRAME GRAHAM raised by a question the desirability of offering a Government reward for the capture of the Whitechapel murderer. Mr. MATTI-11.ms made a long answer. He informed the HMSO that the whole matter of offering rewards for the capture of murderers was gone into when Sir William Harcourt was at the Home Office, and after an exhaustive inquiry, the conclusion arrived at was that the practise was, on all grounds, an undesirable one, and tending rather to frustrate the ends of justice than forward them. He assured the Hefts that no efforts would be spared either by the Home Office, or by Scot- land-yard, to bring the perpetrators of the Whitechapel outrages to justice.

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION.
div.p: THE PARNELL COMMISSION.

Mr. W. H. SMTU, in answer to a question from Mr. Labouchere, stated that it, would be necessary to bring in a supplementary estimate next year for the Special Commission, but in the meantime the expenses would be borne out of the tomPorary Commission vote. No sum had been contributed, either directly or indirectly, ont of the Secret Service Fund; and, as to access to official documents, precisely the same facilities had been iren to the solicitors for The Times and to the solicitors for the Parnellito members. PUBLIC BUSINESS.

Mr. Lasoucazas asked the First Lord of the Treasury whether it was contemplated to introduce any new Government measures during the present session in con- nection with Ireland? Mr. W. H. SMITH said ho would make a statement on Thursday next as to the legislative proposals of the Government.
SUPPLY.-THE LAW OFFICERS AND PRIVATE

div.head: PRACTICE.
div.p: PRACTICE.

The consideration of the Civil Service Estimates in Committee of Supply was restimed.—Mr. BRADLAUGH moved the rejection of the secret service vote, which, however, was carried by 214 votes to 94. The Committee then took up the English votes. On the vote for Law Charges (277.776), Mr. lierrox moved to reduce the salary of the Attorney-General for non-contentious business from £7,000 per annum to £5.000. and that of the Solicitor- General from £6.000 to £4,000, and argued that even with the reduced salaries the law officers ought to give up private practice and devote their whole time to the service of the country.

Mr. H. FOWLIa. quotimr, from a return recently laid on the table of the House. showed that the average salary of the Attorney-G,moral during the last ten years had amounted to about £12.000 a year, and that of the Solicitor-General to over £lO,OOO a year, which, he maintained, ought to secure their whole time and attention. - -
Mr. HALDANE suggested the appointment of a Minister of Justice. . . . . .

...... Lord R. CHURCHILL remarked that the discussion had convinced him that it would be unwise to alter the present system. It was of very little economic moment to the country whether the law officers undertook pri- vate practice or not, but it was of the hiehest import- tance that the best men at the Bar should be obtained for the offices. On a promise being made by Mr. Smith that the sub- ject should receive attention, which elicited the approval of Mr. John Morley, who said there was a very general feeling in favour of forbidding the law officers of the Crown carrying on private practice, the motion was withdrawn. - .

A similar motion, in regard to the Department of the Public Prosecutor, was defeated on a division. The report of Supply was agreed to. On the motion for the second reading of the Augmen- tation Act Benefices Bill, the debate was adjourned, and After the tran,,cf;on of some further business, the House adjourned at 12 21 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TuBsDAT.

. The Lord Chaneellor took hes seat, at 40 p.m. Lord fnrrnerly Sir John Savile. Ambassador at Rome, took i ton his elevation to the peerage. The Victoria University Bill was read a third time and passed. Tux OATIIS SiOz.tiTeßit moved the second reading, of the Oaths Bill. He wished to see affirmation take the place of the oath of allegiance, though in courts of justice oaths must he retained.—The LORD CITA N- CELLOR said in Committee he would move certain amendments.—The bill was read a second time. The House adjourned at 6 0 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS—TUESDAY. The Speaker took his seat at 30 p.m. . _
Sir Joust SWINBURNE presented a nurnber of petitions in favour of Sunday closing—most of them from War- wickshire. _
Mr. Pritchard Morgan, introduced by Mr. Osborne Morgan and Mr. Arnold Merle,. took is seat, amid Onnositinn cheers, for Merthyr, in the place of the late Mr. Henry Richard. QTJESTroNs.

Mr. MATT/INWS was asked a question as to the distri- bution of the Metropolitan police, to which he replied that he had no reason to believe that the force was over- worked or under-manned. The distribution was made according to the needs of particular localities, and was not based on the population. He added that his infor- mation was derived horn Sir Charles Warren. While Sir Jas. Fergusson was giving some information to the House, Mr. Gladstone entered the chamber; and the members of the Opposition present received him with loud and sustained cheers. The prosecutions of the Salvation Army at Rugby were the subject of a series of inquiries, emanating from Mr. Cobb. Mr. Marritaws, however, intimated that he could give no pledge that the Government would take steps to amend the law relating to obstruction. Mr. BRODRICK, replying to Mr. Duff, said that orders for additional guns for ':be navy had been given to Sir W. Armstrong and Sir J. Whitworth. The order in- cluded guns over nine inches in diameter. THE VAN AND WHEEL TAX Nor ABANDONED. Mr. GOSCREN declared that there was no truth in the statement made in the newspapers that he had decided to abandon the van and wheel tax. He considered him- self pledged to the proposal, and did not consider that »e was in is position to withdraw it.

div.head: SIR CHAS. WARREN'S RESIGNATION.
div.p: SIR CHAS. WARREN'S RESIGNATION.

Mr. M ATTHEWS then proceeded to make a state- ment concerning the circumstances under which Sir Charles Warren resigned his post as Chief COM- tuissioner of Police. He read the letter which he had addressed to Sir Charles, calling his attention so the rule prohibiting Government servants from publicly discussing Departmental affairs, and point- ing out to him that his article on police admin- istration in ilfurrag's Magazine was a breach of the regulation. The reply of the Chief Commissioner was also submitted to the House. Sir Charles, it appeared, refused to recognise the right of the Home Office to exercise any control over him in regard to this matter, and so tendered his resifmation. The Home Secre- tary said that he made the explanation in order to dispel any doubt as to the cause of Sir Charles War- ren's resignation, which was due only to this inci- dent 4 and had no connection whatever with any other matter. At the instance of Mr. Conybeare, he denied the report that the post of Chief Commissioner had been offered to Mr. Howard Vincent, adding that all the various conjectures which had appeared in the public prints were, so far as he had seen them, in- correct. SUPPLY.—LEG AL REFOR4S.RE_QUIRED.--*NARROW

div.head: GOVERNMENT MAJORITY.
div.p: GOVERNMENT MAJORITY.

The House afterwards went into Committee of Supply. On the vote for the expenses of the Supreme Court of Judicature, Mr. JEnnitztis condemned the way in which the officers of the Court were paid. In many offices the work was extremely light, and the salary extravagant. lie insisted that immediate steps should be taken to bring about a reform. He moved a reduction of the vote as regarded the salaries for the personal officers of the judges. Lord R. CIItritCHTLL condemned the tactics of the Government in waiting to take the division until the majority of their supporters could be brought up. If the division were taken now, the vote would not be passed in its present form. fie said that the cases cited by Mr. Jennings were disgraceful, and an outrage on the taxpayers. The Government ought not to press the vote now, but withdraw it until after they had given serious consideration to Mr. Jennings's statement

The ArroattEr•GEttsast, adrnitto'cl the report of the Royal Commission showed that many legal offices re- quired overhauling, both with regard to the work per- formed by the occupants, and the hours of attendance. 'rho alterations tout(' not be made immediately, or in a summary way, but on every opportunity reforms would

be made. He then defended the emoluments of the offices that had been adverted to in connection with the office of Lord Chancellor, the Court of Chancery, awl other legal offices, and said the Government fully recog- nised the necessity for changes, and, so far as they were able, the reforms required would be carried out. Mr. OHLDERS said what was wanted was some Minister who should have control over this large ex- penditure, and who should be responsible to ,Parliament for the proper disposal of the money—Mr. Jim/4mm con- tended that the gross extravagance he had complaine,i of had not been met by the Attorney-General. He urged the Government to consent to a formal reduction of :the vote, and thus pronounce judgment on the present system.-7\7,". LABOUCHIPME said i!entlernen en the Minis- terial benches were good at tnaking Fpeeciies on economy. Nit when it came to voting on the subject, their views altogether changed. He condemned maintaining useless offices sueb as those attending on the Lord Chancellor. The committee expressed a strong opinion against the present system, but the Lord Chancellor would continue to job his familv—(latighter)—and ether legal func- tionaries would distribute their patronage, which they looked upon as perquisites, amongst their friends. Mr. H. H. FOWLER urged the Government to carry out the recommendation of the Select Committee, namely, that in public offices the working hours should be seven hours per day. It had been mane a rule in the Inland Revenue Department, and he did not see why it could not be extended to all other Departments. He also suggested that an Attendance Hook should be kept at all public offices, for the highest as well as the lowest offi- cials. _

Mr. JACKSON promised the Government wonld con- tinue, as vacancies arose, to ab-ilisk useless oS!,es.= MT. SMITH said the Government were quite in accord with the wishes that had been expressed. The present discussion would strengthen thcir hands, and he assured the Committee that vacancies, as they arose, would not be filled up, without it was necessary for public service such should be done.—The House then divided— For the Amendment Against l4B-19 The announcement et the numbers was received with Opposition cheering. Mr. BRADLANGH drew attention to the inconvenience of the Judges leaving London to try trifling cases at the assizes.—The SOLICITOR-GF:NFRAL said a bill had passed the other House, which would remedy the incon- venience. _ _

Mr. ROISKRTSON thought something ought to be done to remove the impression entertained by inacy persons, that unclaimed funds in the Court of Chancery were of enormous magnitufe.—Mr. JACKSON hoped the notice now taken would prevent the public from being misled by theenormously exaggerated statements of advertising agents. Ile would see if it was possible to publish annually a statement of the total amounts and number of claimants.—The vote was agreed to. On the vote for the Wreck Commission, Mr. JACKSON, replying to Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, said the filling up of the vacant commissionership was still under consideration. —The vote was agr:ed to, as were votes for county courts and land registry. On the vote for Revising Barristers (England). Mr.. RITCIIIE, replying to a question, said the Government were not satisfied with the present system of registra- tion, and intended legislating on the subject as soon as possible—the vote was agreed to. OR the, vote for Police Courts (London and Sheerness), a Tong discussion arose on the necessity of at once im- proving cell accommodation at police courts.—Mr. PIC'KERSGIIL moved the reduction of the vote by £lOO, kV the proposal was rejected by 150 to 91, and the vote agreed to. In the course of a discussion on the conduct of the police at the Trafalgar-square meetings, Sir W. LAWSON ArOLlgly urged the Home Secretary to appoint a civilian to the command of the police.—Progress was then reported. The Places of Worship Sites Bill was withdrawn. The House adjourned at 12 5 a.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. • The Speaker took the chair at a quarter-past twelve o'clock.

Mx METROPOLITAN POLICE.—The consideration of the Civil Service Estimates in Committee of Supply was continued, and the doings of the London police were again discussed. Mr. CUNNINGRAME GRAHAM warned the HOME SECRETARY that if the police ;ontinued to interfere with popular rights it would be impossible to keep the indignation of the people within bounds, and declared" before God and the House of Commons that he had stood between the HOME SECRETARY and death many times." Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT, referring to the resig- nation of Sir CHARLES WARREN, said his magazine article was an entire mistake. No one was so dangerous or mischievous as an alarmist, and he believed there was no foundation for an alarmist spirit in refe- rence to the population of London. He advised the HOME SECRETARY to beware of reconstructions, holding that our police system was founded on as little inter- ference with the civilian population as was consistent with the necessities of the case. As to the attacks to which Mr. MATTHEWS had been subjected for not offer- ing a reward in the Whitechapel murder cases, Sir Winikm said he had never known rewards for the detection of crime to be of any good. The attacks on the police and the Holm SECRETARY in this matter were most unreasonable and unjust. On the report of Supply Mr. CONTREARE and Dr. TANNER objected to its being taken at that hour, leading Mr. SMITH to declare that the responsibility for the prolongation of the Session must rest with those who raised such objections. The report was eventually agreed to, and the House ad- journed at 6.15. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY.
The Speaker took the chair at five minutes to three o'clock.

QUESTIONS.—Lord GEORGE !Loci vrox,questioned by Mr. HOWELL, said that when the programme of ship-building adopted in 1885 was reduced to manageable proportions the Government would bring forward a fresh pro- gramme of their own, laying its full details before the House, in the hope that the continuity of the shipbuild- ing policy then sanctioned might not be affected by any change of Government or the election of a new House of Commons. Baron H. DE Wonms, in reply to Mr. CHILDERS, read Lord KNursFonn's answer to the ol.jection of the Queensland Government to the appoint- ment of Sir H. BLAKE as Governor.

„. ..... £5,000,000 WANTED.—Mr. Surat, after announcing that the limits of the present session would not permit of the Government proceeding with certain measures— amongst them the Tithes Bills and the Board of Agricul- ture Bill,—said they intended to ask the House to pro- vide an additional sum of £5,000,000 in extension of the provisions of the Irish Land Purchase Act, and he hoped the House would be able to dispose of the matter in the course of next week. The Chief Secretary would next Monday ask leave to introduce the bill, which the Govern- ment proposed to proceed with de die in. diem. The Government would at a later stage ask the House to consider the Employers' Liability Bill, and he hoped te find the oppor- tunity sought by the hon. member for Shields for discussing the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors (Sunday) Bill, and also an opportunity for considering the question of perpetual pensions. Mr. GLADSTONE intimated that when the Irish Land Bill was introduced next Monday night a proposal of a different nature would be offered as an alternative proposal from the Opposition side of the House. It would be proposed that the House should deal with the question of arrears, and apply to Ireland the principle which had been applied with such great advantage in the case of the Scottish crofters. Surrtz.—After a short discussion on the Government's programme of business, Committee of Supply on the Civil Service Estimates was resumed. In the course of the proceedings Colonel Biunommi moved to reduce a policy vote by £1,900, on the ground that that sum had already been paid by the Bolton Corporation, and that if the vote was agreed to, the sum would be received twice by the county of Lancaster. Mr. Sruawr WORT.. LEY expressed a hope that some arrangement in the matter would be come to between the county justices and the borough authorities, and the amendment was withdrawn. Mr. Dir.LoN complained of the conduct of Dr. BARIt, and moved the reduction of a vote by the amount of that gentleman's salary as surgeon at the Kirkdale Gaol. Mr. BALFoun defended his appointment of Dr. BARR, and eventually Mr. DILLON'S amendment was defeated. Subsequent discussion embraced the question of reformatory and industrial schools and London police affairs.

Dressmakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's. which for strenght is nneotialled.—Adet. The valley of the Stour was inundated on Wednesday. Part of Blandford was two feet under water, and miles of country round Wimborne were submerged. The river has overflowed its banks at Bath, inundating the adjacent lands. MURDER IN IRELAND.—A shocking murder is reported from Dunmanway, county Cork. A man named Lynch, who had charge of an "evicted farm," was, while driving home the cows on Tuesday evening, shot by some person concealed in a " boreen." H staggered a distance of thirty yards and then fell dead. The mur- der was not discovered till his body was found on Wednesday morning. For all kinds of domestic sewing. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY,
GEN E RAL NEWs.
Mr. Henry George. author of 4‘ Progress and Poverty," sailed from New York on Saturday in the Eider for Eng- land.

The Home Secretary has refused to commute the sentence of death passed on Eichard Bart Lott, for murdering his wife at Poplar. After s strike, lastinz seven weeks, the men have re- sumed work at the Waterloo Main Colliery, Leeds, new rules introduced by the employers having been with- drawn.

Mr. Saunders, a magistrate for Hertfardshire and ex- High Sheriff, died suddenly of heart disease whilst join- ing in the service at Sayford Church, near Hertford, on Sunday. The Medical Officer of Health for Manchester (Mr. (John Leigh) died on Sunday, at h's residence, nenr Bowdon. He had held the office from the time of its creation in 186 R. All work at the Enfield Small Arms Factory is being rapidly completed to make way for the new magazine rifle, the manufacture of which it is believed will be commenced abont Christmas.

The house and shop of Morton Brothers, cheese. mongers, Church-street, Camberwell, London, were nearly destroyed by a gas explosion on Sunday afternoon, and Mr. Ralph Morton was blown some distance and Injured. "Professor" Higgins, the Brttish rival of Baldwin, made a successful descent by means of his parachute at Coventry on Saturday morning, Half a gale of wind was blowing, but Higgins ascended in his balloon about 3,000 feet before he cast off. There was a great crowd of spectators. The business of the International Trades Union Con- gress concluded in London on Saturday. Resolutions were adopted in favour of eight hours as the maximum limit of labour per day, what was called international legislation of labour, and arbitration for the settlement of disputes between nations.

SHOCKING RESCLT OF A QUARREL...--Samllel Perry, No. 2 court, Merridale-street, Wolverhampton, quarrelled with his son-in-law, named Connell, early on Sunday morning. The latter threw a lamp at him, cutting .wen his head and breaking the lamp, the oil flowing over him. It Ignited, and he was so severely burnt that he is not ex- pected to recover.

NVest Hartlepool, tke flourishing port on the north- Aast coast, has the reputation of possessing the largest warehouse for eggs n the kingdom. Speaking on the subject the other day, the Mayor of the borough (Alderman Gray) said that last year 12,000 tons of eggs, Dr about 204,009,000 single eggs, were imported into West Hartlepool.

SROCEING MUTILATION By A MOTnEII.—On Mon- day, the Woolwich police burt open a room in Ogleby-street, and found the body of a child with her arms and legs cut off, and missing. Ljs nith. a half- otarved single woman, aged 22, the last occupant of the room, was arrested, and stated she burned the head and limbs. The father was a soldier, with whom she had lived. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT BIRMINGHAM:A destractive ere occurred at the Britannia Carriage Works, Saltley, Birmingham, on Sunday. The tire was discovered by a boy who went to feed some cats living in the store- room. The fire brigade was summoned, and succeeded in preventing the fire spreading, bet the building and about £4,000 worth of stores were destroyed. The damage is covered by insurance. FLOODS us DEVONSHIRE: Two MIN DROWNED.—CIyst Valley is under water, and the road from Tapsham to Woodbury is covered to the depth of three and four feet in some places. The water has not yet covored the Great Western Railway. The river Exe is very much swollen, and the Creedy, Culm, and smaller rivers have in some places overflowed their banks. Two men have been drowned in the overflow Waters of the Culm. One of them has left a widow And nine children.

The Prince of Wales, who is on a three days' visit to f.ord Hind'ip, at Doveridge Hall, Derbyshire, arrived in Derby on Monday, for the purpose of attending the, races. Although the visit was a private one, the town was decorated with fla.gs, and his Royal Highness was enthusiastically received. Amongst the guests invited to meet the Prince were Lord Hartingtom the Duchess of Manchester, Lord and Lady Randolph Churchill, Count Kinsky, and others. SUICIDE OF • LIVF.RPOOT. GENTLE:SUN.—A Liverpool gentleman, Mr. C. P. MeHey, committed suicide at his residence, Aigteirth, Liverpool, on Saturday. For some time Mr. Melley had been under medical treatment for nervous depression. On Saturday, his constant at- tendant left him for a brief interval, and on his return found him dead, with a pistol by his side. Deceased was nearly 60 years of age, was formerly a member of the City Council, and a member of the well-known firm of Meiley, Forget, and Co., cotton brokers.

SERIOCTIE FARM FlRM—About seven p.m. OR. Monday idformation was received at the Ahrine.ham Fire Station that a fire Was raging at Ashley Hall, on the estate of Lord Egerton of 'Batton, in the occupation of Mr. Chas. Sherwin. On the arrival of the brigade it was found the flames had get hold of the outbaildings, in which were stored many hundreds of tons of hay and straw. The stock was removed to a place of safety. Much farm produce was destroyed, however, and the damage to gathered crops and buildiegs is estimated at nearly £2,000. The origin of the fire is attributed to a spark from the thre.shing machine. NARROW FECAPN FROM DVATTL—TWO men, named .iames Etheridge and Henry Nixon, had a narrow escape Crewe station on Sunday. They were employed in Axing some pipes between the rails when a train ap- proached unobserved. and both were knocked down, and fell under the iishnan of the engine. The engine, which was ening at a slow speed, was quickly stopped, and the me, were extricated. Both were found badly crushed. Etheridge had one side of his face smashed in, the cinders being ground into the flesh. They were conveyed to the railway hospital, and attended by the company's surgeons.

FATAL REVOLTER ACCIDENT.--A GIRL KILLED BE HER Ritornaa.—A painful shooting case occurred on Satur- day, in the house of a respectable family in Chatham- street, Liverpool. Mrs. Lang, a widow, sent her daughter upstairs to search for a book in an old lass. Not at once finding it, the son, aged 17, set about rummaging the chest, an.d came across a revolver belonging to his de- ceased father. Little thinking it was loaded, he pointed it at the head of his sister, aged 16, and, pulling the trigger, shot her through the head. The bullet shattered the girl's forehead, and in five minutes she expired. TIIRRATENED STRIKR IN THE SALT TRADB.—The work- ing men in the.employ of the Salt Union whose wages were reduced by the new proprietors when they came into possession of the undertakings in Cheshire, are agitating for better terms of employment. Several of the trades union leaders. including Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., and Mr. Champion, the Socialist, are helping the men to organise. On Saturday, an enthusiastic and largely-at- tended meeting was held at Northwich to consider the question. The proceedings were private. It his trans- pired, however, that the men are determined to striko unless their demand for higher wages aad shorter hour., are granted. Tun GLASGOw ExurntTlON.—The Glasgow Inter- national Exhibition, which was opened by the Prince. and Princess of Wales on the Bth of May, was closed on Saturday night. Considerable interest has been taken in the closeness of the attendance to that of the Colonial Exhibition two years ago. In order to swell the total, a number of season ticket-holders resorted to the expedient of passing repeatedly through the turnstiles an Saturday, with the result that the registers indicated an attendance of 60,767 ticket hollers, while the total number of season tickets issued was only 45,269. The sggregate attendance for the season has been 5,743,379 ss against 5,550,745 at the Colonial Exhibition, and 5,765,137 at Manchester last year. It is officially estimated that the Glasgow surplus will be £t0;000. There were 38,000 season tickets issued at a guinea, and 7,269 at half a guinea. EXECOTION OF AN OLD MAN: A STEENING INCIDENT. —An old man, named Levi It,chard H,,,stt, ssas hssss Ii N.wgate, on Tuestay, for the murder of his wife at Poplar. The culprit was 66 '.,..r aua kspt small shop. He had be-n drinking heavily. and, because his wife refused to give him --osss, he beat her brains out with a It no r as she lay in bed. Be afterwards cut his throat, but recovered. The doomed man, who had slept Sou Nlly, prayed oarnestly with the cliapla;, . ay morning, and asked the sheriffs, when the,‘ visited h s cell, to give his 'eve to his relations. Havins been pini 'tied, the old mite walked to the scaffold without two,. A: shorter dron than usual was given, but he appeared to die instantly. The rope tore open the old wound in the throat, causing a sickening sensation among those whose duty required them to be present.

GIVEN GRATIS 10 ar.t..—The following important fact cannot be too frequently impressed upon the minds of suffer- ing humanity, that M. Gould, 14.13. P., of Bradford, has for some time past, and is now, giving the Hop Prescription for Bitters to all applicants who send a stamp for postage. div.head: 11l -_
div.p: OVEIVBER 17, 1888.
THE WHITECHAPEL TRAGEDIES.- THE DORSET-STREET VICTIM.

In reference to the murder of Mary Jane Kelly, in Dorset-street, Spite Melds. many persons state that she never left the house 26, Dorset-street, after she entered it at .midnight on Thursday. Others, who were com- panions of the deceased, state that she came out of her house at eight o'clock on Friday morning for provisions, and that they were drinking with her in the Britannia Tavern at ten—an hour before her mutilated body was found. The hour at which the murder was committed is thus a matter of the first importance. A woman, named Kennedy, who was staying with her parents at a house in the court, opposite the room in which the body was found, makes a statement, which, if trustworthy, fixes conclusively the time ef the murder. She says that about three o'clock, on Friday morning, she entered her parents' house, and noticed three persons at the corner of the street, near the Britannia public-house. There was a young man, respectably dressed, with a dark moustache, talking to a woman, whom she did not know. There was also another woman, poorly clad, and without any head covering. The man and woman appeared to be the worse for liquor, and she heard the man ask, "Are you coming ?" whereupon the woman went the opposite way from that the man wished her to go. Kennedy did not retire to her parents' house for some time, and about half-past three, she heard a cry of " Murder " from the direction of Kelly's room. The cry was not repeated, and she took no further notice, until she heard of the murder. There is good reason to believe that the unhappy woman Kelly was a native of Cardiff, where her family, according to her statement, were well-to-do people. She is stated to have been very well educated, and an artist of some pretensions. On her arrival in London, she made the acquaintance of a French person residing at Knightsbridge, who initiated her into the Course winch has led to so tragical an end. At this time, she drove out in a carriage, and made several visits to Paris. It is not known precisely how she drifted from this position to the life she led at the East End; but she appears to have lived with a woman named Buky. The two women shortly afterwards went to the house of the female at Knightsbridge, and demanded her trunk, con- taining dresses of a costly description. At this time Kelly is stated to have indulged very freely in intoxi- cants. She next resided with a Mrs. M‘Carthy, Penning- ton-street, which placa she left about eighteen months ago, for her last residence in Dorset-street. Mrs. Mc.Carthy believes that Kelly, when she left her, went to live with a man in the building trade, who, Mrs. McCarthy believes, would have married her. Some short time ago she was aroused about two o'clock one morning by Kelly, who was accompanied by a strange man Mrs. Mc.Caithy admitted them to her house. Since then Mrs. Mc.Carthy has never seen her. . .

Mrs. Mc.Carthy, the owner of the house in which the murder was committed, received, on Monday, the follow- ing postcard, bearing the Folkestone postmark : " From 'Jack the Ripper.' Folkestone (the word Folkestone is printed). November 11th, 1888. Dear Boss,—l am getting on the move lively, baint I man, good job lact time. Get better each time. A good job I played off three ladies. One died, two frightened. Next time a woman and her daughter. Ta ta. dear hoes." At the foot is made a sketch of a man stabbing a woman, who is lying on the ground. The postcard, as the bad spelling indicates, is the work of an illiterate person, who is desirous of adding to the terror which • exists among the residents in Dorset-street No import- ance can be attached to this silly communication; but Mrs. Mc.Carthy, whose nervous system has received a severe shock by the events of the past few days, is greatly alarmed at the threat which it contains.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF SIR C. WARREN.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF SIR C. WARREN.

Sir 7-d-iicre:en-s-e-aii-n his resignation on Saturday. After the statement by Mr. Matthews in the House of Commons on Thursday last, regarding the publication of the article in "Murray's Magazine," that Sir Charles Warren had been requested to observe the rule of the Home Office as to the publication of works on matters relating to the service, Sir Charles Warren took counsel with his friends on Saturday, and the result was that on the same even- ing he sent in his resignation, couched in the briefest language, to the Herne Secretary, stating as his grounds for doing so that he could not accept the reproof admin- istered to him. On Monday, all his books and ;3apers were removed from the Chief Commissioner's office at Scotland Yard, and this was the first intimation at Scot- land Yard that he had relinquished the position. A PARDON OFFERED TO ACCOMPLICES. The following has been Issued:—" Marder.—Pardon.— Whereas, on November Bth or 9th, in Miller-court, Dorset- street, Spitalfields, Mary Jane Kelly was murdered by some person or persons unknown, the Secretary of State will advise the grant of her Majesty's gracious pardon to any accomplice not being the person who contrived or actually comtatted the murder, who shall give such evidence as shall lead to the discovery and conviction of the person or persons who committed the murder.— Signed, Citenuct WARREN." DESCRIPTION OF THE SUPPOSED MURDERER

It appears that a man, apparently of the labouring class, with a military appearance, who knew Kelly. on Monday lodged with the police a detailed account of an incident which attracted his attention on the morning of the murder. His story has been sifted, and the nar- rator cross-examined, and he adheres to it firmly. For this reason the police believe the clue to be a new and important one. The informant stated that on the morn- ing of the 9th he saw Kelly in Commercial-street, Spite Melds, in the vicinity of where the murder was committed, in the company of a man of respectable appearance. The man was about sft. 6in. in height, and 34 or 35 years of age, dark complexion, and dark moustache, curled upwards at ends. He wore a long dark coat trimmed with astrachan, a white collar with black necktie, in which was affixed a horse-shoe pin. He wore dark gaiters with light buttons over button boots, and displayed from his waistcoat a massive gold chain. The "highly respectable appearance" of the man was in such contrast to the appearance of the woman that few could have failed to notice them at that hour of the morning. This description, which agrees with that given of the person seen with Kelly by others, is much fuller in detail than has yet been in the posses- sion of the police, and much importance is attached to it. THE INQUEST.

The inquest on the body of Mary Jane Kelly, the victim et the Dorset-street trnedy, was opened, nu Monday, at the Shoreclitch. Town Rail, before Dr MacDonald, M.P., coroner fer North-east hliddlesex. Great interest was taken in the proceedings; but the room in whioh the inquiry was held barely sufficed to aecommodat e the jury and the numerous representatives of the Press who attended. _ _ .

The jury, having been duly sworn, proceeded to view the body, which presented a horrible spectacle; the vari- ous organs having been put in their places, and the terrible wounds sewn up hy the medical men who have had charge of the case. The jury also visited the scene of the murder, in order more clearly to understand the evidence of those who discovered the body. Mr. Vanier Flant represented the Wbitechapel Vigilance Committee. and Inspector Abberline was pre- sent on behalf of the police. The Coroner complained of the unfounded statements ' in the Press ns to alleged communications between him- self and Mr. Wynn Baxter, with regard to jurisdiction. Joseph llaxnett, labourer, deposed: I identify the body of the deceased as that. of a young woman with whom I lived for eight months. I separated from her on the 30th of last month. I left her because she brought a prosti- tute to live in our room. I saw the deceased last between 730 and 745 p.m. on Thursday. We were on friendly terms. Before leaving I said I had no money. The de- ceased was sober. The deceased told me her father's name was John Kelly, gaffer of an ironworks in Car- narvonshire. She was born in Limerick, was married in Wales to a man named Davis, killed in a colliery ex- plosion. After leading an immoral life in Cardiff, and afterwards in a gay house in the West End of London, she went to France for a short time, and then came to the East End. She lived with a man named Morganstone, near the Stepney Gasworks, and afterwards stayed at a bad house, where she was visited by a man named Joseph Kelly, who lived in Bethnal Green-road. She used to ask me to read to her about the Whitechapel murders, and I did so.

At this point the Coroner said Dr. Phillips had written asking whether his attendance would be required. He (the Coroner) thought it would be well that Dr. Phillips should attend to give formal evidenc as to the cause of death, but he need_ not go into the_details.

John Bowyer said: About 10 45 a.m. on Friday, I was sent by my master, Mr. Me.Carthy, to ask Jane for rent. I knocked, and got no ntisvrer, so I put my hand through a broken win' low curtain, and saw flesh on the table'and the body on the bed. I told Mr. McCarthy, and we fetched the police. John Mc.Carthy said : I an a grocer and lodging-house keeper, in Dorset-street. About 10 45 1 sent the last witness to the deceased for rent. He came back, and said he knocked at the door, and getting no answer looked through the window, and saw blood. I went and looked myself, and Saw the body of the woman. I could see nothing fora little time, but when I recovered I accompanied my man to the police. An inspector came with me to the heuse.. I do not know that Barnett and deceased had any serious quarrel. I let the room at 45. 6d. a week. Deceased was 295. in arrears. I often saw deceased the worse for drink. When drunk she became noisy, and sang. Mary Ann Cox deposed --I live at 5, Miller's Court, opposite the deceased. About midnight on Thursday, I saw deceased in Dorset-street. She was very much the worse for drink. I saw her go up the court with a short stout man, shabbily dressed. He carried a pot of ale, wore a black coat and hat, bad clean-shaven chin, sandy whiskers, and moustache. Deceased wished me "Good night," and went into her room. I beard her singing the song, "A violet I plucked from mother's grave.' I afterwards went out of my room. Coming back at one o'clock, she was still singing. I again went out at two o'clock. and she was still singing. At three o'clock I returned. The light was out, and all was quiet. I did Dot sleep a wink that night. I heard someone go out at a quarter-past six, but I don't know from what house. I should think the man I saw with Kelly was about 35 or 36. If there had been a cry of "Murder" I should have heard it ' ,

Elizabeth Porter said: I live in the room over tile-de- ceased's. I went home about 1 30 a.m. on Friday. About 330 my kitten came across my face, and just as T pushed it away, I heard a suppressed "Oh, murder," ap- pearing to come from the court. I did not take portion lar notice, as I frequently heard such cries. Caroline Maxwell, wife of a lodging-house deputy kb Dorset-street, was next sworn. . . . _ _
The Coroner cautioned her to be careful, ea ber evidence differed from other statements made.

Mrs. Maxwell then deposed: I saw the deceased 0 the corner of Miller's-court shortly after nine o'clock on Friday morning. The deceased told me she felt iH and had been sick I went with my husband's breakfast. On my return I saw the deceased speaking with a man outside the Britannia public-house. I cannot give a par- ticular description of the man. He wore dark clothed and a sort of plain coat. The deceased wore a dark skirt, with velvet body, and shawl, but no hat. The man was short ar.d stout.

Sarah Lewis, laundress, said: I saw a man waiting outside Miller's-court about 2.30 a.m. on Friday. I re- mained in the court all night, and about 4 o'clock I heard a woman cry "Murder." On Wednesday night I was with a female friend, when a well-dressed man, carrying a black bag, asked us to go down a passage We were afraid, and ran away. He had a black moustache, and was very pale. On Friday morning, as I was going to Miller's-court, I met the same man with a female In Commercial-street.

Dr. Baxter Phillips, divisional surgeon of the Metro- politan police, said: I was called to Miller's-court on Friday morning, about 11 o'clock. The police forced open the door of the room, in which, on the bed, lay the mutilated remains of a female, lying two-thirds over towards the edge of the bed nearest the door. From subsequent examination I am sure the body had been removed after the injury which caused her death from one side of the bed to the ether. The large quantity of blood under the bedstead, and the saturated condition of the bedding neareat the wooden partition led me to the conclusion that severance of the right carotid artery, which was the immediate cause of death, was inflicted while the deceased was lying at the right side of the bed, and her head and neck in the right hand corner. That was as far as he intended to carry his evidence that day. Otalj After a brief adjournment, Julia Wenturney said: I am a charwoman, and live at Miller's-court. The de- ceased told me she liked another man other than Joe Barnet, and he often came to see her. I was at home during Thursday night, and had there been any noises I should have heard them.

Maria Harvey, laundress, said: I have slept with the deceased on several occasions, and never heard her ex- press a fear of anyone. Inspector Beck, H Division, said: I accompanied Dr. Phillips to the howe. Ido not know that the deceased was known to the police. . . _ .

Inspector Abberline. Scotland Yard, deposed: I went to Miller's-court at 1130 on Friday. When there I received an intimation that bloodhounds were on the way, and I waited till 1 30, when Supt. Arnold arrived, and said the order for bloodhounds had been countermanded. The door was then forced in. In the grate were traces of a woman's clothing having been burnt. My opinion is they were burnt to give sufficient light for the mur- derer to do his work. The Coroner said this concluded the evidence offered that day. The question was whether the jury had not already heard sufficient testimony to enable them to de- termine the cause of death. His own opinion was they might conclude, and leave the case to the police. The jury, after a moment's consultation, returned a verdict of "Wilful murder against some person or per- sons unknown."

div.head: LIST OF THE EAST-END MURDERS.
div.p: LIST OF THE EAST-END MURDERS.

Seven women have now been murdered in the East- end under mysterious circumstances, five of them within a period of eight weeks. The following are the dates of the crimes and names of the victims as far as known:- 1. Last Christmas week.—An unknown woman found murdered near Osborne and Wentworth-streets, White- chapel. 2. August 7.—Martha Turner found stabbed in 39 places, on a landing in model dwellings, known as George-yard Buildings, Commercial-street, Spite Melds. 3. August 31.—Mrs. Nicholls, murdered and mutilated in Bucks-row, Whitechapel. 4. September 7.—Mrs. Chapman, murdered and muti- lated in flanbury-street, Whitechapel. 5. September Nl—Elizabeth Stride, found with her throat cot in Berners-street. Whitechapel. 6. September 3a—Woman unknown murdered and mutilated in Mitre-square, Aldgate. 7. November 9.—Mary Jane Kelly, murdered and mutilated in a house in Miller-court, Dorset-steet, Com- mercial-street. Spitalfields.

The Richt Hon. Stephen Wolfe Flanazan, late judge of the Landed Estate Court. Ireland, lt,v; been appointed a Lord Justice under the Privy Council in England. A voting firmer niined Patrick Larkin has been arrested on suspicion of beina concerned in the murder of the herd Gilligan, near Athlone, making five men now M custody. A farmer and some labourers who were removing potatoes to an evicte,l farm, which the former had taken at Ardee, were attacked on Saturday by armed men and obliged to run for their lives. "-• ••

On Monday, Mr. ltedmon,l, M.P., was unconditionally released from Wexford Gaol, on account of ill-health. Mr. Redmond had still three weeks to serve. The only complaint lie makes is that he was compelled to exercise with common criminals.

_ On Saturday, at Sligo, Mr. O'Connor Morris, County Court jitdge, heard the :wpm! of Mr. M'llug,h, Mayor of Sligo, against the two sentences of four and six months' imprisonment passed upon him by the resident magis- trates for publishing an article in his paper, the Sligo Champion, inciting to boycotting. His Honour confirmed the sentences. An ag.ent from the Argentine Republic for some time past has been orcanising a movement to promote free emigration from the tooth of Ireland to Buenos Ayres. Between 200 and 300 from Limerick alone were about to emigrate, but, owing to a Pastoral issued by Bishop O'Dwyer, a large number have already desisted, and the rest are expected to follow. On Saturdav night, a yOung man named Cunningham, when proceeding home F run Dundalk, was shot. The bullet lodged in the abdomen. He is reported to be dying. The police heard the noise, and arrested a num- ber of men, on one of whom wa, (*minda six-ehambered resolver, but the police did nct know until Tucsday that anyone had been. shot. There are seven men in custody. MYSTERIOUS STIOOTING AFFAIR. _ _

.... - A mysterious shooting affair is reported from Dundalk Reports of firearms were heard shortly after midnight on Sunday morning, near Dundalk Junction railway station, and the police found seven men gathered thereon with six chambered revolvers. They were arrested for discharging firearms, but at nine o'clock it was found that a man had been shot on Saturday evening near the same place. This was a young man named Cunningham, who had been stopped by four men, and fired at, one shot penetrating the abdomen. His deposi- tions were taken. and Vu' prisoners were remanded. on Tuesday, under the Whiteboy Act. They were all members or local branches of the Young Ireland Society, among the members of wlOcli and of the local branch of the Gaac Athletic th-e has been much quarelling.-The death was a- nr uuca4,oa Tuesday, of the young man Cunningly: !e, w-24 B,lh in the abdomen at Dundalk, on Saturday flict,r, bj cne Of a bend of men seven or whom aro In cue.loy. MR..SSIEEHAN, M.P., AGAIN ARRESTED.

Great excitement tmevails in Killarney over the arreS4 of a publican named O'Connor. for receiving rents under the "Pan of Catrusaign." & campaign receipt book has been found in his possession, with the names of four Kenmore tenants in it. They all paid a deposit of £l, and one lodged a gale's rent, less 40 per cent. One of the tenants, named Denahy. has been arrested, and warrants have been issued against three others. It being a fair day there was a crest number of people in the town, and several shopkeepers actcd in the capacity of rent collectors. Mr. Sho.hatt, M P., has again been ar- rested, and an application for bail refused. Messrs. Flynn, Gilhooly, and o'!irien M.P.'s are staying in the town, and several ether arre-as aria expected. No reply has yet been given to the challenge of the agent, Mr. Leman, whi(Ai was to the etTect that the tenants never asked for a larger reduci ion t han they are now getting- -20 per cent. Several secretly paid their rents on Mon- day, and others, it is understood, are sending theirs by post. .

div.head: PARNELL COMMISSION.
div.p: THE PARNELL COMMISSION.

The Parnell Commission sat again on Tuesday, 'when the President said that the Court had decided that statements made to employers by employes regarding property under their charge were admis- sable as evidence, but not as a proof of facts. Documents claiming compensation for malicious injury were also admissable The President also said the contents of the " Times " box ought to be dirclosed. The documents rejected by Mr. SO&II1e6 148 spurious might give assistance when compared with the letters attributed to Mr. Parnell.—Mr. Lockwood having concluded his cress-examinatien of Sergeant Langford, Captain Kennedy gave evidence respecting his experiences in 1879. Wit- ness was urged by the lotal branch of the Land League to give up the farm, but he declined on the ground that he could not get ground elsewhere. He Was accused for being a landgrabber. He gave evidence at the trial arising out of those pro- ceedings, andwasunder police protection, and was boy-, ootted,—sergeant Brown who is stationed atMulla, gave confirmatory evidence, and in reply to Sir C. Russell, said that the meetings of the League were held in the chapel yard, except on wet days, when the meetings were i held n the chapel. He attended the meetings, and was civilly treated. He never moved any resolution.—James Mannion of Letterfrack, a farmer, was next called. The witness avowed himself to have been a member of the Fenian Society, and said that he knew several members of the Land League who were Fenians. The members of the Fenian society had a sign by which they could tell each other. He was sworn in by a man named Bohan. He gave evidence of attending several Land League meetings. After one of the meet- ings he went with a party of men at night to the house of a man named Coyne. This man had taken out pro- cesses against a man named Lyden, and it was arranged that Coyne was to be well beaten and the processes taken from him.—Peter Flaherty, examined by Mr. Murphy, said he was a farmer living in county Galway. Ile was asked to join the Land League by James Hana, and did so, paying money and receiving a card. This was in 1880. He attended meetings of the League. The most prominent men taking part in the meetings were the two Ruanes and Macdonald. After becoming a member of the Land League he was sworn in as a member of another society.—At the close of this witness's examination the Court adjourned.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

Michael Hoarty, who was a member of the Committee of the Land League at Shenagis, county Galway, gave evidence as to proceedings at meetings, and said the object of the League was to get reductions of rent and to get the land at Griffiths valuation. He attended a, public meeting of the League when Meaney made a. speech. Witness was a Fesuan for about four months. He did not know whether any other members of the League were Fenians. In July, 1883, witness's turf was burned, and afterwards moonlighters attacked his house. In cross-examination the witne3s said Vat the distress in the district in 1887-8 was so severe that people could not possibly have lived and paid their rents. The Committee of the League, in his district had nothing to do with outrage. A man named Ford, formerly in the army, and after- wards employed by the late Mr. Latty, described an attack on Mr. Lattv's house on the night of November 7, 1881, when shots were fired, and said he went out with a gun and shot a man who was afterwards con- victed. District Inspector Murphy, of Woodford deposed to outrages on Lord Clanricarde's estate, and was questioned about the Plan of Campaign. On being cross-examined he said he did not remember complaints of intimidation for refusing to join .he National League, but people complained that they were hampered in their actions.

The Town Council of Warrington were occupied Yesterday week, as is usual on the ninth of ISTovember. in electing a Mayor, and appointing Committees for the ensuing year. Alderman Strrrox, as was anticipated, was unanimously re-elected to the office of chief magistrate. This was smooth sailing, but afterwards the Council 'wandered into a bewildering discussion on one of the Standing Orders. Various amendments were moved, but none of them met the views of the majority of members; and ultimately the Regula-

ton which had provoked so much criticism was adopted as it was first submitted. The Council emerged from the fog in which they had been enveloped to find that it was a case with the members of "as you were,: An attempt was also made to "amend' the Sanitary Committee, but nothing came of it except the substitution of Councillor F A. Roszars for Mr. J. V. TAYLOR. Seeing that Mr. TAYWR, through not being a, burgess, could not vote on the Committee, it was like making a virtue of necessity to let him go. Councillor F. A ROBERTS from his special know- ledge will be a distinct acquisition to the Com- Mittee, which, as the great spending department, Might, with advantage, be further strengthened.

13u-t the chief tug of war was as to the proposal to Place Councillor W. BOLTON on the Watch Corn- blittee. Councillor BOLTON is a brewer; he is the owner of several ofi-licensed houses, and he tss an interest in a full-licensed house. Councillor Idosors moved that the name of Councillor W. Tinsley be substituted for that of Mr. Bolton; an this led Vs 'something like a scene. Coun- cillor Flood seconded the amendment, and was followed by Councillor Bolton himseif, who con- tended that if he was not fit to sit on the Watch Committee he. was not fit to sit on any Corn- inittee. He is apparently incapable of perceiving that the watch Committee is the only Committee that has to do with the police and the carrying
out of the licensing laws-; and that it is because
his private interests are likely to conflict with public interests that he is better off the Corn-
mitten than on. He could see that at did not look
Well, a few weeks ago, for Mr JOHN PIHRPOINT to take a seat on the Licensing Committee, because _
he was not wholly disinterested; but Councillor BoLrox fails to perceive that he is sinning in the

same way in taking a seat on the Watch Corn- Inittee. It was an insult to his constituents, he .said,to objet to him. But is he quite sure of that? How if they should conclude he insults them by showing more regard for his own interests than for theirs

There was a good deal said about a perfectly legitimate suggestion from the Warrington Tem- perance Federation that it was inadvisable to place a brewer on the Committee. That, too, was denounced as an insult by Councilor JOLLEY, who has yet to learn the elementary fact that a bur- gess is as much a part of the Corporation* as he is himself. However, he got a lesson on the sub- ject from Councillor H. ROBERTS, who was to the point in reminding the members that the electors were their masters, and that the resolution from

the Temperance Federation was both respectful and respectable. We have re-read the resolution 'complained of, and we are at a loss to discover the ground of complaint. It runs as follows "That the members of the Warrington Tempe- rance Federation, assembled in annual meeting, regret to learn that it isproposed to appoint to a place upon the Watch Committee of the Town •Coulicii a gentleman who is a brewer and the owner ,of several licensed houses.'. They trust that the embers of the Town Council, acting in the best Interests of the community, will not confirm the appointment; and further resolve that a copy of this resolution be sent to all the members of the Town Council." It will be noted that Councillor BOLTON is spoken •of as "a gentleman." Now, that may be stretch- ing a point, but it surely does not " insult " him or "vilify" his character. As to Councillor JoLLEy he is always feeble when he tries to use strong language; -and it is also Peculiar to him that he is most illogical when he seeks to be most convincing. it was a "bull" of the finest proportions to Argue that because Mr. BOLTON grows auriculas he .couldn't have a desire to serve himself by going •on the Watch Committee. Councillor VOISEY Also placed himself in a false position when he 'contended that the Temperance Federation had

no right to issue their resolution. Can it be that he is under the impression that now he has become • 40. Town Councillor he is too exalted to be approached either by letter or otherwise Meet- ings may be held and letters written with the 'Object of influencing the views of members of Parliament; but-as to the Town Councillor he is an altogether different order of be.n.; ; he is a 'red person; the "divine right" of kings has departed from thrones and settled upon him! Shocking as it may seem as coming from a Coun- cillor, Mr. HENRY ROBERTS calls this " bosh " and we are just afraid that ordinary mortals will agree with him rather than with Messrs. JOLLEY and VOISEY.
Councillor W. Pierpoint was very plain-spoken O n the subject of Councillor Bolton's proposed 'aPpointment, and so excited that gentleman that

, he said the speaker was telling "a deliberate falsehood." At this point the Mayor intervened, but he did not, as he should have done, ask Coun- cillor Bolton to withdraw his unparhamentary language ; so, by way of protest, Councillor Pier- point declined to say another word. When the question was put to the vote, the amendment was lost. The Town Council of Warrington are of opinion that it is a judicious thing for the trade to be represented on tho Watch Cointnittee, and this in lace of the fact that there has been an I increase of convictions for drunkenness amongst males during the past year to the extent of 46 per cent., and that, going back a dozen years, drunk- enness amongst females has increased 100 per' cent! What have "the clergy and ministers of all denominations" to say to this? And what have the burgesses to say? Do they think that it will strengthen the hands of the policeman whose duty it may be to report against the licensed houses belonging to Councillor BOLTON ? . Will it strengthen the hands of the Chief Constable who looks to the Watch Committee for instructions for the better enforcement of the law ? It is not, we submit, a question of the character of Councillor Boxrorr. It is a question of the wisdom of selecting out of a score, for a vacant place on the Watch Committee, the one man who, above all others,may be called to sit injudgment upon a case in which he is personally interested. Councillor VOISEY says that whatever the Watch Committee do will have to come before the Council. But Councillor Vorsnv is in error. The Watch Com- mittee has special and peculiar powers :much of its business has relation to the law and to the police, arid does not come either before the Council or the public. We blame Councilor BOLTON for thrust- ing himself, as he has done, upon the Committee; but we blame the Town Council more for making an appointment, the character of which has been found in the past to be bad alike in principle and in practice.

THE HOME SECRETARY brought the question of the resignation of Sir CHARLES WARREN before the House of Commons on Tuesday. It seems that the HONE SECRTARY and the late head of the Metropolitan Police Force, could not "hit it," and it has ended in Sir CHARLES having to go. There is an old saying that when two men ride a horse one must ride behind. In this case both men wished to ride before, and as the SECRETARY declined to give way to the CONSTABLE, the CONSTABLE has cleared out of the partnership, There have been several differences with Sir CHARLM WARREN. He has been altogether too military and autocra- tic; and the result is that, as chief of a civil force, he has proved a failure. His conduct naturally provoked much hostile criticism, and to this he replied in an article in "Murray's Magazine." In taking this course it appears that he acted contrary to the instructions of a circular drawn up in 1879. It was issued for the guidance of "Officers attached to the Depart- ment," and requires that "no officer shall publish, any work relating to the Department, unless the sanction. of the SECRETARY of STATE has been previously obtained for the purpose." Sir Cukax,Es was told that this applied to every officer in the force, from the COMMISSIONER downwards; but Sir CHARLES repudiated the right of the HOME SECRETARY to apply such R circular, in his ease. He would not, he said, have accepted the post had he known of its existence; and tendered his resig- nation rather than submit to such instructions at the hands of the HOME SECRETARY. The resigna- tion has been accepted, and Mr. MATHEWS has had his way; but the matter can hardly be said to be at an end. It is obvious that dual control of the London police does not work well. The HomE SECRETARY appoints the CHIEF CON- STABLE, and is nominally his master; but, on the other hand, no capable CHIEF COMMISSIONER would submit to be ordered about by a Secretary who knows little or nothing of pollee work. The worst feature of the present mode of managing these things is that neither of these Officers of State is in touch with the people of London, who are treated as though they were so many sheep to be barked at and bitten as one or other of the shepherds may direct. Something in the name of Local Self- Government is being given to the metropolis, and will come in force in January; but it is so wretchedly incomplete that it leaves the questicn of the control of the police exactly as we find it to- day. The remedy for the bad state of things which has made the police of the metropolis so unpopular must go beyond the resignation of a chief. It would be an advantage, perhaps, if Mr. MArrEEws would follow the example of Sir CHARLES WARREN and resign; but what is really needed is that the police of London should become an integral portion of the government of London. That is the lesson of the mis-management which has been witnessed in the metropolis for so many years.

Glasgow Exhibition was brought to a close on Saturday. Thole will be a surplus of no less than £40,000 for th 3 promotion of science and art. Well done Glasgow! -- Tom King, the pugilist, appears to have fought his way through life to some purpose. He has just died, leaving personal eitate behind him to the value of £64,000.

The bailiffs of Vienna have seized Sarah Bern- Wardt's wardrobe for income tax. They have not seized Sarah; she is so thin they could not lay hold of her. But as for her wardrobe—why, that is bulky as a haystack.

The "Pall Mall Gazette" publishes a long list of American girls who have made matrimonial conquests of the English aristocracy. It used to be a stock gibe at tile democrats that they were " Americamsing our institutions"; it is the aris- tocrats now who are doing that—in another way.

Let Company-mongers beware. Mr. Justice Kay has ordered the repayment, by the Faure Electric Company of the sum of £2,500 which had been paid to a broker by way of commission on the allotment of shaies. His lordship said "it was in the nature of a bribe to get rid of shares," andhis lordship is right. Law and equity are in agreement for once.

Unmatched gloves have become fashionable in Paris. This will suit Mrs. Cleveland to aT. It is stated that, as the wife of the President of the United States, she has done so much hand-shaking that her right, hand requires a glove two sizes larger than the left. Her hands don't match, and she will therefore be in the fashion without wearing gloves that are odd as to shade.

The members of the Warrington Farmers' Club were usefully occupied on Wednesday in discussing the question of representation on the County Council. If they will only move quickly, select good men, and not too many of them, there is no doubt as to their securing a fair number of repre- sentatives. They must recognise that in their case "Union is strength," or they will find them- selves attacked in detail and beaten.

It seems that Mr. Gosehen is to be let down easy in the matter of backing out of the unpopular wheel and van tax. This week the Tories have themselves been signing a memorial in favour of surrendering it. This is to be the bolster upon which the Chancellor of the
_ Exchequer is to take, his fall. But ho may not find the fall easy after , all. Poor Goschen I He is not like the famous guard; he does not die; he surrenders.

France is to be snuffed out; not by Germany, but by French neglect to increase and replenish the earth. A medical journal makes it put that so few French children are born, there will be no Frenchmen in existence 500 years hence. Five hundred years is a good long term, and it is just possible that some ingenious Frenchman will meantime hit on a plan for keeping up the supply. Let us hope this will be so; our lively neighbours cannot well be spared. •

The Oaths' Bill was read a second time in the House of Lords on Tuesday, on the motion of Lord Spencer. His lordship expressed himself as personally willing to go beyond the scope of the bill; but tke Lord Chancellor intimated his intention of whittling it down stillfurther. There is therefore some danger yet of its failing to become law; but there is consolation in knowing that if it be lost, it will have paved the way for a still better measure when the Liberals come into power. '

The Tories are ready to talk about economy, but they will not vote in its favour. On Monday ten Conservatives only supported Mr. Jenning's motion to reduce the vote for the salaries of the Supreme Court of Judicature, although it was shown by Lord R. Churchill, as well ,as by the members for Stockport, that officials were receiving large sums of money every year when they had really nothing to do. The Government narrowly escaped defeat, but it was in consequence of the solid vote of the Liberals.

Speaking at a ward meeting at Warrington, on Monday evening, Major Litton said :--" Alto- gether he thought they were going on in a most satisfactory manner, and, therefore, when the time arrived they could not do too much in help- ing to return as the member for Warrington a good Conservative with a good sound head on his shoulders." Just so; it is usual to be on the look out for men of this kind; but is it not rather hard on Sir Gilbert Greenall ? Compari- sons are apt to be odious.

A contemporary says :—" Mrs. Drew, who con- tributes to the Woman's Gazette a notable article in favour of women's rights, is the most Gltd- stonian of all Mr. Gladstone's family. For many years before her marriage she was the right-hand man' of her father, and it may be interesting to those who write to Mr. Gladstone to know that every letter of the daily eighty which on an aver- age are delivered at Hawarden is opened by Mrs. Drew, whose services as secretary free her father from a considerable proportion of the inetitable worries of so extraordinarily large a correspond- ence."

Referring to the way in which the English girl is being cut out in the market, " Truth " says : "I should say that the main reason is that the American girl is not so missy as her English sister, and that she is brought up to run down her own game. In England, the notion 'still prevails that a girl is sure to get into mischief if she has not a mother or something of that sort at her elbows. She herself resents this, and takes it out in fast conversation and slangy ways, so that she becomes a singular mixture of a doll 'and a tomboy." That is something for English girls to think about; but it it the " truth ?

It is regarded as "bad form" to dispose of presents by presenting them again. But the Pope is an exception to the rule. He rightly. regards the enormous number of Jubilee gifts which he has received as gifts to the chair of St. Peter rather than to himself individually. He is there- fore making use of them by presenting them again to various churches taking care not to send French articles to France, or German articles to Germany: In this way, fresh forms of art will be introduced in various countries. His Holiness is showing himself in this matter as wise as he is generous. ,

• Mr. J.Burnett, the Labour Correspondent of the Board of Trade, has issued a report whi ch contains s. large amount of vajuable information as 'to the work of Trades Unions. He remarks that the facts presented " will tend greatly to correct Ole generally prevailing notion that the sole object of TradelJnions is to foster and encourge strikes, and that most of their funds are applied to that purpose." • He shows that they are really Mutual Benefit Societies. But the most interest- ing feature of the report is the evidence which it affords of the growing demand for labour. Trade is certainly improving; we are in for a good time, if not for a "boom."

Mr. J. Carvell Williams, has been teaching the young idea how to shoot by alecture on "Progress from Toleration towards Religious Equality." 'ln the colonies, he said, the work of Disestablishment was almost complete. All the changes described had been advantageous to the Church as well as to the nation, though they had been strenuously opposed by the former. In closing, he said that while many of the branches had been lopped off the upas tree of State-Churchism they had yet to strike at the root, and for the sake of religion as well as for the sake of Noncomformity. Nothing had happened to justify a relaxation of effort to ' secure that end, while there was everything to encourage ceaseless labour until their principles had been firmly rooted in the opinion and in the legislation of the British people.'

GOVERNMENT PnosEctrnort OF COLLIERY MAN- AGERS.—At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Friday, before Messrs. A. Sinclair and A. Walmsley, the Whitecross Colliery Company, Limited, and Mr. Hobert Turner, their 9anager, were each summoned under three informations laid by Mr. Henry Hall, Government Inspector of Mines, for allowing a shot to be fired in one of their mines with an explo- sive which would inflame gas, and with allowing an iron rammer to be used in the process of charging or stemming for blasting.—The magistrates dis- missed the whole of the cases against the colliery company. and also the first-named against Mr. Turner; but for allowing men to use iron rammers instead of copper rammers, Mr. Turner was fined 10s. and costs in each of two cases. SEEKING CHEAP LEGAL ArovicE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday James Marsh, of Hay- dock, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly in Clipsley-lane, on the 27th Oct. Defendant pleaded guilty, adding that he had some bother with a woman about some fowls. He wished to ask for a little information, was a woman allowed to keep-- Mr. A. C. McCorquodale J.P. : Keep to this case please,—Defendant: Yes, but is a woman allowed to—The Magistrates Clerk: You have pleaded guilty. What about the drunkenness—were you drunk ?—Defendant; Yes, I have pleaded to that but I want to know—The Clerk: Well, we cannot answer questions here. Go to some lawyer and he will tell you. —Defendant: Yes, but he wants 6s. Bd.—(Loud laughter.)—Defendant was then fined ss. and Cogs. THE RAINFORD HALL ARBITRATION.—The action brought by Messrs. J. L. Wolfenden and Samuel Wolfenden, St. Helens, executors for the late Messrs.l Harris, contractors. against Lieut.-Colonel R. Pilkington, J.P., ofvßainford Hall, in respect of the ' dispute during the re-erection of the hall, which was referred from the May assizes to arbitration, has just been concluded. •The arbitrator, Mr. Lewis Williams, awards as follows :—The plaintiffs are entitled to recover trom defendant in respect of their claim in the said action the sum of .£3,000, and I do further award and find that the defendant is entitled to recover from plaintiffs in respect to his counter claim in the said action the sum of .C 2,000 and I do further award and order the defendant to pay to the plaintiffs the sum of £l,OOO, and I do further award and order that the costs of the said reference, as well as those of the plaintiffs as those of the defendant, and the cost of this my award to be borne and paid by the defendant.

SUDDEN DEATH AT WIDNES. Mr. Brighouse, the County Coroner, on Tuesday held ,an inquest at the Market Gate Hotel, Widnes, on the body of Thomas Mooney, aged seven years, son of William Mooney, labourer, of Major Cross-st. On Saturday the boy, who had enjoyed good health since birth, was seized with convulsions, and Dr. O'Keeffe was called in. He became unconscious on Sunday morning, and died in the even- ing. A verdict of natural causes was returned by the jury. CATHOLIC CONCERT AT WIDNES —ln aid of St. Mary's Catholic Cleirch a concsrt was given in Widnes Volun- teer Hall on Monday evening, and there was a capital attendance. The artistes were Mdlle. Dumas, contralto, Liverpool ; Miss Belle Pryde, soprano, Liverpool; Miss ' Dwyer, Widnes; Mr. Will Kearns, reciter and versatile comedian; Mr. McLoughlin, tenor;, and Mr. Jones, baritone. A long awl interesting programme was gone through, awl the audience evidenced their appreciation, frequently malting the vocalists. The comic sketches of Will Kearns were a source of much merriment.
