A DISHONEST DOMESTIC SERVANT AT WIDNEB.—A domes- tic servant named Elizabeth Nutt, 18 years of age, Whose home is at Pennington's-row, Runcorn, was brought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with stealing 225., belonging to her mistress, Ellen Kristin, greengrocer. Albert-road. She was further charged with stealing a quantity of under clothing, valued at lfis., the property of Elizabeth Scott. Oak- land-st. About seven o'clock on Saturday, night, the 23r.1 inst., Mrs. Kelsall gave the prisoner 225. with which to redeem several articles which were "in pawn," awl she did not return.. The same night the prisoner went to the house of Scott from whom she received the clothing for her Mistress. She was appre- hended by the Runcorn police, and stated that she had lost the clothing in a railway train, and iG was after- wards recovered. As the prisoner had been previously convicted, she was sent to gaol for two months. RUNCORN DOCK Tunws.—A Carnarvon Shipowner. writ- ! ing to the "Liverpool Journal of Commerce," asks-- ! Have the dock authorities at Runcorn the right by Act of Parliament to turn a vessel out of her berth when dis- charging to make room for another, and, if so, can you tell me where to find the Act ? Should a vessel get neaped by This favouritism. have I claim for compensa- tion? [According to the printed statements we find that vessels using the-Duke of Bridgewater Dock or the Old Quay Dock are to be berthed and discharged by turn "on arrival." We understand that this practice has been, as a rule, Properly observed ; but if b is broken to favour any ship or particular owner, without the most justifiable cause, the owner of the vessel so compelled to change berth, or to move off into the basin, would have an excellent plea on which to found a demand for dam- ages. ED. J. C.)—From the "Liverpool Journal of Com- merce." .

STUBBS' FURNITURE CEE4M.--For giving a brilliant gloss to all kinds of mahogany and French polished furniture with half the usual labour, me Stubbs' Furniture Cream. Sold in bottles, id, 2d., and 3d.—lsaac Stubbs. Lowlands-road. Run corn.—Advt. A BOATMAN'S Row am TOP Loces.—Thoma,s Theobald, a boatman, was summoned to Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of assaulting Hannah Giles, wife of John Giles, a boatman in the employ of Messrs. Simpson, Davies, and Co.—There was a cross summons charging Giles with assaulting Theobald. Mr. A. Linaker appeared for Giles and Mr, A. Browne (Warring- ton) was for Theobald. It appeared that the boats managed by Giles had the right of road up the Top Locks, and was alleged that Theobald was so exas- perated that he had to wait, that he struck the woman several blows on the face. He use such force that she was thrown to the ground, and received such injuries to her jaw that she had had to eat "soft food" ever since. For Theobald, it was shown that the woman had a violent temper and had frequently caused disturbances. On the present occasion she gave Theobald two blows on the face, and threatened that she "could do for any— like him." Theobald only struck her in self defence. —The Bench after hearing the evidence dismissed the case against Giles, and fined Theobald Ss. and costs 245. Tun SLEEPING ACCOMMODATION OF A RUNCORN LODGING House.—At Runcorn Petty. Sessions on Monday, Martin Gilligan a common lodging house keeper, Cooper-st., was charged with having failed to cause every room in his house, which was appointed for use and occupation as a sleeping apartment by two or more married couples, to be so furnished or divided that every bed in occupation should. be effectually screened from the view of the occupants of any other beds.—The defendant pleaded guilty.—Mr. W. H. Linaker, Law Clerk, said the Inspector on the night of the 6th Nov. found two married couples sleeping in the same bedroom of the defendant's house, and there was not sufficient protection or screening.—The defendant said he was suffering from an abscess on the hip, and had not earned a farthing for 13 weeks. His wife was in charge of the house on the night in question and she did not know she was doing wrong. He had kept a lodging house for four years.— Mr. Linaker said he had learned from the Inspector that the man's story Was true, and he, therefore asked the Bench to impose as small a penalty as they could justly, and he weal not claim his fee.—Mr. Brundrit said after four years' experience the defendant's wife ought to know the requirements of the byelaws, but taking into consideration the statement of the advocate, they would only impose a fine of 103. including cogs. THE TROUBLES OF A RUNCORN SOLDIEE.—On Monday at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Wm. Ashby, a man of fine physique and respectable appearance was charged with being drunk and disorderly on the sth inst.—P.C. Bourne give evidence in support of tho charge, and said the defendant had broken the cipor of one house open, and had forced his way into another. He admitted that the person who had fetched him into the street had told him this.—The defendant, who had an impediment in his speech, said that on the day in question, after finishing his work, he found that every article of furniture had been removed from bis house during his absence and that his wife had left. He thought he had a right to break open the door, to gain access. He afterwards found his wife in her father's house, and she told him that she was afraid whilst he was in drink. That was the first time he had over indulged in a glass of ale. He had served his time as a non-commissioned officer in the Army and had been in South Africa and Zululand. He did not wish to plead a falsehood—he aspired to some- thing higher—ad he emphatically denied that he was drunk. The constable did no know him and seeing his excited state, and hearing his speech he concluded that he was drunk.—The Bench considered the defendant bad received great provocation, and might have been much excited. The .case was dismissed. The decision was received with applause in Court. Rtreconst CHURCH INSTITUTE CONCERT.—In connection with the Runcorn Church Institute, a concert was given in the National School, on Tuesday evening. Consider- ing the state of the weather and the counter attractions in the town, the attendance was satisfactory. but the merits of the entertainment merited a much larger auditory. 'fke programme was conceived and carried out by Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys and his friends, and was as follows :—Pianoforte duet, "Poet and peasant," Miss Taylor and Mr. Wynne Humphreys; duet, "Whets the wind blows in from the sea," Miss Lizzie Owen and Mr. Frank Whitworth ; violin solo, "Sonata in 4," Mr. H. D, Herrin,e ; song. "Three Fishers,' Miss Ethel John- son; recit and aria, "Arm, arm, ye brave," Mr. Frank Whitworth; flute solo, " Barcarolle," Mr. T. A. Bazley song, "rears," Miss Lizzie Gwen ; violin solo, "Elegy., Mr. H. D. Herring ; pianoforte duet, "Soirees musicales," Miss Taylor and Mr. Wynne Fitimphreys • song," Forget, forgive," Miss Ethel Johnson; flute mho, "Gavotte," Mr. T. A. Bazley • song, "The Bedouin love song," Mr. Frank Whitworth; song, "The Worker." Miss Lizzie Owen; violin solo, '4 Moreeau Charitant," Mr. H. D. Herring; song, "Daddy," Miss Ethel Johnson; trio for violin, flute and piano "Hungarian Airs," Messrs. Her- ring, Bailey and Wynne Humphreys; solo and chorus, t' God save the Queen," Miss Lizzie Owen and audience. From start to finish the concert was a rich musical treat. Both vocalists and instrumentalists were amateur musicians.of the highest class, and the various items were rendered in a style that would have excited the admira- tion of the most critical audience. Those present dis- played their appreciation in an enthuisastic manner, and Mr. Humphreys and his friends were most cordially thanked for their services. Runcorn.— Advt.

ALLEGED ROBBERY XT RUNCORN.=OR Thursday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Mary Williams. a married woman, was remanded on a charge of stealing a brush handle, value 3d., belonging to George Duckett, lodging. house keeper, Church. BETHESDA MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUHROHN.— At the meeting of the members of this society, on Mon- day, the Rev. J. D. Thomas read a paper on "An Ideal Mutual Improvement Society." Mr. T. Handley, the president. occupied the chair., NEW ENAMELLED IRON WARE.—Gartand, Ironmonger,' Warrington.—Adet. RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.—On Thursday evening the first rehearsal of the members of this newly-formed society was held in the Bethesda Lecture Hall, Runcorn, when there was a good attendance, and a most favour- able commencement was made. THE EARLY CLOSING MOVEMENT AT RUNCORN.—The hairdressers of the town have formed themselves into an association and an arrangement has been come to whereby they will close their shops every Thursday afternoon at one o'clock, commencing on the 22nd just. ST. AMBROSE (WIDNES) IMPROVEMENT SOCTETY. —At the weekly meeting of this Improvement Class. on Thursday evening, a large number presented them- selves to hear a paper read by Mr. Joseph Treacy, the subject of his discourse being "Oliver Cromwell." A portion of the evening was spent in impromptu speak- ing. HAYNES'S RANBSEWN WATERTIGHT NAVVIES BOOTS, from 12/6 to 1.6/- 42 and 44, Horsemarket-,t., Warrington. Advt. ACCIDENT AT RuNcoart—Whilst assisting to raise a sunken lighter at Bottom Locks, on Tuesday, John Ford, of Cemetery Lodge, fell off the gates into the lock. Fortunately there was about 4 feet of water in the lock a the time, or the man would have been instantly killed. He sustained serious injuries to . the arms and hands, and was badly cut about the face. THE RECENT ACCIDENT ON RUNCORN BRIDGE.—We are glad to be able to report that the lady who met with the unfortunate accident on Runcorn Bridge last Friday evening is gradually improving. She is only partially conscious, but the symptoms are much more favourable. Several doctors have been in attendance since the occurrence. Hopes are entertained that she will re- cover. The name of the lady is Mrs. Dowe, of London. PETROLEUM STORES—Garland, Ironmonger, Warrington and Harlestewn.—Advt. OBSTRUCTION BY A WIDNES FURNITURE DEALER.— Samuel Claff, furniture dealer, Victoria-road, was sum- moned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, charged with obstructing the footpath.—P.C. Porter deposed that on the 31st October he saw on the parapet, in front of the defendant's shop, a large quantity lof goods, including three tables. The parapet, which is eight feet wide, was altogether occupied.—The defendant was fined 2s. 61. and costs, Bs. 6d. ST. MARY'S IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, WIDNES.—The usual.weekly meeting of this society was held at the Waterloo-road schools, on Tuesday evening. The curate (the Rev. John Connel, 8.A.) presided. The plague of "Murrain "was discussed in connection with the list of the plagues of Egypt, after which the "Plants of Pales- tine were expounded on by the Chairman. Mr. Bing- ham gave some useful information about " Arithmetic," and Mr. Connel gave a lesson in geography, descriptive of Ireland. Altogether a very pleasant evening was spent ROBBERIES FROM A WIDNES Scrtoor..—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Catherine Kerwin, of 8, Margaret- st., was charged with having stolen an ulster, belonging tc Thomas Tansey, of 58, Ann-st. The ulster was worn by Tansey's young daughter, who placed it in the usual place whilst at school. On leaving, the ulster could not be found. It was afterwards discovered that the prisoner, who was the school cleaner, had pledged the article at Mr. Neil's 'shop. There were five similar charges to be brought against the prisoner, who was remanded until Monday. Fon boors AND Slums of every description go to Haynes', Horsemark et-st.. Warrington.—Advt. SHOCKING ACCIDENT ON A FLAT AT WIDNES.—A flatman named John Oakes who lives in Pleasant-st., Lugsdale, Widnes, was working a winch on board his fiat on Thursday, when the handle slipped from his grasp and struck him two violent blows on the head and face. The skull above the eye was broken in to the extent of three inches, a ghastly gash ,disfigured his cheek, the cheek- bone being fractured, and one of ids eyes was almost severed from its connection. Yesterday afternoon he was in a much better condition than those in attendance hoped for. He is a single man, 30 years of age. CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY, WIDNES. —The weekly meeting in connection with this society was held in the Waterloo-road Schools, on Thursday elming. The Rev G. H. St P. Garrett presided. There was a very good attendance. The first part of the pro- ceedings was of a devotional character, an address being given by the Vicar on the religious bearing of the society's work. An excellent address was also delivered by the Rev. Mr. Thomas, on the fallacy of drinking intoxicants in the hope of gaining health and comfort. Suitable hymns were sung by the members, after which a number of members were initiated.

The first annual general meeting of members was held in the New Lecture Hall of the Club, on Mondayevening. Mr. J. Morrison, the presi- dent,occupied the chair, and there was a good attendance. Mr. Frank Cave, the hon. secretary, presented a balance sheet which shawed that the club financially was in a flourishing condition. The balance sheet was adopted by acclamation: Thirteen of the old Committee were re- elected ; four new members being added. After this business a concert took place, Mr. H. B. Shares fulfilling the duties of chairman. A capital programme was gone through, the following members taking part :—Messrs. J. Morrison, Caldwell, T. Singleton, F. Wareing, Hanlon and J.G.Kkldie. The usual votes of thanks were accorded at the conclusion. LIGHTHOUSE LAMM—J. S. Garland, Lamp Works, 51, Bridge-at.. Warrington.—Adrt. CARDIFF PRIZE CHOIR AT RUNCORN .—This celebrated combination of Welsh singers have fulfilled a three days engagement at Runcorn Fublic Hall during the past week, commencing on Tuesday.. There VAS A 3hange of programme on each evening, and crowded audiences have ga•hered to listen to some of the most sweet and tuneful music ever carolled forth. The choir, consisting of nine voices, was well balanced, and the glees and choruses rendered were delightfully harmonious pieces of vocalisation. The individual members sang some of the most beautiful songs and solos in the English and Welsh language,and the encores were frequent and enthusiastic. The performances of Master Aneurim Jenkins, R.A.M., (the boy harpist) were a pleasing feature of the entertain- ments. Should M. Flocking, the conductor, decide to again visit Runcorn he may depend upon a most hearty welcome from.the music loving public. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the cemetery lodge, on Wednesday afternoon. There were present—Messrs. W. H. Rogerson (in the chair), J. Flandlev. S. Taylor, W. Littler, W. Whittaker, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The minutes of the Finance Committee were presented. from which it appeared that the total amount received during the month ending October 25th was £27 ss. 11d., and the payments £9 16a., leaving a balance of £l7 9s 11d. Accounts amounting to £2 7s. 2d. were recom- mended for payment. The minutes were adopted. It was shown by the monthly statement that the interments during the seven months ending October 25th numbered 197, corresponding period last year 204, or a decrease of seven. The receipts during the same period had been £lBB 135., corresponding period last year £217 or a decrease of £2B 10s. This was the whole of the business. ."Twe Jonv Boat" Boor, twelve months' wear guaran- teed. Usually sold at 13/6. our price. 10/8.—Haynes'. Horse. market-at.. Warrington.—Advt. TTIE CIMITCAL TRADE Atl'D THE SALT SYNDIC- ATE.--The "Standard " says :—A struggle between the chemical manufacturers of Widnes and St. Helens and the Salt Syndicate is intensified every day. The manufacturers of Whines have secured one important advantage. A combination of them have obtained the saltfields on the seaside, at Fleetwood, Lancashire, and in a short time they will he able to supple themselves with all they require. The salt will be conveyed all the way by water at moderate freights. • PRRSENTATION OF A. PORTRAIT TO WIDNES.—An interesting incident occurred at the meeting of the Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday last. At the con elusion of the ordinary business, Mr. Carey stated that at a reception given by Mr. H. Wade-Deacon. in the Town Hall, some time ago, the walls were adorned with two portraits of gentlemen to whom Widnes had been greatly indebted in the past. One of these portraits was that of the late Mr. W. Gossagefather of the present Chairman of the Local Board. and there was a general feeling expressed that that portrait should he permanently hung in the Boardroom. Mr. Corsage was unable to make a gift of the portrait. but he had had a copy made, and if the members were willing, it was ready to be hung on the wall that day. The late Mr. :William Gossage was a gentleman of whom the public of Widnes would ever think of with gratitude and pleasure, end no one was more worthy of honour by the Widnes people.—Mr. Carey proposed that the Chairman's kind offer be accepted.—Mr. S. Sadler seconded the proposition which was carried by loud acclamation, and the portrait was brought into the room and fixed over the mantel- piece at the end facing the chair. Those who had the privilege of the acquaintance of the late gentle- man declare the portrait to be wonderfully life-like, and an accurate copy of the original. It is enclosed in a handsome massive gold frame. and will add much to the dignified appearance of the Boardroom. HAYNES 8 HANDSEWN WATERTIGHT NAVVIES' BOOTS, from 12/6 to 151-. 42 and 44. Horsemarket-st.. Warengton.—Advt.

• A great meeting was held at the Cannon-st., Hotel, London on Wednesday evening, to protest against the Van and Wheel Tax Bill. Lord Dufferin, referring in a speech at Simla to the defence of the Empire, said that the Indian frontier was now in a reasonable state of preparation to resist an attack.

div.head: RUNCORN_ THEATRE ROYAL
div.p: RUNCORN_ THEATRE ROYAL

-- A special session for the purpose of hearing an application for the renewal of the licence to the Theatre Royal, was held at the Police Court on Mon- day. The ma,gistreZes on the Bench were Mr. John Brundrit, chairman; Major Hazlehurst, Messrs. C. Reynolds, A. Thomas and Jas Handley. Mr. Wynne Humphreys, solicitor, said he had again to apply for a license to the Theatre Royal, Runcorn, this time on behalf of Mr. Butter Stanhope, who for the past ten years had been the lessee of the Theatre Royal, Birkenhead. The alterations and repairs required to be made by the magistrates, had been carried out. and the superintendent of police had expressed himself quite satisfied. He (Mr. Humphreys) took it that if Mr. Waldron had applied the Bench would have granted the license as a matter of course, and the only thing he should have to do would be to satisfy them as to the character and qualifi- cation of Mr. Stanhope. Mr Stanhope was determined that the place should bear a high character as regarded the entertainments, and he had spent a considerable sum on repairs and decorations. Hitherto the fees for the license had been very heavy, and he asked the Bench to encourage Mr. Stanhope by reducing the charges as low as possible.—ln reply to Mr. Brundrit he said the total charge would be £2 Bs. 6d.' including the fees for the special session. The charge for the license • alone would be 265. 6d.—Superintendent Hollingworth said the 1 alterations had been carried out as required by the county surveyor. He had made inquiries and Mr. Stanhope was a person.in every way qualified to hold a license.—Mr. Brundrit said the license would be granted and the fee reduced to a guino,.—Messrs. H. Coward and R. Abel became sureties with Mr. Stanhope for the good conduct of the house. From our announcement columns it will be seen that the Theatre Royal will be re-opened this (Saturday) evening with the drama ,‘ Gombeen's Gold," which has been performed before Royalty.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. F. 11. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. E. Carey, T. Handley, D. Wright, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood, It Cook, F. C. Liddell, F. Heyes, J. Taylor, H. Gaskell jun., J. Houghton, S. Sadler. J. T: Allan (clerk), T. 1 Eigginson (surveyor), I. Carr (gas engineer), J. Dickson (nuisance inspector.)

MARSH -BROOK SEWER. Mr. Carey reported that die Committee appointed to deal with the setting up of the sewer, had had an interview with the representatives Of ilutchinson's trustees who had undertaken, as a temporary expedient to flush the sewer at two different places. They hoped 11 that this would do some good.

div.head: SIIND-AY CLOSING.
div.p: SIIND-AY CLOSING.

The Clerk read a petition in favour of the Sunday closing of public houses which had been forwarded for the Board's seal to be affixed.—Mr. Gaskell said he sympathised with the object but he thought it was not a matter that the Board could deal with.—Mr. Heyes agreed with Mr. Gasket'. This Was strictly a political matter, and it was a question upon which there was a great difference of opinion in the community. It would be a pity to introduce an element of discord into the elections of members by electing them on account of their temperance principles or otherwise. Be moved that the letter lie on the table.— Mr. Gaskell seconded the motion which was carried unanimously.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL!.
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCIL!.

The Chairman cies—crrailie steps tfat had been taken to induce the magistrates of Lancashire to give Widnes a better representation on the County Cduncil. The , magistrates of the Wes. Derby Hundred were of opinion that Widnes was being very badly treated and they did all in their power to get an alteration made in the decision of the Committee of the magistrates that had only apportioned Whines Division one member. They , were, however, unable to get, any alteration made; but it was suggested that where the representation was insucient, as in Widnes. Leigh, and Barton, that the membn elected shOuld be made an Alderman at the first meeting of the County Council, and then these divisions would have to send a second member to the Council. Of course they in Widnes were not satisfied with this because they did not feel that it was imperative on the Council to make those gentlemen aldermen, and as far as he was concerned he thought they wonld not do so. He would be speaking the feeling of the Board when he said they should not rest content with what had occurred but that they should in every constitu- tional and proper way follow up this matter until they got that representation which a constituency of 30,000 people, and a constituency yearly increasing in rateable value, demanded. He proposed that a vote of thanks should be accorded to the magistrates of the West Derby Hundred who had so nobly supported the cause of Widnes. The chairman also paid a tribute Ito the strenuous efforts made by the committee of the Board.—Mr. Handley seconded the proposition with pleasure. He was sure that the magistrates who took the matter in hand worked very hard for the interests of Widnes, as did alsck some members of the Board, and especially the Clerk, Mr. Allen.—The motion was carried.

_ GAS AND WATER COSIMITTEE.-PATENTS BY MR. CARE. The minutes of the Gas and Water Committee con- tained the report of the engineer (Mr. Carr) who stated that with regard to the fuel economiser at Stock's Well, he had during the past month checked the quantity of slack now ' being used, and found.the saving to be 18.9 per cent. ov a the consumption previous to the intro- duction of the economiser. The amount saved per annum was 500 tons of slick at ss. 9d., and equalled £143 15s. The mean rainfall for the month was 1-325 inches, and the water in stock was 6,197,732 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month had averaged 18.33 candles. Letters had been received from Messrs. Savce and Randle, alleging damage to Appleton quarry Wall through the lar:ag of ;as main, and giving notice that the Board would be held responsible. In- structions were given to deny liability. Letter, 24th October, from the Dinsmore Gas Co., Limited, enclosing a copy of a resolution passed by them cancelling the charge for the use of their patents under their agree- ment dated 16th July, 1888, because of the services ren- dered them by theadoption of the patents by this Board. Letter, let November, by the said company asking for permission to show their appreciation of Mr. Carr's ser- vices by a suitable recortipense, and stating that all improvements on their patents will be at the Board's service free of charge. Instructions given to thank the Dinsmore Gas Co. for their offer and to ask them to duly endorse the agreement to that effect. Recommended that permission be given Mr. Carr to sell his patents to the Dinsmore Gas Co., Limited.—The minutes were adoped on the motion of Mr. H. Gaskell.

div.head: NEW NAMES FOR OLD STREETS.
div.p: NEW NAMES FOR OLD STREETS.

- The Highway Committee recommended that the fol- lowing alterations be made in the name of streets : John-st., Mill brow, to Parr-st., James-st., Mill brow, to Cliffe-st., Davies-st., Moss Bank. to Brown-st., Elizabeth-st., Moss Bank, to Moss-st., Gerrard-st., Waterloo-road, to Albion-st., Gerrard-st., West Bank, to Wright-st. Recommended that the name of Lugsdale- road be applied to the whole of the road from its junction with Alforde-st. to its junction with Widnes-road at Kaludah terrace.—That the name Warrington-road be applied to the road from its junction with the aforesaid Lugsdale-road to Gorsey-lane, and that the name Halton View be applied to the road from the old level crossing at Mill Brow to the junction of Walter-st. The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Sadler.

NIGHTSOIL REMOVAL. On the recommendation of a joint Committee of the Health and Highway departments, instructions were given to apply to the Local Government Board for per- mission to convert part of the market building into a stable, to enclose a portion of the surrounding land, and for sanction to borrow money necessary for the purpose. Also to borrow money for the cost of five horses and five c.rts, and other minor requirements in connection with the removal pf nightsoil. Mr. John Sadler was instructed to prepare specification, detailed plans and quantities.

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer reported to the Health Committee that during October there were 97 births and 37 deaths being at the respective rates of 38.8 and 14.8 per 1.000. There had been six inquests during the month. In company with the Sanitary Inspector he had visited the manure works at MORS Bank and saw the owner, who promised to do everything in his power to abate the nuisance complained of as arising from his works. A case of typhoid fever and one of smallpox had occurred and both patients were promptly removed to the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital; and so far as he was aware no second case of the latter disease had occurred in the township.—The Sanitary Inspector reported that a case of scarlet fever had also been taken to the Hospital. There were also three children at 21 Sankey-st. suffering from the disease. but the parents refused to have them removed tope Hospital. FINANCE.

The minutes of the irina-n-c-e-Committee which were approved on the motion of Mr. T. Hanley, recommended that application be made to the Local Government Board for sanction to borrow money for the improvement of West Bank-st. and Milton-St. Accounts amounting to £4,396 75. 4d. were passed for payment.
A DISTURBANCE AT _THE_SALVATION . ARMY
CITADEL.

• Before Mr. J. Brundrett and Mr. Charles Reynolds, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, George Shaw, a young man. was charged with having on the 4th inst. conducted himself in an indecent and violent manner in the Salvation k Army Citadel, during the celebration of divine service. His brother James Shaw was charged with assaulting Arthur Plevin, an officer of the Army.—Evidence was given showing that the defendants and several 1 companions are in the habit of attending the meetings of the Salvation Army for the purpose of disturbing the congregation. On the Sunday afternoon in question, George Shaw had an instrument composed of two pieces of tin with a rag placed between, and with this he was makingmost disagreeable noises, and hiscompan- ions were laughing loudly. Ileyin went to him to remon- strate with him on his aiduct, when the brother imme- diately attacked him, and a great disturbance occurred.

The captain and lieutenant, who are women, were so alarmed that they fainted, and the service had to he abandoned for that afternoon. The defendants deined the charges. They admitted having laughed at some- thing one of the women was saying, but were not in possession of any instrument, and there was no disturb- ance until Plevm attempted to forcibly drag George Shaw outside.—The testimony pf the witnesses having been heard. Mr. Brundrit said the cases were clearly proved. If the defendants did not believe in the tenets of the Salvation Army they ought to keep away, and not make a disturbance, which the magistrates believed they had been in the habit of making.—Each defendant was fined 10s. and costs.

div.head: ROSBERIES FROM WIDNES MARKET.
div.p: ROSBERIES FROM WIDNES MARKET.

Charlotte Logan. of Stitnll-1-;;;e: - ;;;;;--b-r-ought before the Widnes magistrates, on Monday, charged with having stolen a pinafory, worth Sid. belong- ing to Alfred Walklr, of Manclvster. The prisoner was further charged with stealing a blacking brush, and a quantity of wool worth Is. 10d., the property of Peter McKinley, of Bridge-st.. St. Helens. On Sat- urday night, the prisoner went to Walker's stall, in Widnes Market, and enquired the prices of various articles. She complained that he "wanted too much," and as she was leaving the stall, P.C. Massey saw her stoop, pick up a pinafore, and place it in her basket. The prisoner then walked away and the Con- stable, keeping a watch upon her saw her take the other articles from McKinley's stall, and place them in her basket. The Constable took her into custody, with the articles in her possession.—The prisoner contended that she had paid for the woll and the pinafore and she was was abour to pay for the brush when the policeman apprehended her. She was fined 20s. in each case, or a month in goal, in default.—William Byers, of Water-st., was charged with having, on various dates in September, stolen four pairs of boots, value 235., the property of Paul Goldstraw, auctioneer, of Liverpool, who is a stall holder in Widnes Market. On the 29th October P.C. Massey went to the prisoner's house to apprehend the prisoner on another charge, and during his search of the premises. he found two pairs of boots, which Goldstraw identified as having been stolen from his stall. Thera were also two pawn tickets relating to boots. The pri- soner acknowledged that he had stolen two pairs of boots and he was sentenced to a month's imprisonment.

NATIONAL LIFE BOAT INSTITUTION. CONCERT AF RUNCORN. A concert, promoted by Mr. and Mrs. Norbury, of Bowdon, was given in Runcorn Public Hall, on Monday evening, with the object of increasing the funds of the Royal Life Boat Institution, of which Mr. T. J. Mitchell, of ELM. Customs, is local hon. sec. The fame of Mrs. Norbury's noble and self- sacrificing labours on behalf of the gallant life- boatmen, had preceded her, and notwithstanding the boisterous state of the atmospheric elements, the hall was well filled with an audience gathered to give her a cordial welcome, and to contribute their mite to an institution in which Runcorn, as a port, and as the home of many a brave sailor, is deeply interested. A capital programme was pre- sented. The recitals of Mr. and Mrs. Norbury formed a conspicuous and most enjoyable part of , the evening's entertainment. Mrs. Norbury exhi- bited a power of expression and a dramatic instinct that stamps the true artist, and after each of .her elocutionary efforts she was re-called by an enthu- • siastic audience, and she bowed her acknowledg- ments. In the murder scene from "Macbeth," and in the 'School for Scandal," her abilities had full scope. and as the tragical Lady Macbeth, and the gay and reckless Lady Teazle, she was equally successful. The parts of " Macbeth " and "Sir- Peter " were ably recited by Mr. Norbury. This gentleman also recited several other pieces, notably • Jud Brownin's account of Rubinstein's piano; which convulsed the audience with laughter owing to the admirable powers of description displayed by the reciter. The musical portion of the enter- tainment was no less deserving of commendation. Miss Zanetti (of Sir Charles Halle's concerts), a vocalist possessing a full clear soprano voice, gave an artistic rendering of "Tell me, my heart." for which she was re-called. Later on the same lady sang "The last rose of summer," with a pathos that called forth a hearty encore, and she raised the audience to a high pitch of enthusiasm by her singing of "Home, sweet home." Mr. Peploe (of the Manchester concerts) is the possessor of a bass voice of good, quality ' and great power, and he gave a capital inter- pretation of "The diver," and "Down in the deep." In response to an encore for the latter song, he sang "The storm fiend" in faultless style. Mr. Daniels, also of the Manchester concerts, contributed "The White Squall" and "The Sailor's grave," in which his expressive tenor voice was heard to great advan- tage. He also sang "Maids of Merry England" in response to an enthusiastic encore, in a charming manner. A couple of duets and a trio completed the , programme. Before the audience departed Mr. Norbury took occasion to thank the audience on behalf of his wife and himself for their hearty applause, and more especially for their kind patron- age of the institute they were advocating. His wife and he had raised about .£3OO towards a new - lifeboat, and had provided a lifeboat fr Ramsey at a cost of .£7OO. ',Applause.) A friend had also given them £3OO towards building a house for the lifeboat at Ramsey and also for providing reading and recre- ation rooms for the lifeboat crew and fishermen. (Applause.) He understood that some people in Runcorn were desirous of providing a mission room for sailors, and he was sure that would be a good thing if it could be accomplished. (Hear, hear.) He wished to state that Mrs. Norbury and himself . would be happy to come to Runcorn to take part in an entertainment for the purpose of raising . funds to carry out that excellent work. (Applause.)

div.head: BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE-
div.p: BRUNSWICK WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVE-
MENT CLASS.

The " Gentlemenl;-E'ven-iii-i"--in connection with the aboi'g took place on Wednesday evening. The room was crowded at the time advertised to start, and after a few remarks by the Chairman (Mr., Simister) the quartette party was called upon to render the piece "Evening," by De Call. This was sung with much expression, and well merited the hearty applause that followed. "Thy Sentinel am I" was next rendered by Mr. J. Birkett,whose sweet and expressive vocalisation was much appreciated. After a recitation by Mr. Rhodes, entitled "The Diver." which was given in masterly style, the Brothers Guest rendered a selection of instrumental music, their effort being a most successful one. Then followed a dramatic selection, Oliver Gold- smith's "She Stoops to Conquer" being the piece set down on the programme. Seven gentlemen members of the class took part in this, and they were listened to with the greatest attention, the only drawback in the piece being its extreme length. The characters represented were "Sir Charles Mar- low," Mr. Molyneaux ; "Mr Hardcastle." Mr. Perm "Young Marlow," Mr. Jones; "Hastings," Mr. Moulton; "Miss Hardcastla," Mr. W. Millington; "Miss Neville," Mr. Wardle; "Maid," Mr. Hayes. Mr. Williams was most successful in his song "The White Squall," and "The Children's Home ;" then followed the old English part song" Here's a Health unto His Majesty," which caused much laughter. Shakespere's "Mark Antony's Oration" was next. recited by Mr. F. Eden, after which Mr. Morris sang "The Three Blind Sailors of Bristol City" and the "Chief Mate's Story," in capital style, and was well 'received. Then followed Bishop s ever fresh "Now by day's retiring lamp." The glee was rendered in a most powerful manner, and the audience testified their appreciation by a hearty round of applause. Votes of thanks to those who had taken part and to the Chairman brought to a close a very pleasant evening. Mr. Millington had charge of the literary, and Mr. J. Birkett the musical, portions of the pro- gramme. Tke decorations were splendidly carried out by Mr. Read. Mr. Wynne -Humphreys pre- sided most ably at the pianoforte.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIMISDAY.—Before Mr. G. Pilkington. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—The following persons were fined Wand costs for drunkenness :—John Moon, Moon-st. ; Mary Lester, Farrant-St. ; Mary Smith, Irwell-st. ; Thomas Flvde, Dixon-st. ; Thomas Fox, Cholmondeley-st. ; Annie Hewitt, Underwood-st. ; Edward Loftus. Water-st, ; Thomas Caulfield, Thomas Finnerty, George Mellon. and Thomas Walsh, New-road, Dutton. Rachel Connoßey, Sankey-st., and John Smith, Irwell-lane, were each fined 108. and costs. For being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart, George Hewitt was fined 7s. 6d, and costs.—Edward Hvnan. Victoria-A., and James Ince, Halebank, were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, in the usual sureties,for creating a breach of the peace. Mary Jane Doyle. Sankey-st., and Sarah Jervis, Water-st.. were similarly dealt with for creating a disturbance in Sankey-st. Terence Doran, of West Bank-st., was also bound over to keep the peace for creating a disturbance, and a warrant was issued against Martha Doran. who was wanted on a like charge. ASSAULT.—Charlotte Beard was summoned for assaulting Eliza Flowers, on the 12th inst. It was alleged that the women were neighbours. and on the date named the defen- dant accused the complainant of having called her a thief, and thereupon knocked her down and severely beat her.—The./ defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months.

On Thursday- Joseph Arch unveiled a bust of Mr. Glad- stone at the Shipley Liberal Club. Mr. Goschen, speaking at West Bromwich on Wednes- day night, replied to Mr. Gladstone's speeches in the Midlands. He said the right hon. gentleman's method .of controversy was to put aside argument with a wave of the hand, to deal in generalities, and to litep the. country in the dark as to his policy.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of raatehes played on Saturday must be sent to the head once, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning

PARR V. WARRINGTON OLYMPIC.—Parr visited Warring- ton with a weak team, to try conclusions with Warring- ton Olympic. The home team won the toss, and Vose started the ball for the visitors. At half-time Parr had scored two miners to their opponents nil. In the second half tkere was plenty of scrummaging but the game elided in a draw—Parr, two minors • Warrington Olympic, three minors. WIDNES Sr. MARY'S V. 4TR L.A.V.—WEsr LANCA.• swizz JUNIOR COP (FIRST RouNn).—The above-named clubs faced each other at Wavertree on Saturday after- noon in very windy weather, to play the first round in the West Lancashire Junior Cup competition. The Volunteers lost the toss, and J. Whelan set the oval rolling with a strong wind. When half-time was called, the score stood—Widnes 1 goal and 1 minor to the Volunteers nil. When the last blow was sounded the visitors proved victorious, the result being lgoal, 1 try, and 3 minors to nil.

RUNCORN V. MANCHRSTRR Roans.—This match took place at Runcorn, on Saturday; but owing to Brazen- dale, H. Hughes, W. Hughes, W. Faulkner, and G. Wainwright being engaged in the inter-county match at Birkenhead, the strength of the home team was greatly interfered with. Throughout the game, however, the play as exceptionally fast, the forwards giving a splendid example of their powers. W. A. Riley obtained the ball in mid-field, and ran in finely, the run being a thoroughly good one. Broady, however, failed to con- vert the try into a goal. Minors were afterwards obtained by the home team, these being secured owing to the long kicking of Riley, Crompton, and Davies. For the Rangers Mehan played a capital and spirited game. In the second half Riley was [he first to show form by putting in a splendid run and a kick, thus forcing a:dead ball. Davies, too, was to the fore, but the Rangers put in the saving clause twice in succession. At the close of play the result was as follows: Runcorn, 1 try 6 minors; Rangers, 1 minor. Wintals v. Swarrox.—The first-named club, having a vacancy on their list, arranged to play a match for the benefit of the Widnes Cricket Club. Mr. 5. Pollitt, of Swinton, visited Widnes, with a team composed entirely of Swinton players, on Saturday afternoon. Widnes could only put a poor team into the field. Farrell kicked oft for his men, and continued pressure lasted for some time, during which several minors were registered. The play now assumed a fast character, each goal being visited in turn, but without any favour- able result. Marsh's shot at goal from a free kick proved a failure. Hartles now attempted a drop at goal, but nothing accrued from it except a minor, as the leather just struck the post. Fortune next favoured the Widnesians, and Farrell managed to secure a goal by a really smart drop. Half time followed, with the scores standing—Widnes, 1 goal and 6 minors, to Swinton 1 minor. In the second half the home team seemed almost to carry everything before them, and were very- successful in their play, adding three tries and nine minor points, while the Swintonians were equally as unsuccessful in not gaining a mark, and were obliged to retreat with a big defeat, the score being— Widnes, one goal, four tries, and 15 minors, to Mr. Pollitt's team one minor.

RUNCORN Recssavion v. Tuzenomr.—On Saturday these teams met on the ground of the latter. The weather was anything but favourable, there being a strong gusty wind blowing. Runcorn won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. A bad return was notice- able, and a line out was formed in the home 25, and the Recreations rushed the ball over, and obtained a touch down. From the kick off, scrimmages followed in neutral ground. A free kick for Tuebrook ensued, and Burton, the Runcorn three-quarters, relieved by a well-judged kick into touch. Edwards essayed a cross run; but his career was checked. This was followed by a similar run on the part of Morris ; but Houghton brought him to earth. Dribbling succeeded this, and the Runcorn team obtained two touch downs almost immediately afterwards. After a free kick to Tuebrook, Burton returned. Vickers put in a dashing run, but owing to the splendid packed game in midfield, and an excellent dribble, Runcorn scored another minor under the posts. Further scrim- mages took place, and S. Houghton arnindst loud cheers dropped a goal for the Recs. Kearsley afterwards secured the ball, and a free kick followed. At half-time the score was; Runcorn, 1 goal 4 minors; Tuebrook, nil. In the second half the home team secured three minors. Morris, Edwards, A. J. Pearson, and Bleasdale played a fine game for Tuebrook, whilst S. Houghton, Cawley, J. Jones, Burton, and Morris were the cream of the Recrea- tion teams. Result.—Runcorn Recreation, 1 goal, 5 minors; Tuebrook, 4 minors. WARRINGTON v. WIGAN' "A " TEASES.—ThO Warring- ton "A " team journeyed to Wigan on Saturday, with the intention of spoiling another record, and succeeded in accomplishing this task. An exceedingly fast game was witnessed. Two 30's, having been agreed upon, and Wigan having won the toss, Lsherwood kicked off against the wind, Hall returning, and Carrington follow- ing well up forced Jolley to touch down. The latter player dropped out, and Mitchinson replied to Warring- ton 25, where he again gained possession and kicked, Wigan being allowed a free kick owing to an infringe- ment of the off-side rule, another minor accruing from the kick at goal by Kearsley. Appleton and Mather gained a lot of ground after the drop out by tall kicks, the latter collaring Halliwell before he could get the oval jaway. Shortly after Jolley received the ball, and scored a deicl ball I'm' the visitors. Halliwell dropped out, and Adamson making his mark Isherwood took the place, but Mitchinson returned to Speakman, who kicked into touch at centre. Holland, Belshaw, and Wells by a smart dribble caused play to be located in Warrington 25, but Hayes, Molyneaux, arid Donohue removed to neutral ground. Appleton now had his kick charged down, and the home forwards again invaded the visitors' quarters,where Kersley was allowed another kick at goal for off-side play, a minor only been registered. Jolley dropped out, and smart following up by F. Bate and Creaghan caused play to rage in the centre, where Speakman put in a grand run and kick, which caused the home team further trouble. From a scrimmage near the posts Lawless passed to Speakman, who dropped at goal, but Yates charged it down, and this player, with Carrington and Hodgson, dribbled to centre. Hayes, Adanason, and Isherwood replied to Wigan 25, were Mather was granted a free kick, and (7r-di:gain, Bate, and Dollolnie Fatalie'mil over the line, only to see Murphy run it out and kick to Appleton. who punted into touch at Wigan quarter flag. Speakman was next prominent with a fine effort and pass to War burton, the pair running the ball up the field' Half-time Was called, the score standing Wigan 3 minors to Warrington 1 minor. After the interval Mitchinson restarted, Jolley returning into touch. Houghton dribbled nicely to the Warrington line, but Speakman replied by a good kick to centre. Williamson put in a spirited run, Lawless bringing him down. Tie visiting forwards went away with a rush to the home line, where from some loose play Adamson kicked to Warburton, who dropped a goal, Mitchinson kicked off, Jolley returning well. A grand pass by Mather to Speakman enabled this player to get away, and finished by passing to Appleton, who ran the oval to the line. Wigan get another free kick, and Warburton being the recipient, had another shot at goal, a dead ball resulting. Creaghan improved matters by a smart dribble, but Hall and Bithell were on the alert, and brought the oval back again Lawless and F. Bate dribbled nicely to Murphy, who kicked to Bibby, this player making a grand run and kick. Warrington were here granted a free kick, a miner being recorded from a kick by Jolley. Molyneaux relieved his line by a good kick, and Bibby put in a smart run to centre. Lawless passed finely to Appleton, who made the run of the day, getting over the Wigan line, Hall pulling him touch-in-goal. Adamson returned the drop-out, and Halliwell and Jolley exchanged kicks, play resting in Wigan 2§, where Warburton and Bibby tried hard to get through, Murphy having ultimately to teach down. After the drop-out, Mitchinson made a grand run and pass to Yates, causing play to rage in the visitors' quarters. Adamson, however,replied by a good kick, and collared Murphy before he could part with the leather. A smart pass by Speakman to Bibby enabled the latter to run to the line, and when time was called, Wigan were having the worst of the game, the score being—Warrington, 1 goal 5 minors; Wigan, 3 minors. Teams :—Warrington : Full back, Jolley; three-quarter backs, Appleton, Speakman, and Bibby; half backs, Lawless and Mather; forwards, Adamson (captain), Donohue, Hayes, ereaghan, Molyneaux, Isherwood, Beard, Eyes, and Warburton. Wigan: Full back, Murphy; three-quarter backs, Hal, Halliwell, and Williamson ; half backs, Mitchinson (captain) and D. Yates ; forwards, Hodgson, Peck. Holland, Carrington, Bithell, Houghton, Belshaw, Wells, arid'

div.head: WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

The first meeting of the season of these strong West Laipashire Organisations took place on Saturday, when a:large crowd assembled at the Wilderspool enclosure, Warrington. The meeting hat been eagerly discussed, as both teams had this season experienced a long series of success. The " wirepullers," as the Warringtonians are familiarly termed, had, up to Saturday's contest, played nine matches without a defeat, having won Seven matches, whilst the two remaining ones had been drawn. amongst their victones may be recorded those of Tyldesly, Rochdale Hornets, Coventry, Askaro- in-Furness, Manchester Free Wanderers, Widnes, and Carlisle; whilst Broughton Rangers and Oldham have been left undecided. On the other hand, Wigan have had a brilliant run, Crompton, Tyldesley, Manningham, Tottington, Kendal Hornets, Widnes, Oldham and

Barrow all having to submit to the colliery representa- tives, whilst only in one instance have they had their flag lowered, and this by a strong team under the direction of Mr. T. R. Sutton of Manchester. Long before the advertised time to kick off crowds wended their way to the spacious enclosure, and every vantage of spacer was occupied. Special trains were run from Wigan, and it was estimated that close on 2,000 joum yed to witness the match. Both sides had repress tatives in the county team against Cheshire, Dillion on the Warring- ton side, and Atkinson on behalf of Wigan. However, the last named was enabled to place a strong team in the field; but Barnes, Handles, and Creaghan were absent from the Warrington ranks. Soon after the advertised time to kick off bothsides made their appearance. It was estimated that nearly 13,000 people were present, and the greatest excitement prevailed. Wigan started against a pretty strong wind, the ball gravitating in touch at the Warrington quarter4lag. A free kick to the Warringtonians allowed the oval to be taken to the half-way flag; but smart play by Seddon placed Wigan at their original position. Free kicks were hereabouts very frequent and a pass from Halliwell to Seddon saw the latter taking an ineffectual drop at goal. From the drop out the Wigan men con- tinued to harrass the Warrington defence, and after give-and-take play, Daniels relieved his side by a smart punt to neutral ground. Not to be denied, the visitors still kept up an aggressive attitude, and although Antrobus, Massey, and Jolley each in turn tried to evade the opposing backs, a good passing motor ment by Seddon, Halliwell, end Bullough finally ended in Hatton scoring the first tangible point for the visitors, Slevin failing to augment the point. On re-starting Fair. Turner put in a tall kick to the Wigan lines, and it seemed as if the Warringtonians were going to equalize straight away. However, wild play afforded relief, and Antrobus with neat work again improved the position of his side, but only a minor point rewarded his efforts. Ashurst responded to the drop out, and although the battle waged fierce on the Wigan line, try as they would the homesters could not cross the line, and half-time was called with the score—Wigan one try one minor to Warrington one minor. On resuming hostilities it was thought the Warringtonians were in fora severe drub- bing. However, this proved incorrect, for against the wind they played with exceptional pluck. Frank Turner started, his brother stopping Slevin in his reply. Free kicks afforded relief to the visitors, but the War- ringtonians would not be denied, and after a fierce struggle under the bar, Halton had his kick charged down, the ball ultimately going over the bar. A loud cheer welcomed what was thought to be a goal, but the disappointment was great Nshen it was announced that only a.minor point had been recorded. This piece of bad luck did not discourage the " wirepullers," for again the Wigan citadel was threatened. Antrobus and Speak- man were to the fore with some pretty work, and although Daniels was afforded a chance of exhibiting his skill he was easily stopped by the smart tackling of Seddon. Jolley was to the fore with smart kicks, and although Slevin neutralized by a smart kick to the Warrington quarter-flag, Antrobus and Jolley by pretty exchanges again placed the visitors on the defence. The Wigan team now had a turn, and a strong kick by Slevin was quickly followed up by Hunter, and a misunderstanding by the home backs allowed the Wigan man to score a some- what easy try, Halton failing at goal. Seddon responded to the kick-off, and passing by Antrobus, Evans. and Jolley again gained ground, Topping afterwards saving. The game was now virtually over, and though the War- ringtonians tried all in their power tq gain the lead, they could not keep thevisitors out of thelr2s,and a drop at goal by Halton forced another minor. Eventually the game concluded as follows :—Wlgan, 0-2-4; Warrington, 0-0-3.

Undoubtedly the 'defeat of the Warringtonians can only be attributed to the combination of the team being disturbed. The display on either side was anything but brilliant, and taken on the whole the match was many degrees below that of the previous week against Brough- ton Rangers. The forwards were beaten time after time, both in the pack and loose, and the exclusion of Randles and Creaghan from the team came in for some severe criticism. Massey played splendidly at full back, and the high opinion formed of him a few weeks ago was certainly justified. Of the three-quarters Jolley and Evans did fairly well, but Daniels was outclassed. Antrobus was the pick of the half backs, whilst in the forward division, Fair. Turner, Ashton, and Littlewood are deserving of credit. On the Wigan side Slevin, Sed- don, Halliwell, and Wardle are worthy of notice. The following were the teams :—Warrington: Massey, back; DanioLs, Evans. and Jolley. three-quarter backs; Speakman and Antrobus, half backs; Fair Turner, Ash- ton, Povey, Littlewood,Nevins,Frank Turner, Unsworth, Ashurst, and Holmes, forwards. Wigan: Topping, back; Slevin (captain), Seddon, and Bullough, three- quarter backs; Hunter and Halliwell, half backs; Cat- terall, Wardle, Lowe, Halton, Hatton, Dempsey, Swift, Telford, and Bibby, forwards. Referee Mr. Lord, Broughton Rangers.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The county match, Lancashire y 7 Cheshire, which took place on Saturday. at Birkenhead, was a very one- sided affair. Cheshire were "not in it," and Lancashire overwhelmed them with a score of eight tries and one minor to nil. A more decisive score than this could scarcely havo been wished for, and the score pretty well indicates the game. It was not a case of ill-luck on one- side endpoints on the other, as the game was one-sided from beginning to end. Mr. W. Dillon has again been selected to represent his County in the match Lancashire v. Northumberland, to be played at Newcastle to-day (Saturday.) The St. Helens Associationists met and decisively defeated Southport High Park by six goals to two. The visitors came with a splendid reputation, but they were over-matched from start to finish. The winners played a better game than on any previous occasion during the present season' and an improvement in the combined play is evidenced each week. Eeriest iwn journeyed to Bolton on Saturday to play the return match with the Bolton Rovers, who received a " drubbing "at Earlestown, earlier in the season, by about a dozen goals to one. This was net the difference in the scores last Saturday, but the play was almost as one-sided, as Earlestown pressed during the greater portion ctf the time, but could only manage to win by Ulna goals to on. • he Haydock club occasiorOla national surprise in the football world on Saturday, by their victory over the famous Darwen team in the Lancashire Senior Challenge Cup competition. The match was played at Haydock, but not a single individual anticipated the success of the home eleven. However, the colliery lads rose to the occasion, and playing with great determination and energy were finally declared the winners of the most exciting match in the history of the Haydock club by three goals to two. . .

The St. Helens (Rugby) Club were opposed by Stock- port on the Denton's Green enclosure, on Saturday, but, as in other places throughout the country, the new rules interfered with the ordinary play. No major points were scored, St. Helens having six minors to Stockport three, at the call of "No Side." It is rather singular to note that•all the St. Helens points were notched in the first half ,and the visitors' in the second period. Early in the second half Dearden, one of the home players, met with an accident by which one of his arms was broken. The home eleven had the best of the play, but had hard lines in several attempts to score. . . _ _

The St. Helens Recs. had Lancaster as their "guests," but the latter came shorthanded—or shortfootedf—and with two substitutes only numbered 14. Nothwithstand- ing this drawback, an interesting game was played and the victory of the Recs. was a popular one. Playing with the wind in the first half the home team "piled on the agony "to the extent of two goals and eight minors to nil. The visitors were unable to make any dangerous headway in the second period, and finally retired beaten by two goals one try and nine minors, without a single point to their credit.

It is proverbially a rather dangerous operation to "change horses while crossing a stream," and in football it is equally risky to make much of a change in the ordinary team just before playing an important match. A chan,ge of this kind may be said to have,at least to a certain extent, led to the defeat of Warrington by Wigan on Saturday. The alteration was,of eourse,to some extent compulsory, as W. Dillon. one of the best forwards, had been selected for county honours, but Barnes and Bandies and Cragan were a good deal missed. The absence of three or four of the ordinary players impaired the combination of the home team, and gave a good opportunity to the " colliers " for breaking the hitherto unbroken record of the "wire-pullers," which they accordingly did. It is quite certain that the new Rugby rules are not winning enthusiastic approval, and one is inclined to believe that the game between Warrington and Wigan would have been a more interesting affair had it been under the old remulations. There was 'very little in it of what is sometimes called " scientific " play, and the continual keeping of the ball in motion seemed adverse to sustained combination. More practice may remedy this, but as yet the new code has not by any means been unanimously endorsed by the spectators, who, after all, I as they supply the "sinews of war," are the mainstay of football as of other popular games.
