THE MANCHESTEIt SHIP CANAL.
GENERAL PROGRESS.

I On Wednesday it was just .twelee months since the first sod of the canal was cut. On the 11th of November last year a number of the Directors went over to Eastham and inaugurated the great work. Nothing could have been more simple than the ceremony. There was not a flag, not a note of music, net two words of a speech, h A even a cheer. A spade which had seen some service, and bad neither an lebony handle nor a silver blade, was handed to Lord Egerton by Mr. Walker, the con- tractor, and with this honest. implement the Chair- man of the Company, without 'Apra ado, delivered the first sod from its mother earth. The spade passed in turn to the other Directors, and each cut a sod. Mr. Leader Williams, the engineer, tipped a barrow containing the product of these labours, and, the ceremony was at an and. The minute recording the proceedings states that the Directors afterwards discussed "ordinary business." The neoessary rude- flees and bareness of all this is relieved by a single touch of sentiment. The spade with whieh the first sods were cut finished its work that morning, and now hangs, we believe, in Tatton Hall. Mr. Walker lost no time in buckling to his work. For some time he had been getting materials together, and within a week of the inauguration ceremony he had two thousand men on the ground. As the opera- tions opened out, the forces were gradually increased, and at present the number of men is over 10.000. The men, however, represent but a small portion of the force brought to hear in this great digging enterprise. The bulk of the excavation is being done by the steam digger, and of these mighty workers 85 have been pressed into service. Three of them are of German make, two come from France, and the rest are of English construction. In addition to these, 100 locomotives and 5,000 waggons are constantly at work, and the lines of rails put down for temporary purposes cover about 200 miles. So much effective strength has never before been brought to bear upoa a contract of this kind, and as a matter of course the amount of work. done has been enormous. The whole course of the canal is now in outline, and in some places the excavation is in a rough way complete. The progress made during the year is. we believe, regarded as emin- ently satisfactory, and. there is every reason to believe the work will be finished to time. Mr. Walker has a name for getting done' within the limit of his contract, and in the present undertaking his reputation is involved as it never was before. It was on the site of the entrance locks that the Direc- tors cut the first sods. The particular spot has long since disappeared, and the whole look of the place has changed The excavation in the great lock has been carried down to the invert level, a depth of about fifty feet. Further excavation will be necessary for founda- tion purposes, but the work is so far forward that tbe construction of the lock gates is in progress. It is duff. cult to give readers an idea of the great red gulf the steam digger has made here. The width of it is about 400 feet, and the average depth 35 or 40 feet. Its width of 400 feet it keeps for a distance of about 600 feet—the length of tbe largest of the three locks—and then tapers off into the ordinary width of the canal. In construct- ing locks of different sizes the engineer is, of course, not open to the charge made against the man who drove a large hole in his kitchen door for the cat and a smaller one for the kittens. Vessels of small tonnage could of course enter by the great lock, but it would be at an unnecessary expense of Water. The great red gulf we speak of is a scene of enormous activity, and in fare of the blinding smoke of locomotives and steam diggers it is not easy to grasp the details At the lowest level the new red sandstone has been reached, and the final exca- vation will have to be done by blasting. But as a great , deal of stone will be needed here for building purposes, lit is no doubt convenient to have it at hand. Most of I the marl and stone now coming out of this vast quarry , goes towards Poole Hall, where the canal has to be taken across a deep bight in the coast line. Some progress has been made with this work, but the embankment is not vet above high-water level. The number of men on the hastham section is about 1,000, and for their accom- modation a village ,of wooden houses has sprung up lunder the shelter of the hill. A new chapel, on much more handsome lines than the first hasty erection, has been built, and under the auspices of Mr. Morris, one of the contractor's agents, a reading-room has now been provided. Between Ellesmere Port and Holpool Gutter the exca- vation has in various places been taken out to the full depth of the canal. Between Holpool Gutter and Weston Point the German steam digger has done good work, and is to have the assistance presently of one on the French system. The sluices at the river Weaver are to be started soon, and at the lock at Weston Marsh the work is so far forward that the concreting of the walls is now going on. On the Runcorn section progress is most noticeable at No Man's Land. Between Randle's Sluices and Latchford a great deal of blasting has been done, the rock coming nearer the surface here than at some other points. The diversion of the Mersey at Latchford Locks has been finished, and a start has been ' made with the railway deviation, which begins at a point near Warrington and ends at Thelwall station. Section N 0.7 was the last section to begin work, but in the four months much has been done, especially in the excavation of' the Irlam locks and the work connected with tho deviation of the Cheshire Lines Railway. The docks at Salford are in a forward state. As readers know, they are to consist of three branches open- ing out of the canal, which at this point is much wider than usual. The excavation of the mid branch is nearly complete, and on the Trafford-road side the concreting of the wall is in progress. The other branches are not so far advanced. The river will give some trouble at this point, and extensive works are in progress to take it out of the way for a time. The material dug ou; at Salford is mainly gravel, with clay and rock a the bottom. The gravel and rock will be used in making the concrete walls. The rest of the spoil is in part deposited on land near the Racecourse, and in part sent down towards Stickins Island, where the diversion of the river is now complete. To a wonderful extent the various sections have so far turned out, as one might say, self-contained, each able to use up and dispose of its own spoil ; and in a work extending over so many miles this is, of course, a matter of no small consequence STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

The German navvy in its new position is making con- siderable headway, the soil being extremely light and sandy, and the cutting it is engaged in making deepens rapidly. The spoil excavated is removed by rail to Acton Grange, where it is tipped on the spoil banks. The recent wet weather has flooded the old Runcorn Canal, and under Twenty Step Britt) the line of rails is submerged in a pool nearly two feet deep. The American navvy which has been for some time standing opposite St. Thomas's Church has been taken to pieces and removed to another section. One of the two excavators at the head of the cutting, near the Chester-road, has also been removed to about one hundred yards further back, along the cutting, where it is engaged in widening the proposed channel of the canal. The navvy engaged in commencing a second lift at Morley Common has extremely hard werk,and on account of the heavynature of the soil is unable to cut very deep.

_ MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE. On the Moore section, operations are almost entirely confined to the spoil banks. In the early part of the year the work was so raiply pushed on that the greater part of the work (that of excavation) is almost corn- pleteci. On the Runcorn side of the level crossing at Moore, a large amount of labour is being employed. At Acton Grange, where rock is being worked along the whole length of the section, the excavations progress in a steady, if slow fashion. The railway embankment has now reached a considerable height and is plainly visible from the other side of the present railway.

THE STRONGEST E IDEN CE. From The Blackburn Times. William Henry Holden, residing at 26 Whalley Old-road; Blackburn, has ever since 1872, at fre- quent intervals, been aubjeoted to indescribable suffering, owing to attacks of intense pain and swelling in his feet. Everything that was recom- mended for the ailment, which was of an acute rheumatic nature, was used; but the remedies applied proved futile. A few weeks ago, Mr. Holden, hearing how the life of Mr. William Buchanan, one of the Cunard Steamship Company's engineers, had been saved by St. Jacobs Oil, after he had been given up by the Liverpool doctors to die, and had been at times deprived of his reason by suffering, resol- ved to try this Oil, and procured a bottle from Jackson and Co., chemists. To his utter amassment, and that of all the members of his family, the excruciating pain and terrible swellings left after only a few applications of the remedy had been made, and he young man is now free from his sufferings. "The change brought about by this bottle of St. Jacobs Oil is simply wonder- ful," remarked Mr. Holden, "and I gladly state that it has done more in a single minute than all the remedies we had used before that time had accomplished in four- teen years. This may seem like a broad statement, but it is the plain, simple truth." It may here be stated that the leading newspapers of Manchester and Liver- pool have recently reported similar remarkable cures. Among these is that of Mr. John Tetlow, a well-known resident oT Oldham, who had long been so seriously afflicted with rheumatism that he was unable to walk. He was bent with agony. A single bottle of St Jacobs Oil effected such a marvellous change that he is not only free from pain, but, although sixty years of age, he can walk as well as ever. So delighted was he with his relief, that he personally sent a testimonial to the pro- prietors, The Charles A Vogeler Co., 45 Farringdon-rd., London, with full permission to have such use made thereof as they wished. The case of Mrs. Ann Watson, of Upper Pitt-st., Liverpool, is another instance. The lady writes that she had been entirely deprived of the use of her feet owing to rheumatic troubles of long- standing. Physicans could do nothing for her, and all- medicines which she used were without avail. St Jacobs Oil was finally used with the same astonishing results as in the instances above reported. She can walk as well as ever, and is in perfect health. Facts like the foregoing speak for themselves. And it must be admitted by all, that so valuable a discovery as that herein referred to deserves to be made known every- where.

div.head: SAN KEY DROWNING MYSTERY.
div.p: SAN KEY DROWNING MYSTERY.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Black Horse Inn, Sankey Bridges, on Tuesday, touching the death of Catherine Davenport, aged 28, whose body was found on Saturday morning, floating in the Sankey Canal, near Bewsey Lock.— Hannah Davenport, mother of the deceased, said she lived at 48, Rolleston-street. Her daughter was 28 years of age, and had been living with her since February last, excepting at intervals when she went away for her health. On Friday evening her daughter was rather low-spirited, but occupied herself with household duties until about half-past six, when she went out, after getting ready the tea. She did not return and witness looked for her, but, as she was not to be found, she thought that she might hqve gone to spend the night with one of her friends. Next morning, however, witness heard that her daughter was at the Black Horse, Sankey Bridges, and, on going there, found that she was dead. Witness did not think that deceased had any idea of taking away her life. She had, however, very bad health, being troubled with chronic bronchitis, and she was also troubled about not easily getting a place as domestic servant. Witness did not know of any one who bore I the deceased any ill-will. The girl knew the way to the I lock perfectly, having been for some time a servant at Mrs. Chorlev's, of Bewsey.—William Leigh, carpenter, Dallam, saia he was going to his work at about 7.30 on Saturday morning, along the canal bank, when he saw the body of the aeceased floating on the water about thirty yards above Bewsey lock. The top of the head andthe dress of thedeceased were visibleabout twoyards from the banks. He thought that the feet must have been resting On the bottom, as the canal is there rather shallow. Hewent and informed the lockman,and together they get the body out of the water.—P.C.Dugdale, said he was called to the spot and searched the body. He found only some papers which he produced.—The Coroner announced that the papers contained nothing which could have any reference to the cause of death.—Mary Farrell deposed to laying out the body of the deceased. She found no marks of violence whatever on the body. After considera ion the jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned."

div.head: MAYOR AND CORPORATION OF
div.p: THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION OF

WARRINGTON AT CHURCH. In accordance with the announcement made at the Council meeting last week, the Mayor of Warrington (Alderman. Sutton), following a time- honoured custom, attended the Parish Church on Sunday morning, and was accompanied by many members of the Town Council, Corporation officials, and others. A procession was formed in front of the Town Hall about ten o'clock and proceeded to the Parish Church in the usual order. First came the police under the direction of the Chief Constable (Mr. Samuel Hunt), the force consisting of two inspoc tors—Sphiks and Cox—four sergeants Bowen, Rowbottam, Shaw, and Cheney and 26 constables. The firemen, ten in number, followed, being under the direction of Superintendent Turner. The Mayor came next having on his right his chaplain (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), aad on his left the Deputy Mayor (Alderman Pickmere), and behind them walked the following members of the Corporation :—Aldermen Webster, Burgess, Davies, and Chandley ; Councillors F. A. Roberts, Jolley, Flood, Francomb, John Pierpoint, Joseph Taylor, Askton, Monks, Marsh, Blackhurtt, Wright, Percival, Hutchinson, Greenall. Shaw-Green, Tinsley, Bolton, and Jenkins. The following gentlemen brought up the rear: Messrs. Thomas Longdm (borough surveyer);John Fairhurst, jun. (collector), F. Taylor (secretary of the gas department) W. S. Haddock (gas engineer), G. F. P. White (deputy magistrates' clerk), D . Jones, D. W. Finney, Thomas Morris, William Molyneux (Wolverhampton), G. Griffiths, Stanley Higham, T. 0. Speakeman, Alfred , Jolley, James Smethurst, Robert Isherwood; John Griffiths, and John Allen. At the Parish 'Church there was a large congregation. The prayers were read by the Rev. B. J. Willcocks, the lessons by the Rev. C. E. Jackson, curate, and the Litany by the Rector. The sermon was preached by the Rev. S. Wilkinson, who selected for his text the words, "For our conversation is in heaven" (Phillipians ill. 20). In concluding his sermon the rev, gentleman said: This morning you come here as a Corporation, and in your corporate capacity you can do very much for the advancement of God's cause and for the benefit of your fellow-men. ' I am glad to say that, taken as a whole, the Mayors of England do all they possibly can for the good of their fellow-towns- men ; and in this respect we have been especially fortunate in the town of Warrington. Ever since I hen known this town I have always found the Mayors most kind, sympathetic, and generous towards every good work which is taken in hand; and surely we must aH acknowledge that our present Mayor, my old friend, and people's churchwarden at St. Paul's, certainly stands out pis-eminently fer what he has done to benefit his fellow - townsmen. We must remember that it is a good thing to have a sound mind in a sound body, and I think the Corporations of our towns can do a great deal towards the promo- tion of the health and happiness and the morality of the inhabitants. For example : the Mayor and Corporation can do very much towards promoting the cleanliness of the town, and it is very true that cleanliness is next to godliness. And then they can do much for the promo- tion of decency, by seeing that our houses are not overcrowded, and in supplying our borough with good and pure water, which is such a very important matter In everyday life. And much can be done with regard to the lighting of the erects. And then, again, much can be done in exercising a wholesome control over the licensed -victuallers' houses, and by providing wholesome literature in our free library for the benefit and use of all the inhabitants. I believe in all these works the Corporation can do much for the promotion of God's glory and for the benefit of their fellowmen. Of course, I know perfectly well that in all these works there will be opponents, and that when the Corporation undertake any great work for thegood of the inhabitants, especially if it be of an expensive character, then there will be some who will find fault. But, after all, I am quite certain that the Mayor and Corporation , will have the sympathy and the support of the great majority of the ratepayers, and what I say to you, dear brothers, is this—Go on in the good work in which you have been engaged for so many years, go on fearlessly and boldly; and if you do what is right in the end they will acknow- ledge the wisdom of your proceedings, and real good will be done.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT WAR- RINGTON.

The annual meeting of the Conservatives of the North-west Ward was held in Rolleston-st. school on Monday evening. Major Litton presided and amongst those on the platform were Mr. T. Fielaing (of the National Union), the Rev. EL Wilkinson, Councillor J. Pierpoint, and Mr. J. Roberts.

THE JUNCTION' Or CHAIRMAN. • Mr. J. Roberts moved that Major Litton be re-elected chairman of the Ward Committee for the next twelve months. Referring to the position of Conservatism in the town, he said he was sure that when the time came round they should again return their good old friend, Sir Gilbert, or someone in his stead. (Applause.) He was sure they should feel it very deeply at heart when their good old friend, Sir Gilbert, disappeared, and he hoped they ,should have him for many years to come to represent the 'borough. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. Banner seconded the propesal. There was no doubt, he said, that Major Litton was a good Conservative at heart. There were some shams going about—Many of them in fact—but Major Litton said what he meant and meant what he said. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Banner) would say this unreservedly—that Mr. Glad- stone had been one of the greatest humbugs the world oversaw. (Laughter.) If he had done nothing else, with all the great qualifications for which he was held p as a model, there was one bad act he had done which all his good acts rolled into one would not counteract, and that was the granting of outside beer and wine licenses. That had done more harm than anything else that had ever happened in this country. (Hear, hear.)—Councillor J. Pierpoint, in supporting the proposal, referred to the recent municipal elections and the agreement that they should be non-political, and , said that, with respect to one side, he could vouch that I that agreement had been adhered to. The Conserva- tives did not even hold a ward meeting, and they never gathered together for the purpose of nominating candi- dates, and they took no active part in returning mem- bers of their own party. But what did the other side do? They held their ward meeting, although they pro. I mised faithfully they would not act politically. If they would heed him they would not trust the other side, as they were always ready to hold their hole-and-corner meetings. The cat was let out of the bag: with respect to the north-west Ward when one of tho leading members of the Liberal party supported the selection of the two candidates on political grounds. The two north-west ward candidates were brought out politically and not as nominees of the Ratepayers' or any other Association. (Hear, hear.) It was therefore necessary for the Con- servatives to look about and not to trust the other party with too great length of rope, or they might depend upon it they. would do some act of dishonesty with respect to electioneering, as they (the Conserva- tives) had had so many opportunities of seeing they would do. (Hear, hear.)—Major Litton vjas then unani- mously re-elected chairman of the ward, and, after acknowledging the compliment, referred briefly to the general political situation.
_ELECTION OF OTHER OFFICERS.

Messrs. John Roberts, J. Sriiethurst, J. Pierpoint, T. Jolley, and J. Houghton were elected vice-presidents; and Messrs. J. Hough, J. Thornton, G. A. Ward, J. Peers, R. T. Smith, and J. A. Simpson, were appointed delegates to the Council of the Conservative Association. The captains of districts and working committee were re-elected with power to add to their number.

INDEPENDENT ORDER OF ODD. FELLOWS, M.U. A lecture on "The History 'of Oddfellowship Origin and Progress of the Manchester Unity," was recently given by Bro. W. B. Doig, Pro. C.S., of the Birkenhead district, to the members of the Prince of Wales Lodge, Warrington district. Towards the close of the lecture he said :--Between the years 1827 ansl 1838 the Order took firm rout in the minds of the industrial portion of the population of this country, and had by this time bean introdueed into Wales. A great many of the old societies of Odd- fellows had now joined the Manchester Unity. From 300 lodes belonging to the Order in 1827, the number had increased during ' the ten years to 1,500 lodges, and nearly 100,000 members. In October, 1840, a dispensation was granted and sent to Sydney, New South igales, and the first lodge was named "The Strangers' Refuge." Since then the Order has progressed to a very large extent in the Colonies, and many of our brethren have had cause •to rejoice in its existence In such a distant clime. From 1838 to 1844 the society steadily increased in numbers, many of the leading members of the Order mean while endeavouring to inculcate a system of- sounder principles of financial reform; and at the A.M.C. held this year at Newcastle, many very important measures were adopted for the benefit of the unity, several of which the speaker referred to, and also reviewed the progress which had been, made during the past 24 years. On the let of IJanuary, 1865, the number of members was returned at 373,509, with an accumulated capital of £2,000,0009 or a little over ..£5 10s. per member. The returns of 1870 showed the number of member.: returned as 376,580, and from lodges not sending their returns, 33,823; total, 410,403; and a capital of £2,558,735. On let January, 1881, the numbers .were returned as 508,013, and capital £4.881,456, or an average of £9 2s. GO. On the Ist January, 1888, the numbers were 627,594 members ; total capital, including all funds, £6,806,736, an increase of capital am ce 1864 of £4,806,736, and an increase in members of 254,085: During 1887 there was paid in sick benefits £535,989 18s. 7d., being an average pay- ment of 17s. Bid. per member; for funeral claims. £130,646 18. 10d., or an • average of 4s. 20. per member; received in. contributions, £666,712 Os. 9d.. or an average payment of £1 is. Which is the exact average payinent to members for benefits ; but the interest on invested capital realized during the same year was £2.31,747 ss. id., or an average rate. of interest of £3 18s. Hid. per cent., or equal to an annual contribution of 7s. 50. per member. (Applause.) A hearty vote of thanks to Bro. Doig brought the meeting to a close

THE ALLEGED MURDER AT WIDNES. PRISONER BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. Thew Widnes murder case was taken a stage further on Tuesday, when the prisoner John Broome was brought before Mr. Brock, at Widnes Police Court. On Saturday,. the 3rd inst., Broome vas, committed for 'trial on the Coroner's warrant on the charge of manslaughter, but he was now accused of the mere serious crime of wilful murder, although the evidence adduced differed little, and that not materially,from the evidence offered to the Coroner's jury. At the inquest the prisoner exhibited a keen interest in the itestimony of the witnesses, each of whom he scanned narrowly, atid lie was in frequent consultation with his solicitor, Mr. Rideal, through- out the inquiry. His week's experience of life in gaol appeared to have had a considerable effect ' upon him. Although no alteration could be dis- covered in his personal appearance, he seemed to have undergone severe mental suffering, and his , demeanour was *aim even to listlessness. From I entering the prisoner's dock, to leaving it for the cell below, he maintained one attitude, and beyond glancing occasionally at the numerous witnesses examined, he kept his eyes fixed upon Mr. Lewin, the magistrates clerk, as that gentleman recorded in black and white the links in the chain of evidence against him ia the sad and unfortunate tragedy. There were no spectators of the encounter that resulted in the death of Maley, and the charge was built entirely upon statements made by the prisoner himself just after the occurence, The facts, which were given at length in this journal last Saturday, may thus bo briefly recapitulated. For a period of six years the prisoner, whose home is at Appleton village, had been employed at the works of Messrs. Mort, Liddell and Co., chemical manufacturers, latterly as a blacksmith's striker. Thomas Maley, the victim of his alleged violence was a man 63 years of ago, and occupied the position of foreman fitter at the same works, and although he lodged at 76, Church-street, Widnes, for convenience, his residence was at 2 Station-road, Sutton, St. Helens. On Monday afternoon, the 29th October, Maley went to the general office and made a statement to Mr. Thomas Glover, the manager of the works. At this time Maley was bleeding from the nose and had a wound on his hand. In consequence Mr. Glover had an interview with the prisoner, and asked him if it were true that he had struck Maley. - The prisoner replied "Yes; he had the hammer in his hand and he was going to hit me, and if I had not struck him in self-defence ho would have hit me with the hammer." As he admitted striking a person in authority over him, Mr. Glover at once discharged the prisoner, who, however, was brought face to face with Maley. Mr. Glover again asked, "Did you strike Maley "; and the prisoner replied, "Yes, I did, and I have- not finished yet"--a statement which • caused Maley to remark "If you had not taken me unawares, you would not have done this." "Are you ready now," exclaimed the prisoner, putting himself into a pugilistic attitude, but he was restrained by Mr. Glover, who told him it was cowardly to strike an old man. Broome then left to go to the office for his wages, and afterwards Mr. Glover met the prisoner in tho yard, and understood him to threaten that he would wait outside for Maley. He therefore advised Maley not to go home by the usual way. At about ten minutes to six, two hours after the alleged assault, F. H. Roberts, fitter and turner, ' found Maley in the fitting shop in an unconcious state, and he had him removed to his lodgings in a cab. During the afternoon the prisoner informed ' Austin Young, of Church-st., Farnworth, that he had been "sacked for snouting, old Tom." and he told another workman named John Prescott, of 110 Albert- rd., that he had got "sacked for warming old Tom." The prisoner also boasted to Win. Crillon, foreman labourer in the black ash department, that he could use his fists to different men to Maley, and added "The old —has not done with it yet." The only cause sugges- ted for this ill-feeling is that on the morning of the day in question Maley complained of the manner in which the prisoner had cleaned a flywheel, and threatened that he" would find him another job some of these morn- ings." On Tuesday the prisoner absconded from the town, but he was quickly discovered at the house of Mrs. Winters, in Orford-st., Warrington, and he was taken into custody by P.S. Robinson on a charge of unlawful wounding; but Maley died early on Wednesday morning and the matter assumed a more serious aspect. Dr. Hutchinson, assisted by Dr. O'Keeffe, made &pose mortem examination of the body, and these gentlemen deposed that the cause of death was rupture of a blood vessel in the head, and consequent effusion of blood and compression of the brain. The deceased was predis- posed to rupture, and a slight blow would have caused the rupture. Strong excitement, without a blow or a fall, might have caused the rupture.--The prisoner, who reserved his defence, was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes, on the charge of wilful murder.—Mr. Rideal applied that the prisoner should be liberated on bail. He mentioned that the prisoner had a wife and four or five children, and- he had testimonials as to his character and respectability from Dean Finegan, of Appleton, and from a number of neigh- bours--Superintendent Johnson pointed out that the prisoner absconded to another town when the case did not seem so serious as it did now.—After some consider- ation the magistrate decided to grant the application,the prisoner to be bound over in £lOO and two sureties of £5O each. Before , accepting the bail, however, the police were to be perfectly satisfied that the prisoner would be produced at the Assizes.

ROYAL VISIT TO DERBY.—The Prince of Wales visited Derby School on Wednesday' and inspected the building erected as a memorial of his previous visit, sixteen years ago, when he was accompanied by the Princess. The streets were crowded, and the Prince was welcomed heartily not only by the people of Derby but by the students. An address of welcome was delivered by the headmaster, the choir sang "God bless the Prince of Wales," and His Royal Highness was presented with a list of honours gained by the school during the past twenty years. Afterwards he drove to the races with his host, Lord Hindlip. The Prince after concluding his visit to Derbyshire went on to Burton-on-Trent on Thursday, and made a tour of Allsopp's breweries, returning to London by special train in the afternoon.

FATALITY ON THE RAILWAY.—On Thursday forenoon, Robert Howard, 50, met with a shocking death on the Bolton and Liverpool line, near West Leigh Station. Deceased was a labourer, and about nine o'clock went along the line to see the foreman platelayer. How he met with his death is a mystery, the accident not being known until the body was discovered. •

THE "WELLS LIGHT."—A short description of one of the latest systems of outdoor illumination will interest contractors, railway men, and others who are on the look out for cheap and simple methods of lighting. There is a great need for a powerful light which can be set to work without waiting for dynamos or machinery, and which can be readily moved about without breaking any connections or stopping tho light. This need is apparently supplied by the I! Wells Light," which gives a continuous light of about 3,000 candle power, and can be carried about by two men. It consists of a small air-tight steel tank which contains the oil, and from which rises a stand-pipe connected to a generating burner. The oil is forced up the pipe by pneumatic pressure obtained by a small hand pump which also serves to pump in fresh oil when needed. The oil is turned into gas by the heat of its own combustion, and burns in a large white brush-shaped flame which is so powerful that no wind affects it, and which is said to cast no unpleasantly sharp shadows. The whole apparatus appears very simple and strong, and must of necessity be so, since it is used in many important work- ings throughout the kingdom and is generally under the charge of navvies or labourers. The cost of light- ing is, we understand, almost nominal, a specially pre- pared cheap oil being used and burned as before noticed in the economical state of superheated gas. This oil cannot explode, and, being burnt as gas, it never gets I thrown about as in the case in some lamps. We may mention that all the night work done on the Manches- ter Ship Canal has been carried out by means of the "Wells Light," and the proprietors, A. C. Wells and Co., of London and Manchester, are constantly receiving repeat orders from all parts.

THURSDAY HALF-HOLIDAY AT RUNCORN.

- Sir,—The drapers deserve great praise for the way in -which they are keeping the Thursday half-holiday move- ment in this town. If they can close their shops, why cannot all the rest (ironmongers, stationers,grocers, ace.) do it? It wsuld be a great boon to those who are at present working from 8 o'clock Monday morning till U and 12 on Saturdays. Hoping somebody will take the natter up,—l am yours truly, G. H.
Runcorn, Nov. 14th, 1888. WANTED—A PILLAR LETTER-BOX FOR LATCH- FORD.

Sir,—lt has long been ;--n;tter of surprise to the writer, and many other residents on Koutsford-road, Latchford, that no convenience in the shape of a pillar letter-box is provided for the inhabitants along and around this populous and leading thoroughfare. Surely it is but necessary to direct the attention of our postal authorities to this matter to ensure the provision of such accommodation. As near as possible to the site of the late St. James's Mission House would, no doubt, be a good position. Possibly some of your readers interested may add their testimony in favour of the above to that of CORRESPONDENT.

DANGEROUSLY DARK, AND DIRTY STREETS. Sir,—Will you permit me through the medium of your paper to ask the Paving Committee and the Sanitary Authority, if something cannot be done to enlighten the darkness, and to improve the state of the streets and lanes in the neighbourhood of Bank Quay. From Green- St. down Mill-lane, the streets on the right hand side, together with the lane itself, are in a deplorable condition, and on dark evenings, give us a tolerable idea of "Egyptian Darkness." Posts are set up on each side which are really dangerous, for in trying to avoid stick- ing fast in mud you are nearly certain to come in contact with one of those wooden nuisances. Coming back up Mill-lane and entering Lovely-lane, we find the streets on the right and left are dreadful. We notice Selby-st., Price-st., and Earnest-st. where fever was rife a short time ago. Drains are laid, but the grids being mostly above the level of the streets, instead of taking in the water, it is thrown off on the streets in pools, which when absorbed, leave a sediment, which must be detrimental to the health of the seig,hbourhood.—yours 44r.c , Bank Quay, Nov. 14th,1888.
TFIE LITE RECTOR.

div.head: VIDE ET CREDE.
div.p: VIDE ET CREDE.

---- Sir,—A short times ago I ventured for the considera- tion of the public of Warrington to suggest that some- thing might be done to show our respect and esteem for the late venerable Rector, the Rev. W. Quekett, M.A. Since writing that letter, I have heard many express their willingness to subscribe if the list could be started, and one dear old friend of the Rector even suggested that a peal of bells to his memory might be accomplished. I know that the late Rector had a great desire to finish his great work at the Parish Church, by swinging the bells, but it appears never to have been attempted. I don't think that I need hide the name of the gentlgman who now makes the suggestion, for I know his heart is warm in the matter, as is nine. It is Mr. Councillor J. E. Wright. In a word, then,l would humbly suggest that he, and the present churchwardens, under the leadership of the present Rector, test the feelings of the public on this question. I had the privilege of hearing the splendid peal of bells at St. Paul's, London, on the day of the Lord Mayor's show last week, and it is this fact which hastens me to urge that Warrington ought to possess something of the kind in her beautiful Parish Church.
LATE WARDEN.
SHARPERS AND THEIR TRICKS.

---......--- ......., i Sir,—l was much amused by reading n your last issue about the Lancashire man's troubles. One of the tricks (the putting the bun clown the lad's neck) is a very old one, and has been practised in Warrington. -There is another "little game" whioh I think is new to

Warringtonians, and which is being practised now in some towns. It is as follows :—a respectably-dressed gentleman (?) sometimes in clerical dress, is attentively engaged in looking in a jeweller's window. A man evidently under the influence of drink collides with the "parson." The result is that the "rev, gentleman" explores the inside of the window. Now comes a lit le bit of legerdemain worthy of Professor Anderson. One hand palms some gold article, and the gentleman raises this hand and draws out his handkerchief, of course , dropping into his pocket the palmed article. The same ' process is gone through with the other hand ; this time the purse comes out. The unfortunate gentleman ex- tracts himself from the window, bounces in the shoo, and in a manner seemingly honwst, and outspoken, tells the jeweller his woes, offers to pay tor the window,and winds up with a sermon on the effects of intemperance. All this takes far less time than it takes to write it, it all being done with a rapidity worthy of a better cause. Sometimes the jeweller refuses to take any money for the window; sometiines he takes the value. It is all the same, or nearly so, the articles safe inside Mr. Stiggins' pocket being worth many windows. The "rev. gentleman" takes his departure, and has a good chuckle with his inebriate companion about the watchfulness of the police, jewellers, &c. Warrington jewellers beware of Warrington, Nov. 12, 1888.
"THE ROAD TO ROME."

div.head: MR. STIGGS.
div.p: MR. STIGGS.

Sir,—Some of your Frodsham readers will perhaps remember—some months ago—a lecture delivered by a gentleman of this town, entitled "The Road to Rome." On reading " Observer's " letter in your issue of last week, I was a little tempted to draw a comparison between the two. Has that—good intentioned, no doubt —but somewhat too zealous parishioner of ours been roaming again? " Observer " apparently belongs to that class of Churchmen who imaginetheysee depicted the form of the "scarlet woman "in every innovation—from the wear- ing of the black gown, to the singing of the" Old Hundredth,"—a good old tune I admit. The writer himself has, at different times, attended service at the Frodsham Parish Church; but on no occasion has he seen what "Observer" says is there, i.e., " Popery." The several instances he brings forward in his endeavour to substantiate his fixed idea—such as the mode of receiving the communion—are not,in my opinion, points of sufficient gravity, in these pressing times, to raise a quibble ; abour. As for the hymns "Ancient and Modern," they are, I think, taken collectively, one of the best and most appropriate selection of hymns in use. They are so compiled as to suit all classes of Churchmen. If the name of Mary should sound—although I know not why it should—discordant to some Churchmen's views of Protestantism, they can omit it or make a substitu- tion.

In conclusion let me add, if in case" Observer "and a few besides are dissatisfied, while the majority of Churchmen are content to leave such trivial matters alone, they should be prepared to make themselves con- tented, or anyhow,not to observe things in future through a strongly magnifying glass.—l am, yours &c., Nov. 14th, 1888.

"THE STOCKTON HEATH SWELLS AND THE SHOP ASSISTANT." Sir,—My attention has been called to the letter signed "A Passenger" in your issue of Saturday last. I beg to sta.:o I have not received intimation from anyone respecting a young lady not paying the proper fare, nor are our conductors authorized to make any alteration of fares. Had your correspondent communicated with me instead of writing to the paper, every attention would have been paid to him and much unpleasantness would have been prevented.—Yours &c., W. RUSSELL, Manager, Warrington Carriage Company.

Sir,—Under the above graceful and characteristic ' heading your correspondent "A Passenger" once more rushes into print. But what of the story? I fear it will prove to be but apocryphal. The facts are being sifted and care will be taken that the public shall know the rights and wrongs of a matter which has been thrust unnecessarily into notice. " Passenger " should have *len quite sure of his facts before bringing such a charge of meanness against an unnamed "two" of a body of young men so limited in number as those to whom he refers. There are but some twenty involved, and every- one of them is lying to-day under a most unjust sus- picion because of your correspondent's letter. In the interests of fair play, I assert that he had no right, while slinking under his cowardly anonymity, to make a charge in such a way that the Innocent must inevitably suffer with the guilty. If anybody is guilty (which is more than doubtful) the public does not know who it is, and every young man who rides in the 'bus lies under the shadow thrown by " Passenger's " ugly intrusion. But it is likely that investigation will prove the whole affair to have been a comedy of errors, that no one has committed the action charged, and that the only mean- -44,,, nh,,,P Of it. Two questions to the Carnage Co.—Was any com- plaint made as alleged? If so, by whom? Answers to these questions would terminate the controversy. I earnestly hope the young lady will never have a similar trouble (undeniably unpleasant so far as she is concerned) but still more do I wish her a better advo- cate should Stich an eventunfortunately happen.—Yours truly, CHIVALRY. [We have had to strike out a portion of our correspon- dent's letter, as he sought, contrary to rule, to go be- hind the signature of " A Passenger."—En. Ex.]

THE GREAT SALT RING, Sir,—lt Is rather remarkable to thdstl kfilld Ihterest themselves in the cUrrent Wig Of politiettl questions of the day, how apparently apithetie the public are some- times over matters that directly affect their own inter- ests. Truly, we English workingmen, and women, are in some respects a wonderful set of docile bipeds. lam sometimes almost given to think that, were it not for the reviving influence exercised by the press—barring the Tory prints of course —we should lapse by degrees back into the 'good old days' (?) of the 'Corn Law' again. A few of the great controllers of capital can meet in solemn conclave, as instance the recently formed Salt Syndicate, and arrange matters so that they will be able to control at their will an industry the pro- duct of which is one of the chief necessaries of every-day life. We are told by those interested, and by the ignorant, that this Salt Syndicate is not going to affect the price of that commodity only to a trifling extent; ay, there's where the public are duped. Most of us understand the importance of that old adage :—" Every mickle make.; a muckle," and to none does it apply more forcibly in this question than to the poor consumer. I see no reason why we should be compelled to pay twopence a bar more for salt, when there is no scarcity of that article, simply to suit the ends of a few wealthy capitalists. The advo- cates of " Protection" have for years past been trying to allure the country, by somewhat similar reasonings to those the promoters of the Salt Ring are using. The 'Protectionist 'tells us that a tax on the foreign import of wheat, would not be materially felt by the consumers; only a trifle of, perhaps, a halfpenny per lb. Rut most of us have a too recent recollection of what Protection' means to allow ourselves to be bitten twice on the same place. When any public imposition, or taxation, is imposed upon us under the graduating principle, we are too much inclined to minimise its importance. Now, grant- ing that the rise in salt is as yet trifling, what reason have we to supcsAe that it will remain such? None; but on the other hand, there is much to show that the price will advance. All monopolies, whether in salt or any- thing else, are formed for the exclusive benefit of a few at the expense and disadvantage of the many. We shall be prepared to hear next, if these kind of undertakings are sanctioned by the public, of a great scheme to buy up all the coal pits; ay. already we have had a rumour to that effect. Instead of creating more monopolies, I am of opinion that it would be better to do away with one or two already existing; for instance that in land. The Salt Syndicate may be looked upon by some as not important enough to demand public agitation. Granting it so, what of the precedent? As I have before sta.' ed, the prac tics can be carried out to an unlimited extent, and here, in my opinion, lies the danger, which calls for, I think, public disapproval. Trusting that the question will receive further notice L in your columns, I am, yours &c., Nov. 7th, 1888.
PLEBEIAN.

The Marquis of Ripon and Mr. T. B. Potter, M.P., on Wednesday night addressed a mass meeting of the Liberals at Rochdale, chiefly with reference to the Irish question. A resolution in support of Mr. Gladstone was passed. Mr. JAMES Stionx, a clerk in the Warrington Health Department, has passed the examination held by the Sanitary Institute, of London, to qualify for the position of Inspector of Nuisances. THE ARCHDEACON OF WARRINGTON ON MAR, RIAGE.—The Archdeacon of Warrington, rreaching on Sunday afternoon in the Pro-Catheciral,Liverpool, from the second lesson for the day on the marriage in Cana of Galilee, said that marriage has been attacked by the Secularists of England, who were endeavouring to prevent both law and religion from having a voice in the matter. There were two theories—one that marriage was a matter of indivi- dual arrangement, and the other that, though a contract, it should be terminable at the desire of either party. The Church declared that marriage, was of divine institution and preceded by a contract but was in itself the union of two hearts by Almighty God. The law of love was a sovereign, imperative and exhaustive affection. No heart could sustain a dual love The increase of divorce in England was a sad and serious sign of the times; and he reminded them that in France, 100 years ago, before the Revolution, 2,500 divorces were granted in 18 months. He protested against the desecration of the holy estate by its performance in a registry office.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY " ARIEL."

That the portrait of the late Mr. Wm. Gossage, presented to Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, is a speaking likeness; and it is highly appropriate that the features of such a worthy should be pre- served to future generations in our Municipal Hall. He was the first Chairman of the Board on its formation in the year 1865, and his son, Mr. Fred Gossage, has occupied the same dignified posi- tion with credit to himself and advantage to the town for the last six years. May he live to occupy the chair for many years to come! That there ought to be &companion picture to the portrait which will in future look down upon our civic rulers as they labour for the benefit of the town. Naturally there rises up the name of the late Mr. Deacon, father of Mr. IL Wade Deacon, J.P., a worthy sire of a worthy son. No two gentlemen could be named to whom Widnes owes more than to the late Mr. Gossage and the late Mr. Deacon. who were really the founders of the prosperity of the "Chemical Metropolis " ; and the gift of a portrait of the last named gentleman would be received with pleasure.

That Widnesians do not intend to quietly sub- mit to the injustice of having but one representa- tive on the County Council, and the question will be agitated whilst there exists the slighest shred of hope. That the magistrates of West Derby Hundred fought nobly for the interests of the "Black Spot on the Mersey," and have placed the people of Widnes under an obligation they will not fail to repay on opportunity. It is to be hoped they will continue the battle of Right against Might. That there is "death in the cup." A reflection caused by the fearful death of the man Twigg at Widnes on Saturday night. His senses dulled by too much drink, he attempted to follow an occupation needing all his physical facul- ties, and a few minutes after leaving the " noisy jollity" of a public-house bar, he is endur- ing the tortures of scalding which result in his death.

That although it may be against the rules to leave the works, while on duty, almost any night of the week about" closing time" men can be seen issuing from public houses in the vicinity of the works. They are o# the night shift, and have had the last drink of ale until morning; and unfortu- nately the last has perhaps only been the successor of half a dozen other drinks.

That for the men's own safety at their dangerous occupations, a stop should be put to this, which is hereby a matter of discipline to those in authority. That the question of who are to be the candidates for the County Council is at present agitating the public mind at Runcorn, and various names are suggested—amongst others Mr. J. Brundrit, J.P., Mr. James Ifandiey, J.P., Major Hazlehurst, J.P., Mr. John Simpson. and Mr. P. Speakman. That the Conservatives deny having taken any action in the mattter, much less selected candidates, and there are rumours of an intended compromise between the two parties, but, however much they may care, nobody appears to know whin way the " cat will jump." That a township meeting to consider the matter in an unpolitical spirit is not an unlikely event. That " Watch and wait" would appear to be a good motto at the present time.

A RUNCORN YOUNG MAN IN CANADA. Mr. George W. Littler, the son of Mr. W. Littler,of Leinster Gardens, has become settled at Moosomin N.W.T. Canada, and writing recently to his parents he thus refers to the prosperity of the country:— Wonderful how people get on in this country. I know people who 5 years ago had not a dollar who now have farms, implements, cattle and a good balance of money to boot. No taxes, not a cent.; no rent, no game laws, plenty of game, no dog licences nor dog muzzling—no wonder people get on— nothing to do but to find food for themselves. A farmer who has taken rather a liking for me, and who is helping us with our crops, told me to-day that he had cleared over a thousand dollars this year without any help whatever, and I know it for a fact that be has also broken 36 acre of new land ready for next Yegri crop. That's business. Saw a locust to-day. *Not many insects but what are represented here. Wheat averages from 25 to 50 bushels per acre, oats 45 to 60 bushels, 85 has been known. Wheat 50 to 90 cents per bushel, oats 28 to 40 cents. I told you in last letter that manure was at a dis- count. Farmers bury it in holes to get it out of the road. Farmers let part of land rest once in two years. All straw is burnt after threshing except a hit saved for bedding, both wheat and oat straw. Some farmers don't plough the land at all; they just scatter the seed and go over it with the harrow, But it nays to work it more. When the crop is ready for cutting it is cat with a machine, which binds it up into moderate sized sheaves. One machine will find work for two men shocking up behind it. Threshing, the grain costs 4 cents a bushel. The owner of the thresher pays the men of which there are fourteen, and the farmer finds them i food and lodging. The men find their own bed- clothes. Two of the men receive 50 dollars a month, the other 12 receive 30 dollars. They are not fed on bread and cheese, but the best of everything about the place. The twine for binding the sheaves costs 15 cents a pound. and it takes from one to three pounds per acre. The grain is hauled to town in winter whenever it is fit. I don't know whether these things interest you or not. I know it was tedious enough, if I talked about it when I was at home, but that was from books. I now speak from what is every-day life here. It seems strange I talked about it so long, and it has actually come to pass. I think nothing now of walking over the prairie tumbling over hundreds of buffalo skulls, bones and trails. I am quite at home here; do almost as I like. I wish you were all here. Father would coin money. Remember me to friends and relatives. RUNCORN AS IT IS AND AS IT OUGHT TO BE.

TEMPERANCE AND PURITY. The Rev. .J. D. Thomas, pastor of Bethesda Con- gregational Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday evening, preached the second of a series of sermons on "Runcorn as it is and as it ought to be" to a good congregation. The subject was "Runcorn in rela- tion to temperance and purity" and the discourse was based upon the text I. John 11., 16 verse. In the course of his sermon, Mr. Thomas said the two great evils sapping the foundations of health and morality in our country to-day, were intemperance and impurity. Perhaps with one exception England was the most drunken country on the face of the earth. And we did not seem to be content with be- ing drunken ourselves, but we were doing our level best to make others like ourselves. "The Devil in solution," as Shakespere termed it, was being exported from our shores in ship loads to enslave and destroy the poor negroes of Africa and the Mohammedans of India. Then there was impurity which strutted along the streets, sometimes in the gay plumage of a bird of paradise, and some- times like the poor carrion crow, but in eioher cases, it was always ready, with a wolf like fierceness to devour all who fell into its grasp. How did Runcorn stand at the present time in relation to these matters. Perhaps if they compared the town with most other towns in the United Kingdom, they would find Runcorn favour- ably situated. But what of that? "Comparisons are odious," and never more so that when made between persons and places, which are naturally and inherently bad. They must think of what ought to be and not of what was in other localities. That other towns were very much worse than this did not prove that Runcorn was as good as it ought to be. Look, then, at its relation to temperance. The large influx of men in connection with the Ship Canal had probably given to the streets a more sottish appearance than they had formerly, although it must be confessed that on the whole these men were decent fellows and well behaved, but their arrival had not increased the facilities of drink- ing. Indeed, much to the credit of thepolice, there was one house less than aforetime. Still there were in the town at present about 100 licensed houses. These for the most part were in the central streets and thoroughfares, the magistrates having exercised a wise discretion, and a discretion which he hoped they would continue to exercise, in refusing to grant licenses for the newer and more modern parts of the town. But 100 houses, taking the population of the town at 15,000, meant one , licensed house for every 150 people including men, , women and children, a number which far exceeded the real needs of the populace. For remember it was needs, not indulgences, which these places were intended to supply. But the number was not by any means the , worst part of the business. In the light of recent police court revelations and also of his own extended observa- tions and experience, there could not be any doubt that , a great deal of excessive drinking was permitted and , encouraged. Surely it could not be mere accident, that , they saw men, and often the same men, coming out of these houses, hardly able to stand, and seeking the kindly support., of a wall or railing; nor was it , due to any lack of reasoning and priming on , the part of the men themselves. It was because the law was habitually broken and every encou- ragement was offered to over indulgence. The

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 17, 1888.

fact was that if only the real needs of the populace were supplied nearly one half of these houses would speedily be shut up. But another and sadder feature in connection with the intemperance of the town was that so many women were given to drink. They were to be seen standing up with tho men at the bar, or sitting in the taproom, quaffing their potations of ale or supping more potent liquors. And it was little short of being as common to see women reeling along the parapets as it was to see men. But the conse- quences were, if possible, much worse. Whatever the man might be there was some hope of a nation as long as its women remain sober and virtuous. But when the women gave up there was nothing short of the depths of hell for that people. Mothers, women, better suffer yourselves to become the victims of your drunken husbands cruelties then take yourselves of the cup whose:contents are as the poison of asps. Before leaving the matter of intemperance, it was only right that he should acknowledge the very nibble efforts , that had been made in the town to rescue the drunkard and to turn the rising generation in principles of sobriety, by two societies, viz., the Order of Rechabites and the Sons of Temperance. Taking the town as a whole there was a growing sentiment favour- able to temperance, and they owed it very largely to the fact that when others had forgotten its existence, these societies did not fail to bear aloft the banner of sobriety. Alluding to purity, the preacher said there was one thing upon which they might congratulate themselves, and that was, that at the present time there was not a house of ill-fame in all the town. These houses, so far as they were known to the police, had all been pounced upon and their occupants harried out of the neighbourhood. But this was a poor remedy after all. To his own certain knowledge there were many houses which were almost as bad. There were not a few married gentleman in the town who seemed to have forgotten that portion of the marriage service which concluad with the words, "As long as ye both shall live." And there were many others who had not entered into the " Sacred covenant of materimony " and yet were living as man an wife. There were some young women who were mothers before they were wives, and some young men who were fathers before they were husbands. All these things contravened the Christian obligation of purity. And he told them honestly, that, during his pastoral work, he had seen so much of the awful wretchedness arising from this sin that, if he did not lift up his voice against it more distinctly than he had done, he should feel that their blood was upon him. Oh, beware of it as they would a yawning chasm, or dark abyss. Flee from it as Lot fled from the sulphur- ous flames which enveloped and consumed Sodom. And allow him to point out three things which in his opinion tended to prevent the formation of a healthy sentiment respecting purity. One was the impossibility of separating the sexes in very small houses. Another was the indecent behaviour which was too often tolerated between boys and girls. And a third was a certain class of novels in which light behaviour towards women is openly counten- anced. In conclusion, he asked young men to remember that God made woman to be man's help-meet she was to occupy a honorourable and dignified position by his side. She was not to be his toy nor yet his slave. And if ever they should make one of God's daughters the victim of their caprice or passion, the Almighty would punish them for it. More than that, if either, or any of them, had been guilty of unhallowed conduct towards maiden or woman in the past, they were under a two-fold obliga- tion, first to repent of their sin, and, second, to make all the reparation in their power to the victim of their sin. Young men, do not let it be said that they to whom God had given a strong right arm and a heart for heroic purposes, that they had contributed to the overthrow of their sisters' virtue and innecence. Nay, but let it be known that anywhere and everywhere they were their bold and chivalrous defenders. If they proved the tempter instead of the defender, the betrayer instead of the faithful helper, a terrible Nemesis, depend upon it, would overtake them.

div.head: FRIGHTFUL FATALITY AT WIDNES. DEATH IN THE CUP.
div.p: FRIGHTFUL FATALITY AT WIDNES. DEATH IN THE CUP.

An accident of a shocking description occurred at the works of Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.. shortly before midnight on Eaturday. and affords another instance of the sad effects of drinking to excess. It appears that Win. Twigg and Win. Smith, labourers, were in charge of the same job at the works, and were on the night shift. About 8 o'clock, the men left the yard, and got some beer, Smith acknowledging that he had had three pints of ale. On returning from the public-house, the men attempted to carry out their duties as usual. It was part of Twigg's labour to run off from a tank hot " mudliquor,' which is a mixture of chloride of calcium and oxide of Manganese, and about eleven o'clock he went up the gangway to perform this office. In a few minutes there were shouts of di:- tress, and Jas. Dwyer found Twigg immersed in the hot liquor in the tank, and clinging in terror to the platform overhead with both hands. He was quy Yes Cued from his painful position, and con- veyed to the United Hospital, where every atten- tion was paid to him; but he succumbed to his injuries on Sunday night.

- INQUEST. Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body on Wednesday afternoon.— Mr. J. B. Imison was foreman of the jury, and Mr. Joseph Morrison represented the firm. Joseph Twigg, 21, Princess-t.. contractor, deposed , that the deceased was his brother, and was 35 years of age. He had lived at 45, Moon-st. On Saturday night, 1 about eleven o'clock, a man named Dwyer told him there were two men—one was in drink, and the other I was drunk. When he got down to the place he found ' his brother lying in the hut terribly scalded. William Smith, labourer, said he worked with the de- ceased. They went out together about eight o'clock and got some beer. The deceased was not sober, nor was he (witness), at the time of the accident. He (witness) had had about three pints of beer. He had only been in the works a fortnight, and did not I know it was against the rule to go out of the works. He had been at other works in the town, and it was not the rule there. He saw the deceased go up the gangway to the tank, but he did not hear him shout. He was after- wards told that deceased had been scalded. Mr. Johnson sent him (witness) home, because he was drunk. He could not say whether deceased was fit to go to the tank or not. By a juryman: He did not suppose the accident would have occurred had the deceased been sober. _

James Dwyer, of 2, Sutton's-lane, deposed that the deceased "had had drink but was steady enough." There was plenty of light at the tank, and on the plat- form was a handrail to prevent anyone falling in. The liquid was not boiling; it was hot. John Dwyer, of Sutton-lane, said he went to tell Twig, the contractor, that his brother was not capable of doing his.work. Miss Janet Downie matron at the hospital, said the deceased died from scalds and shock to the system. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased met hie death by accident while under the influence of drink; and it was the opinion of the jury that the place was perfectly safe for a sober man to work in.
FRODSHAM.

ST. JOHN'S, KINGSLEY.—It is stated that the Ecclesias- tical Commissioners, in consideration of two benefac- tions, amounting to £1,500, have made grants in augmentation of the benefice of St. John's, Kingsley, Frodsham.

div.p: LYII3I.

TEMPERANCE ENTERT7.INMEITT-S—The first Band of Hope entertainment for the season in connection with the Congregational Church was held on Monday even- ing, Mr. B. Parr in the chair. Readings, recitations, and dialogues, were rendered and Mr. Theodore Nash, of Heatley, addressed the meeting. LIBERAL MEETING.-A meeting of the Liberals of the Lymm Polling District was held in the Congrega- tional School on Saturday, to consider a letter from the Conservative party with reference to the election of County Councillors. We understand that no definite action ' has as yet, been resolved on, but an amicable arrangement will be arrived at between the two parties. BAPTIST MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT BOCIETY.—The usua weekly meeting of this Society was held on Wednesday evening, the president, Mr. Brundritt, occupying the chair. An impromptu speech on " Gas " was given by Mr. W. Cadman, and afterwards a paper was read by Mr. Hurstfield on "The Immortality of Man : is it sup- ported by reason and revelation." A discussion ensued. THE REV. Hum( DAVIES.—The Rev. Hugh Davies preached his last sermon in Lymm, in the Congregational Church, on Sunday. The rev, gentleman received a call from Slack-lane Chapel, near Keighley, a few weeks ago, and will, during the coming week, remove to that dis- trict, where he will take up his pastoral duties in the first week in December. Mr. Davies received a call by the members of the Higher-lane Baptist Chapel some 1:3 tears ago, direct from college, and duly administered the -duties of his office for about 12 years, when he resigned, at which time the members of his church and congrega- tion made him a handsome present as a token of the high esteem in which they held him. FUNERAL OF MR. JAMES GILBERT. The remains of the late Mr. James Gilbert, of Rush Green—who died on Thursday of last week—were on Monday interred in the burial ground of St. Peter's Church. Deceased being a consistent member of the Wesleyan body, a service took place in the Wesleyan Chapel at 1.45, at the close of which all the members of the church present proceeded to the cottage and thence, with the widow and mourners, to St. Peter's Church, where the burial took place. Deceased was in his 48th year. Mr. Gilberts was an ardent Liberal and a fai;hful supporter of Mr. Leadam, at a number of whose meetings he spoke on behalf of and in the interest of workingmen. At a meetingof Liberals held on Saturday a tote of condolence was passed to the bereaved widow, the chairman being requested to embody the sentiments of ' the meeting in a letter and convey them to her. A deputation from the members of the Lymm Liberal Club also followed the funeral to the grave.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Yesterday, an extensive German sausage maker, named Carlos Hertz, committed suicide in Belfast.

The Forth Bridge works sustained some damage, and vessels broke from their moorings in the roadstead. At Kirkcaldy a steamer was driven ashore, and shipping in Firth of Forth sustained considerable dam- age. Lord Tennyson has been laid up with rheumatic gout for nine weeks: He is still confined to his bed at Aid- worth, Haslemere. A seaman named Swan was blown overboard from the Abertay Light Ship, moored at the entrance to the 'Fay, and was drowned,
At Dumferline the roof of a school was blown off, seriously injuring a girl. The roof of a house in Bruce- st. fell into a room where lay a bedridden man, and he narrowly escaped with his life. . .

A Ger Man 'schooner drifted from her moorings in Weyland Bay, Kirkwall, at the height of the storm, but crew were saved. Reports are reaching Kirkwall of other wrecks along the Orkney Coast. DEATU or COLONEL DUNCAN, M.P.—Colonel Duncan, M.P., died at half-past eight yesterday morning. He had sat as Conservative member for Holborn division since 1885. The cause of death was dropsy, supervening on abscess of the liver.

At Berwick a chimney and the gable of a house fell through the roof of an adjoining wine shop, knocking out the front wall. The tall chimney shaft of a cement works was blown down, injuring the roof and steeple of a Baptist Church and other buildings. On the north cast coast of England many vessels had to run into harbours for safety, and it is feared the casual- ties must have been numerous. Cross Channel steamers between Scotland and North Ireland encountered fearful weather, and arrived in port hours late. THR WHITECHAPEL MURDERS: ANOTHER ARREST.—A man was arrested at Market Harborough on Thursday night on suspicion of being the Whi echapel murderer. He is very dark, swarthy looking, and speaks with a slightly foreign accent. The account he has given of himself to the police is not satisfactory. IRISH LANDLORDS.—RepIying yesterday afternoon to a deputation of the Irish leaseholders, Lord Salisbury said Government could not extend the land act so as to include holders of houses of over ninety-nine years. Next session, however, they might be able to deal with the question by adopting some such scheme as was in Mr. Russell's Bill, which proposed to give landlords the option of selling the fee simple of their property, or of going into the land court. At Inchkeith, in Firth of Forth, a barque, 570 tons, bound from Sandshull to London, was wrecked on the rock.. The crew, 11 in number, were rescued by the lifeboat. The Brig Argus, from Rotterdam with timber, and the schooner Carolina, bound to Charleston in ballast, both went ashore at Dysart. Barque Abraham Scull, from Yarmouth, was totally wrecked at King's Horn Four of the crew attempted to swim ashore, but only one succeeded, the others perishing in the tremen- dous break ?rs. .

THE PARNELL COMMISSION.—Most of the witnesses called at the Paraell Commission, yesterday, were farmers, herds, or publicans, who had served processes or taken farms from which former tenants had been evicted and who were consequently subjected to out- rage, which in most instances took the form of shooting in the legs. The feature of the afternoon's proceedings was an altercation between the President and Mr. Timothy Harrington. Eventually Mr. Harrington apologised for the heat he had shown, and Sir James Hannon expressed himself satisfied with his statement.

SRRIOI79 ILLNDSS OP MR. Jomx BRIGHT.—Mr. Bright has had a serious relapse. At a late hour on Wednesday night alarmingsymptoms of congestion of the lungs set in. Dr. Hayle immediately sought the aid of Dr. Drysdale, of Liverpool. Alter their examination on Thursday afternoon they formed a hopeful opinion of his condition, and at night Mr. Bright was rallying again. Mr. John Albert Bright, Mr. Philip Bright, Mr. William Bright, and Mrs. Clarke arrived at One Ash from London on Thutsday. Mr. Bright passed a fairly good night on Thursday but was rather feverish. He was better yesterday morning. A late telegram says :—Mr. Bright is no better this evening. MR. PYNE, M.P., ACCIDENTALLY DROWNED—A first-class saloon passenger travelling by the London and North- Western Company's steamer Shamrock from Holyhead to Dublin, on Tuesday night, either fell or leapt overboard when midway across the Channel, and was drowned. I It is feared that this passenger was Mr. Douglas Pyne, MP. for Waterford. The hon. gentleman had not been in the House of Commons for several nights, and anxi- ous inquiries in Dublin and Lismore on Wednesday only went to confirm the belief that he is drowned. It has been learned that Mr. Pyne, M.P., left London for Ire- land on Tuesday morning, leaving his luggage at his London lodgings. He telegraphed from Holyhead the same evening to Mr. McCartan, M.P., to meet him in Dublin.—The latest news that can be obtained leaves scarcely any doubt that Mr. Pyne was thrown into the sea whilst on the upper deck, by a lurch of the ship. I He bad ordered a meal to be got ready for him before Zoirtz QTI the upper deck. DEWSBURY Etecriox.—The nomination of candidates to fill the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation of Dewsbury, caused by the retirement of Sir John Simon, took place on Wednesday, when Mr. H. 0. Arnold-Forster (Liberal Unionist) and Mr. Mark Oldroyd (Gladstonian) were nominated. Polling commenced at Dewsbury at eight o'clock yesterday morning. During the dinner hour many of the working-men visited the polling stations, and the clerks at each place were busy. Both sides were working extremely hard. The result was declared last night as follows :
_ OLDROYD (Gladstonian) ARNOLD FORSTER (L. Unionist) 3969

Gladstonian Majority 2102 Last election (1886) the Liberal majority was 2,358; but it was then a struggle between a Liberal and a Conser- vative. Mr. Forster has gained a few votes as a Liberal Unionist, but he is still hopelessly beaten.

div.head: STORM.-LOSS OF LIFE AND GREAT DAMAGE.
div.p: THE STORM.-LOSS OF LIFE AND GREAT DAMAGE.

A storm of exceptional.;Uen-ce has raged over the north of England, north of Ireland, and the greater part of Scotland from an early hour on Friday morning, doing enormous damage to property on land, and to shipping at sea and in the harbour at Glasgow. A man named Craig, reputed to be the tallest man in the city, was removing a tottering signboard from a house when he was blown to the ground, and instantly killed. A considerable number of adults and children met with accidents more or less serious in the streets ftom falling signboards, and slates. A chimney stack 110 feet high, at Rollox was blown down, crushing a man named Charteris beyond recognition and slightly injuring other workmen. Sixty feet of roofinr, of the Grand Hall of the Exhibition recently closed was torn away, and buildings generally suffered considerable damage. Steamers going up Clyde were unable to call at the piers, and incoming vessels reported terrific weather at sea.
A MISSING BOMBAY VESSEL. SUPPOSED LOSS OF 900 LIVES.

BOMBAY, -IWO; is felt as to the fate of the coasting vessel Vaitarna, which recently left Cutch for this port with nine hundred passengers on board. She is now a week overdue, and it is feared that she must have foundered, with all hands, in a cyclone.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—FRIDAY: QUESTIONS, &c.—The Speaker read a letter he had received from Ireland announcing the imprisonmeut of Mr. Sheehan in Tralee Gaol. Sir. .1. FERGUSON, replying to Sir. G. POWELL, said further papers relative to sugar bounties would be produced if moved for. Mr. W. SMITH intimated that it was intended to re-intro- duce a bill for the formation of an agricultural depart- ment next session. THE FIVE MILLIONS PROPOSALS.—MY. GLADSTONE gave the terms of his amendment to Government motion to introduce the Land Purchase Bill on Monday. In place of voting ano her sum of five millions, Mr. GLAD- STONE was in favour, in view of recent evictions, of extending the provisions of Land Law Ireland Act, 1887, so as to empower the Land Court to reduce and , cancel arrears of rent found to be excessive, as well as to deal with rents themselves. SUPPLY —The House then went in Committee of Supply on the vote for Science and Art Department. Mr. A. ACKLAND called attention to the teaching of science in elementary schools. He also urged that there should be better organization in secondary schools. Sir H. Roscoz spoke of the deficiency of accommodation at South Kensington. Mr. F. S. POWELL hoped that every assist- ance would be given to Irish local industries. Mr. MUNDELLA regretted there was a reduction in the vote for instruction in art. Mr. ISAACS urged the desirability of helping the new technical institutions which were springing up. After some further discussion Dr. TANNER urged the opening of South Kensington Museum on Sunday. The proposal was rejected by 106 to 41, and the vote was agreed to. On vote for the British Museum being proposed, Sir J. Lurmocx gave an account of the additions irtade.
[LEFT SITTING].

At Pontefract. on Wednesday, Rebecca Mary Smith, domestic servant, was committed for trial charged with the murder of her newly-born female child. The body of the child was found with the skull extensively fractured. TRH EXCITING FIRE IN LONDON.—Flames broke out at two o'clock on Thursday morning, in the shop and house tenanted by J. Bethell, gasfitter, 9/. Central- street, St. Lukes, London. The first floor and staircase were burning before the occupants were awakened, and a scene of great excitement occurred. The inmates threw up the windows and screamed for help, while the smoke rolled out above them. An escape was speedily .brought. and Fireman Stevens, planting it against the wall, ran up, and disappearing in the smoke, soon emerged, carrying a partially.dressed woman, the wife of the tenant. He went in again, and rescued Bethell himself, an old man, who was terribly burnt. He was at once sent to the hospital. The house was almost gutted.
MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN.

Although the weather during the week has inter- fered with the operations, the work has been car- ried on without stoppage. The American navvies at the Big Field are making rapid headway on the second level, and the cutting is lengthening percep- tibly day by day. At present, however, the most important work is being carried on at No Man's Land. About 200 men are busily employed making a deep ' cutting through the centre of the island, and the soil is being used to increase the height of the river hank. At the east end of NO Man's Land, steel rail piles are being driven into the bed of the river for the purpose of forming a coffer dam , and immediately the pile driving is completed a bed of concrete will be laid in. Then will be commenced the work of constructing the liver wall from No Man's Land up to the Old Quay. The engineers' offices at Dukes Field are rapidly approaching completion.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

The greatest activity prevails on this section. The steam navvies, of which there are three kinds, German, French, and Wilson's—are kept incessantly in motion, and the cutting is now upwards of a quarter of a mile in length. The clay, &c., is being used in the formation of a spoil bank, and it has now been filled to a height of 18 feet. The construction of the great lock at the mouth of the Weaver is progressing, and the concrete is being laid as quickly as the difficult circumstances to be overcome will allow.

div.head: NEARLY DROWNED.
div.p: NEARLY DROWNED.

On Saturday mornin—g-a—Cal. i;;;;ed Jane Taylor, daughter of a navvy working on the Ship Canal, and who lives in one of the wooden cottages erected by Mr. Walker at Warburton, was playing at the back, which adjoins the hauling bank, when by some means she fell in the river. It was not seen how she got in, but she was noticed floating down the stream some 100 yards from where she had been last seen. Assistance was immediately summoned, and the child quickly rescued. Fortunately Dr. W. W. Williamson was at hand, and at once attended to the little sufferer, who it is hoped is now out of danger.
